VS
Ambia Khatun and others ------ Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
This rule was issued calling upon the opposite-parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 25-3-2008 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Netrokona in Other Class Appeal No. 36 of 2007 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 14-11-2007 pissed by the learned Assistant Judge, Atpara, Netrokona in Other Class Suit No. 62 of 2005 dismissing the suit.

2. The present petitioner and opposite-party No. 5, Fultara as plaintiff instituted. Other Class Suit No. 62 of 2005 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Atpara, Netrokona, impleading the predecessor of the opposite-party Nos. 1(a) to 1(e) as defendant No. 1 and opposite-party Nos. 2-4 as defendant Nos. 2-4 for declaration that the judgment and decree dated 26-5-1999 passed in Title Suit No. 46 of 1997 is void, illegal, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

3. Plaintiff's case, in short, is that the plaintiffs are co-sharer in the suit land by way of inheritance as described in the schedule 2 to the plaint. The predecessors of the opposite-party Nos. 1(a)-1(e) and opposite-party No. 2 as plaintiffs instituted Partition Suit No. 46 of 1997 impleading the present petitioner and others as defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 4 and prayed for partition described in schedule of the plaint. The positive case of the plaintiffs is they had no knowledge about the alleged partition suit and no notice/summons was served upon the plaintiffs. It is further stated that the plaintiff of the partition Suit by practicing fraud created false notice and showing a notice served upon the defendants but without serving any notice upon the defendant Nos. 3-4 of the partition suit, the plaintiff of the partition suit obtained the decreed. The plaintiffs acquired the suit property by way of inheritance and few days back the defendant No. 2, Hosen Banu and her husband disclosed in the locality that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 of the present suit got decree and further declare that they will take possession of the suit land at the earliest opportunity. Thereafter the plaintiffs on 25-9-2005 obtained certified copy by the judgment and decree of the previous partition suit and confirmed that the plaintiffs of the earlier suit obtained a decree by practicing fraud upon the court without serving any notice and thus the plaintiffs constrained to file the present suit.

4. That the predecessor of the opposite-party Nos. 1(a)-1(e) as defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a joint written denying the materials allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter-alia, that the suit is not maintainable, the suit is barred by limitation and the principle of res-judicata and there is no cause of action to file the present suit. The positive case of the defendants is that the defendant's predecessor filed the Partition Suit No.46 of 1997 and in the said suit the summons and the postal notice was duly served upon the defendants and the defendant No.2 of the earlier suit, who is defendant No. 4 in the present suit contested the said suit with the knowledge of the plaintiffs; that after hearing and considering the materials and evidence on record decreed the suit by judgment dated 26-5-1999 in respect of their share of 30 decimal of land out of total 1.81 decimals of land and preliminary decree was passed accordingly. Against the said decree passed in Partition Suit No. 46 of 1997, the defendant No. 2 of the present suit preferred Title Appeal No.113 of 1999 in the Court of District Judge, Netrokona and who after hearing the same affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial court. With these averment defendants prayed for dismissal of the suit.

5. In the present suit plaintiffs examined 3 witnesses including herself as PW 1 and on the other hand defendants also was examine 3 witnesses including the defendant No. 2 as DW 1. The learned Assistant Judge, Atpara, Netrokona on consideration of the evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit by judgment and decree dated 14-11-2007. Against the said judgment and decree, the plaintiff preferred the Title Appeal No. 36 of 2007 before the District Judge, Netrokona, consequently the said appeal was transferred and disposed of by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Netrokona who by judgment and decree dated 25-3-2008 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial court.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 25-3-2008 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Netrokona in Other Appeal No. 36 of 2007 the plaintiff moved this court and obtained the present Rule.

7. It appears that this revisional application was filed with a delay of 60 days time and same was condoned subject to any objection that may be raised at the time of hearing of the Rule.

8. Mr Syed Ali Asgor, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner mainly submits that the judgment and decree of the appeal court suffers from misreading and non-consideration of the evidence on record. He further submits that the defendants of the present suit obtained the decree in the partition suit by keeping the present plaintiff petitioner in dark and without serving summons upon them and by practising fraud. He finally submits that the court of appeal below failed to consider that the summons upon the defendant No.4 has not been properly served in the suit.

9. On the other hand, Mr Sikder Mahmudur Razi, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite-parties submits that the plaintiff-petitioner has not prayed for any declaration of title and consequential relief in the suit, therefore, the present suit is not maintainable without seeking any consequential relief. He further submits that the impugned judgment and decree do not suffer from any non-reading, misreading and non-consideration of materials evidence on record. He next submits that the present suit was filed challenging the decree of the partition suit after 7(seven) years as such, the suit is hopelessly barred by limitation. He also submits that the defendant No. 4 of the instant suit who was the defendant No. 2 in the Partition Suit No. 46 of 1997 is the full brother of the present plaintiffs and the said defendant contested the said partition suit and therefore the present plaintiffs are fully aware of the partition suit from the very beginning. He finally submits that the plaintiffs filed the present suit only challenging the judgment and decree of the trial court only but not challenged the judgment and decree dated 4-6-2001 passed in the Other Class Appeal No. 113 of 1999. Since the plaintiffs have only challenged the judgment and decree of the trial court as such, the present suit challenging the decree of the trial court is not maintainable.

10. Now, the main question that is to be decided in this rule is that whether the courts below have committed any illegality in dismissing the plaintiffs present suit and whether the summons of the Partition Suit No. 46 of 1997 was duly served upon the present plaintiffs Ayesha Khatun and Fultara, (defendant Nos. 3 and 4) of the previous partition suit.

11. On examination of evidence on record it appears that Adil Hossain (Husband of present opposite-party No.1(d) and father of opposite-party Nos. 1(a) to 1(c) and 1(e) and Hosen Banu (present opposite-party No. 2) as plaintiff instituted a suit for Partition Suit No. 46 of 1997 on 26-11-1997 in the court of Assistant Judge, Atpara, Netrokona impleading Abdul Mazid, Firoz Miah (brother of Ayesha Khatun and Fultara) claiming partition of 1.81 acre of land and the claim of the plaintiffs was only for 30 decimals. Firoz Mia (defendant No.2) contested the said partition suit by filing written statements. His positive case was that Shachuni Kha died leaving behind one son namely AR Afsar and one daughter namely Palisher Ma and by amicable family settlement Palisher Ma got her saham 10 decimals of land in plot Nos.716 and 5 decimal of land in plot No. 27 and extinguished her interest in the remaining property AR Afsar, father of defendant Nos. 2-4 (Firoz Mia, Ayesha Khatun and Fultara) brother of plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 of the present suit and plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 got the rest property of Shachuni Kha and thereafter Ali Afsar transferred 25 decimals of land from plot No. 58 to defendant No. 1 (Abdul Mazid). The plaintiff No.2 (Hosen Banu) transferred 10 decimal land to Firoz Miah by registered sale deeds dated 19-9-1993 and 14-12-1995: The said partition suit was decree in preliminary form on 26-5-1999 and against the said judgment and decree only Firoz Miah preferred Other Class Appeal No. 113 of 1999 and same was dismissed on contest on 4-6-2001. Ultimately final decree was drawn up in the partition suit on 26-4-2001. Subsequently, the decree-holder-present-defendants filed the Execution Case No. 2 of 2010 and in the present Civil Revision said execution case was stayed.

12. It appears that the present Other Class Suit No. 62 of 2005 filed by Ayesha Khatun and Fultara for declaration that the judgment and decree dated 26-5-1999 passed in Partition Suit No. 46 of 1997 by the Court of Assistant Judge, Atpara, Netrokona is illegal and void and not binding upon them. In the present suit Adil Hossain and Hosen Banu, Abdul Matin (son of defendant No. 1 of partition suit) of the Partition Suit No. 46 of 1997 were impleaded as defendant Nos. 1-3 and Firoz Mia (defendant No. 2 of the said partition suit) was also impleaded as defendant No. 4. It was the positive case of the plaintiffs that they did not receive any summons of the earlier partition suit and they had no knowledge about the said partition suit and it came to their knowledge when the husband of the defendant No. 2 disclosed in the locality that very soon they are going to take possession of the plaintiff's suit land. Having came to learn about through the local people, the plaintiff made a search and confirmed about the judgment and decree passed in the earlier partition suit on 25-9-2005. Thereafter, on the death of Adil Hossain, defendant No. 1, his heirs were added in the suit as defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(e). It appears that the trial court after considering the service return, Exhibits-(Ka) and (Kha) found that the summons upon the defendant No.3 of partition suit (present plaintiff No. 1) was duly served and same was received by her husband but the summons upon the defendant No.4 (present plaintiff No. 2) was received by her nephew but it is not clear whether they are joint family member. It was further found by the trial court that the defendant No. 4 is the full brother of the plaintiffs, who contested the said partition suit and also preferred appeal against the decree passed in Petition Suit No. 46 of 1997. Therefore, the plaintiffs were fully aware about the partition suit. The appellate court also considered both the service return as proper. Appellate court after considering the deposition of PW 1 found that they were fully aware of the partition suit. The appellate court also considered the cross-examination of PW 1 wherein she deposed that she heard about the partition suit from her cousin Abdul Mazid. She further stated that Abdul Mazid died 7 years before and after 1 year of death of Abdul Mazid, PW 1 heard about partition suit. So, after the death of Abdul Mazid he came to PW 1 and informed her about the suit which is totally unbelievable and ridiculous. It further transpires that although the present plaintiffs are challenging the decree of earlier partition suit on the ground of non-service of summons upon them, but failed to examine Md Abul Kashem (nephew of Fultara) in support their case. Thus it transpires that the pleadings and the deposition of PWs are contradictory and unbelievable regarding knowledge of partition suit filed by the defendant's predecessor.

13. Learned Advocate for the opposite-par-ties vehemently submits that although the plaintiff in the present suit challenged the decree of the trial court passed in Partition Suit No. 46 of 1997 only, since the decree of the trial court have been merged with the decree of the appellate court passed in other Appeal No. 119 of 1999 and without challenging the judgment and decree of the appellate court, the plaintiffs have only challenged the judgment and decree of the trial court and, as such, the present suit itself is not maintainable. In support of his submissions learned Advocate relied upon the decision of AIR 1987 Patna 733(Full Bench).

14. On the other hand, learned Advocate for the petitioner vehemently submits that the judgment and decree of the appellate court suffers from misreading and non consideration of evidence and materials on record but failed to pin point what are the exhibits which were not considered or which are the evidences misread by the courts below. He also submits that the notice upon Fultara, defendant No. 4 was not duly served upon her. In support of his contention learned Advocate referred a decision of our Appellate Division reported in 63 DLR(AD) 99.

15. I have gone through the decision reported in 63 DLR (AD) 99. It appears that the said decision was passed in a money suit invoking the jurisdiction under section 19(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain and in that decision the decree was passed without any service of summons or even without any attempt to do so. As such, it is a nullity in the eye of law and it is imperative upon any Court of law, which is in seisin of the, mater, to hold so, even without invoking the provisions of section 19 of the Ain or rule 13 of Order IX of the code. Because rule 13 of Order IX envisages at least a service, .even if not 'duly' and sub-section (1) of section 19 also envisages a service of summons upon the defendant. In the present case, it is evident from the Exhibits-(Ka) and (Kha) that the notice of the Partition Suit was duly served upon the defendant Nos. 3-4. Thus the 'case referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case.

16. It further appears that the plaintiff filed the instant suit for simple declaration without prayer for any consequential relief by way of cancellation and without payment of ad-valorem court fees. It also appears that the plaintiffs of the instant suit were parties of the earlier partition suit as defendant Nos. 3 and 4 respectively. In this respect reliance may be placed on the decisions reported in 39 DLR. (AD) 46 and 17 DLR 119.

17. In the case reported in 17 DLR 119 it is observed by a Full Bench that if the plaintiff is a party to the instrument, the Court refuses as a rule to grant such a declaratory relief, on the ground that the instrument, in such a case, need be avoided by cancellation. The plaintiff in such a case is required to pray for cancellation, by way of a consequential relief. Where, however, the plaintiff is not a party to the instrument no such difficulty arises. There he is entitled to a simple declaratory relief. (CP Code, Order II, rule 2).

18. It also transpires that in the present suit the plaintiff-petitioner have only challenge the judgment and decree dated 26-5-1999 passed by die Court of Assistant Judge, Atpara, Netrokona in Partition Suit No. 46 of 1997 which was merged with the decree dated 4-6-2001 passed in Other Appeal No. 113 of 1999 but the plaintiff S did not challenge the decree of the appellate Court. Since the plaintiff in the present suit has only challenge the decree of the trial court, same is not maintainable.

<u>19. It is well settled that when a trial court decrees a suit and the decree is challenged by a competent appeal, the appeal is considered as a continuation of the suit, and when the appellate decree affirms, modifies or reverses the decree on merits, the trial court decree is said in law to merge in the appellate decree, and it is the appellate decree which rules.</u>

<u>20. In this respect reliance may be placed in the case of Jokhan Rai vs Baikunth Singh decided by a Full Bench of three Judges, reported in AIR (1987) Patna 133 has taken the view that in the event of an appeal the decree of the trial Court merges with that of the appellate Court. The doctrine of merger is too well known to call for further elaboration. Indeed, the moment the appellate decree comes into being, the original decree loses its independent entity. Perhaps, one can go to the length of saying that on an appellate decree being passed, the original decree by virtue of merger loses its very existence. In the concept of merger, thereafter it is the appellate decree which subsists. After it is rendered the decree which is enforceable is only that of the appellate Court and not of the original Court. To put it tersely, in the event of an appeal the enforceable decree is that of the appellate Court.</u>

<u>21. On perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the court of appeal below, the last court of the facts on consideration and evidence and materials on record affirmed the judgment of the trial court and these been purely findings of facts based on the evidence on record, this court seating revisional jurisdiction cannot interfere in the concurrent findings of the facts of the courts below. In the present case the learned Advocate for the petitioner failed to point out that the impugned judgment has occasioned failure of justice to the present petitioner. The mere error of law without occasioning failure of justice cannot itself be a ground for interference by this court under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and in that view of the matter, I find nothing to interfere with the same.</u>

22. On the reading of the impugned judgment and decree and having regard to the all aspects of the case and on careful considerations of the entire evidence on record and the decisions cited above, I am of the view that the concurrent findings of the court below should not be interfered with.

23. In the result, the rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

24. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

Send down the lower court records at once.

End.

Vs.
Ayechuddin & Others
full_judgment:
A. T. M. Afzal, J:- The question that falls for consideration in this Rule is whether the learned Subordinate Judge was right in taking the view that the question of abatement does not arise owing to the non-substitution of the legal representives of the deceased plaintiff within the time limited by law in a suit for partition where a decree in preliminary form has already been passed. The question may be put in a more general form as follows : Whether it is correct to say that rules 3 and 4 of Order XXII of the Code of Civil Procedure are not applicable where the death of the defdt. or plff. occurs between the passing of preliminary and final decrees in a suit and that Rule 10 governs such a case.

2. The impugned order in this case was passed in the following circumstances: One Basirannessa, since deceased, along with her minor sons, Opposite Party Nos. 5 and 6 brought a suit for partition, being other suit No. 97/1956 in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Rangpur and the petitioner is a defdt. in the said suit. The suit was decreed in preliminary form on 9-4-60. Plff. No. 1 Basirannessa died on 11-5-62 but no application for substitution of her heirs was filed until 31-1-68. A. prayer for substitution of her heirs was made on that date along with a prayer to treat O.Ps. Nos. 5 and 6 as major. The Subordinate Judge allowed the prayers by order dated 26-4-68 and 0. Ps. No 1 to 4 were substituted in her place besides O.Ps. Nos. 5 and 6 who were already on record.

3. The deft-petitioner filed an application for review of the aforesaid order, being Misc. case No. 54/68, whereupon the impugned order dated 22-2-69 was passed by the learned Subordinate Judge dismissing the said Misc. case.

4. Being aggrieved by the said order, the defdt. petitioner moved the then High Court under section 115 C. P. C. and obtained the present Rule.

5. It appears from the impugned order that it was urged on behalf of the defdt. that the substitution of the heirs of the deceased plff. ought not to have been allowed because the application for substitution was filed long after the period of limitation. The Subordinate Judge observed in his order that the suit being a partition suit in which a decree in preliminary form was passed long before the alleged substitution, the question of abatement did not arise and the substitution in question was not, therefore, illegal. In such view of the matter, he dismissed the Misc. case.

6. Mr. Md. Fazlul Karim, learned Advocate for the petitioner, has frankly submitted that the view taken by the learned Subordinate Judge is based on a consensus of almost all the High Courts of the Indian Sub-continent and it is not his purpose to contend that the said view is untenable. He, however, submits that since there is no reported decision of this court on the point, the question may be examined keeping in view those decisions and possibly the only contrary opinion expressed so authoritatively by a very distinguished Judge of the Sub-continent, namely, Sir Muhammad Sulaiman.

7. Mr. Fazlul Karim has pointed out that all the High Courts of India relied upon the dictum enunciated by the Privy Council in the case of Lachmi Narain Marwari v. Balmakund Marwari reported in 51 Indian Appeals 321: AIR 1924 P.C. 198, but Sulaiman, J. in the case of Anmol Singh v. Hari Shankar Lai reported in AIR 1930 Allahabad 779 upon a close examination of the aforesaid Privy Council case observed that the case before their Lordships of the Privy Council was a case of a. totally different character and their Lordships had not to consider the specific language of the various rules in Order XXII and there was no reason to extend the principle underlying that decision to cases of abatement in a country where the law is to be found in a codified form. Mr. Karim upon placing reliance on the views of Sulaiman, J. and that of Rankin C.J. in the case of Elokeshee Dasee v. Kunjabihari Basak reported in AIR " 1933 Calcutta 696 (to be referred to fully hereafter) has made a tentative submission that it remains to be decided where the we should follow their views in this court in preference to those of other High Courts of India.

8. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Advocate for the Opposite parties, has painstakingly placed before me all the leading decisions on the point and contended on the authority of the almost unanimous view expressed therein that a suit does not abate by the death of a plff. or defdt. after a preliminary decree and failure to bring the heirs on record within the due time. He has pointed out that the principle enunciated by the Privy Council in the aforesaid case has been applied by all the High Courts of India except that of Allahabad and those High Courts further upon a construction of rules 3 and 4 have laid down as aforesaid. He submits that upon the sheer force of logic, to which I shall presently refer, we must prefer to follow the almost unanimous -view expressed by the High Courts of India.

9. Upon a review of the authorities cited before me it appears that at one time all the Courts in India appear to have held that the death of a party after the passing of the preliminary decree may cause an abatement of the suit. But the aforesaid decision of the Privy Council seems to be the turning point & have mounded the views of the High Courts in India. The celebrated dictum of the Judicial Committee was laid down in the context of somewhat different facts. The facts were that the High Court at Patna on appeal made an order by consent for a partition upon certain terms and remitted the suit to the Subordinate Judge for disposal under the decree. Upon the plff. failing to appear on the day appointed by the Subordinate Judge for the matter to be proceeded with, he made an order dismissing the suit he based his action upon Order XXII rule 2 C.P.C. The High Court upon motion set aside that order. While upholding the decision of the High Court, the Judicial Committee made this classic remark:

"After a decree has once been made in a suit, the suit can-not be dismissed unless the decree is reversed on appeal. The parties have, on the making of the decree, acquired rights or incurred liabilities which are fixed, unless or until the decree is varied or set aside."

10. The first important case on the subject which I propose to refer is the Full Bench decision of the Madras High Court in the case of Perumal Pillai v. Perutnal Chetty reported in AIR 1928 Madras 914. In that case the plff. obtained a preliminary decree in a mortgage suit on 18th November, 1921. He then died on 25th February, 1922 before a final decree had been passed. No application had been made or acceded to within three months of Plff's death to add his legal representative to the record. The question referred to the Full Bench was whether on a proper construction of the authorities it could be said that the suit had abated in terms of the provisions of Order XXII rule 3. Courts-Trotter, C.J. while delivering the opinion referred to the yet another illuminating principle set out by Lopes, J in the case of Char man v. Day ( 1883 ) 48 L.T. 907:—

"It is said that, the defendant having die d the maxim action personal is monitor cum persona applies. I think it does not apply in such a case as this. I think "action" means right of action" and if that is the true way of looking at it, the right of action here had been determined before the death of the defendant."

11. Applying the aforesaid principle and upon making reference to the aforesaid Privy Council Case his Lordship gave the opinion that Order XXII rules 3 and 4 do not apply to the present state of circumstances. It was observed that the case in hand was obviously a casuo omissus from the Civil Procedure Code and probably nobody had thought of providing for it.

12. The next important case is another Full Bench decision of the Nagpur Judicial Commissioners Court in the case of Bapu v. Gulabchand reported in AIR 1929 Nagpur 142. The point under reference was whether Order XXII rule 4 should apply in a case where the death of a party took place after the passing of the preliminary decree but be-fore the decree is made absolute; or whether Order XXII rule 10 should apply.

13. It was considered whether after the preliminary decree has been passed, it can be held that the right to sue subsists so as to bring the case within rule 4, Order XXII or not. Reference was made to the afore-said Privy Council case and the Full Bench decision of the Madras High Court. Their Lordships quoted the following important passage from the decision in the case of Lakhpati Kuar v. Daulat Singh ( AIR 1927 Oudh 156 ):

"Decisions of almost all the High Courts in India were cited in support of the view that proceeding after the preliminary decree and before the final decree are proceedings in the suit. We are of the opinion that the precise question which arises for determination in the present case is not answered on the view of the rule of procedure taken in these decisions. The question which we have to decide is whether the provisions of Sub-R.(3),R.4, 0.22, Civil P.C. applies to a suit in which a decree of the Court preliminary in its legal characteristics has come into existence and death occurs in the rank of the defendants subsequent to such a decree. According to our judgment the said sub-rule has no application to such a case. The word "suit" in 0.22 must be given a restricted meaning. We think it means only such proceedings as antecedent to the passing of a decree, preliminary or otherwise. This interpretation is supported by the language and import of several rules of the said order. The first rule is that the death of a' plaintiff or a defendant shall not cause the suit to abate if the right to sue survives. Obviously no question of "the right to sue" can subsist in a suit after a decree is delivered by the Court in that suit. As soon as the Court pronounces judgment the plaintiff's original right to sue disappears if he has failed and it merges in the decree if he has won transit in rem judicatam."

14. The answer to the reference was that rule 10, Order XXII applies in a case in which the death of the defdt occurs between the passing of the preliminary and final decrees of the suit, and not rule 4 of that Order.

15. Sulaiman, J had occasion to consider the question in the case already referred to above in the following year i.e. 1930. The Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court was hearing an appeal by the puffs from an order of the court below actually dismissing the suit which was treated as an order refusing to set aside an abatement against the contesting defdts only. In a mortgage suit, some of the defdts died after the passing of the preliminary decree and their heirs pointed out that their names had not been formally brought on record. The puffs filed an application to bring the legal representatives on record. The heirs took the plea that the suit had in fact abated as against them because no application for substitution of names had been filed within the time allowed by law. The Subordinate Judge acceded to this contention, and holding that the suit had abated, dismissed the suit as against the contesting defdts.

16. It was argued in the High Court upon the authority of the aforesaid Full Bench case of the Madras High Court that after a preliminary decree had once been passed there was no question of abatement at all. Their Lordships observed that in the said Full Bench case, the specific provisions of the Code, apart from those contained in Rules 3 and 4 appeared not to have been examined. With reference to the dictum of the Judicial Committee, it was observed that it fully applied to a compromise decree passed between the parties. It was further pointed out that although if a partition suit is to become infructuous no fresh suit can be instituted on the same cause of action, nevertheless if the property remains Joint and undivided there is nothing to prevent a co-sharer, subsequently on a fresh cause of action, from again suing for division of the joint property and for the separation of his share. To hold that his right to get a partition is extinguished would be tantamount to holding that the property has become impartible. Sulaiman J summed up his discussion of the Privy Council case thus:

"It is therefore clear to us that the case before their Lordships of the Privy Council was a case of a totally different character and their Lordships had not to consider the specific language of the various rules in 0.22 and we see no reason to extend the principle underlying that decision to cases of abatement in a country where the law is to be found' in a codified form."

17. His Lordship then gave his own reasons, contrary to the reasoning of the Madras, Nagpur and other High Courts that—

"A decree in a suit may be either preliminary or final. A decree is preliminary when further proceedings have to be taken before the suit can be completely disposed of it is final when such an adjudication completely disposes of a suit. There cannot therefore be the least doubt that under the Code of Civil Procedure now in force the suit does not terminate by the passing of the of the preliminary decree but continues till it is finally and completely disposed of by the passing of the final decree. This point has arisen in numerous cases in connexion with the period of limitation which should be applicable to applications for the “framing" of a final decree and it has been unanimously held by all the High Courts that the proceedings are not by way execution but in the suit itself. We need only refer to a few cases of our own High Court on this point: Abdul Majid v. Jawahir Law (8) (1911) 33 All 154; Moti Lal v. Ram Narain (9) (1917) 39 All 551 Gajadhar Singh v. Kishan Jiwan Lal (10) (1917) 39 All 641; Nizamuddin Shah v. Bohra Bhim Sen (11) (1918) 40 All 203; Ahmad Khan v. Mt. Laura (12) (1918 40 All 235. Now when the suit is still continuing even after the passing of the preliminary decree, it is difficult to see how 0.22, R.4, cannot be applicable to it. It expressly states that the Court "shall proceed with the suit" There seems to be no reason to restrict the meaning of the word "suit" in this particular rule and say that there "suit" means the stage in the suit up to the passing of the preliminary decree only and not thereafter."

18. His Lordship noticed that in the Allahabad High Court the view has been consistently held that the death of a party after the passing of the preliminary decree may cause an abatement of the suit, and then upon a review of the background and current opinion of the other High Courts concluded thus:

"We are accordingly of opinion that there is nothing in the case of Lachmi Narain v. Balmakund Marwari (3) which can be taken the overrule these previous decisions. We must therefore adhere to the view which has so far been strongly expressed by the High Court as we are not bound, by the opinions expressed by the other High Courts."

19. In the following year, Sulaiman, C. sat in a Full Bench in the case of Mahabir Singh v. Narain Tewari, A 1931 Allahabad 490, and reiterated his views thus:

"The last point suggested in the order of reference is as to the question whether there could be an abatement of a suit between the passing of a preliminary decree and the preparation of the final decree. The rulings in India were all one way and laid down that under the new Civil Procedure Code the suit continues till the final decree is passed and it can abate before that contingency happens. A dissentient note was struck by a Full Bench of Madras High Court in Perumal Pillay v. Perumal Chetty (18) A.I.R. 1928 Mad. 914 after the pronouncement of their Lordships of the Privy Council in Lachmi Narain Marwari v. Balmakund Marwari (19) A.I.R. 1924 P.C. 198. The same view appears to have been followed in Calcutta and Oudh. In Anmol Singh v. Hari Shankar Lal (3) A.I.R. 1930 All 779 in concurrence with King, J., I held the decision of their Lordships of the Privy Council did not upset the previous rulings of the Indian High Courts, and explaining the ratio dividend of the case pointed out how that case was distinguishable. Another Bench of this Court in Bahadur Singh v. Nanak (4) agreed with that view and came to the same conclusion."

20. Rankin C. J does not seem to have expressed his views finally in the decision referred to above, A 1933 Cal. 696. His Lordship noticed an earlier decision of the same count (Nazir Ahammad v. Tamijuddin Ahammad A 1929 Cal 430) holding that a suit does not abate after a preliminary decree which to some extent was based upon the aforesaid Privy Council case of Lachmi Narain Marwari v. Balmakund Marwari. As to the case in hand, he observed that this is a partition suit and that nothing, which can be done in this partition suit, can prevent the plff. from bringing an-other partition suit. With regard to the ruling referred to by himself he observed that whether the said ruling was right or not was a matter which could only be settled by a Full Bench. The decision of the Judicial Committee, he observed further, could in no way be said to conclude the present case.

21. In the case of Priyabala Dassi v. Sarajubala Choudhurani reported in AIR. 1936 Calcutta 540 a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court concurred with a decision of the Patna High Court (1931 Patna 57) upon relying on the aforesaid dictum of the Privy Council, that Order XXII rule 3 did not apply in the case of a proceeding for ascertainment of manse profits after a decree in a preliminary form had been passed inasmuch as after the decree has been passed, the suit could not be dismissed, unless the decree has been reversed, and no question of abatement could arise in such case even though one of the parties dies after the preliminary decree is passed and no legal representative is brought on the record within the time allowed by law.

22. Beaumont C.J. of the Bombay High Court dwelt upon the question in the case of Dawara Ali Jafarli Saiyad v. Bai Judi reported in AIR 1940 Bombay 318. Upon noticing the views of different High Courts including that of Sulaiman J and the observations of the Judicial Committee, he opined that the "observations" are no doubt of general application but the question must ultimately turn on the construction of the relevant rule which in that case was rule 4 of Order 22. Rejecting the contention that the phrase the suit shall abate as occurring in rules 3(2) and 4(3) is mandatory and applies to cases under consideration, his Lordship in a forceful and incisive exposition of the rules, in the facts of that case, laid down thus:

"The use of the definite pronoun show that the suit, which is to abate, is the suit referred to in the earlier part of the rule, and that is a suit in which the right to sue either does not survive against surviving defendant or defendants alone, or does survive, in the case of the death of a sole defendant. Now, where a preliminary decree has been passed, it seems to me that it is quite inappropriate to talk about the right to sue surviving. The rights of the parties are crystallized by the preliminary decree. The mortgage is established, the mortgagor has a right to redeem, and in default the mortgagee is given certain rights. It is no longer open to the plaintiff to sue in respect of his original cause of action; all he can do is to enforce his rights under the preliminary decree. No doubt an application for a final decree is not technically an application in execution of the preliminary decree, but it is certainly not an application in respect of the original right to sue. It is an application to enforce the rights under the preliminary decree and though the suit may be continued for that purpose, it seems to me inappropriate to refer to the right to sue as either surviving or not surviving. Therefore, on the language of 0.22 R.4, I feel no doubt that the rule does not apply to a case in which a preliminary decree has been passed;

23. A Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Bhusan Chandra Mondal v. Chhabimoni Dasi, AIR 1948 Calcutta 363 upon similar reasoning as noticed above found:

"On that view of the matter we hold the cases of the type which we have before us do not come within the provision of 0.22, R. 4 and for the same reason within the provision of 0.22, R.3. According to the language of 0.22, R.10, these cases where death occurs after the preliminary decree must come within the rule, viz, R. 10 and there is no period of limitation fixed with regard to the matters coming under the said rule. This view of ours would not create any inconsistency where the death of a party occurs during the pendency of an appeal for, in that case, the words "right to appeal" will have to be substituted by reason of the provisions of R.11 in the place of the words "right to sue" occurring in R. 3 & 4. The view that we are taking is the view that has been adopted in all the High Court excepting in the later decisions of the Allahabad High Court:

The Division Bench reviewed all the previous decisions of the Court and observed further that:

"In view of the decisions of two Division Benches of this Court which are binding on us and in view of the fact that all other High Courts except the Full Bench of Allahabad High Court in 54 All. 25, have taken the view which is in accordance with the view we are taking, we do not think that we would be justified in accepting the contention of the petitioner be-fore us on the first point."

24. Mr. Mahmudul Islam has brought to my notice yet another Division Bench decision of the Calcutta High Court that in the case of Tara Pada Roy v. Shyama Pada Roy reported in AIR 1952. Calcutta 579 where once again the principle laid down by the Judicial Committee was referred to and it was held that once a preliminary decree is passed by a, Court it has no Jurisdiction either to pass an order dismissing the suit or to record that the suit has abated as the heirs of one or more of the original and necessary parties had not been substituted within the statutory period.

25. Upon a review of the authorities it becomes clear that in answering the question in hand, although a reference has always been made to the aforesaid pronouncement of the Judicial Committee, but in the ultimate analysis, the construction put upon the rules has decided the issue. The crux of the matter seems to be that whereas Sulaiman, J. has held that a suit does not terminate by the passing of the preliminary decree but continues till it is finally and completely disposed of by the passing of the final decree and therefore, it is difficult to see how rules 3 and 4 of Order XXII can be said to be inapplicable to it, all the other High Courts seem to have put more ex-phases on the phrase 'right to sue' surviving or not surviving upon the death of a party. Beaumont C.J., in my opinion, has fully answered the main reasoning given by Sulaiman J. The learned Chief Justice has held that where a preliminary decree has been passed it is not appropriate to say that 'the right to sue' survives because the rights of the parties are crystalised by the preliminary decree. Of course, an application for a final decree is not technically an application in execution of the preliminary decree and the suit continues as found by Sulaiman J. but it is certainly not an application in respect of the original right to sue. Indeed the Plffs original right to sue disappears if he has failed in the suit and it merges in the decree if he has won. Thus the original right to sue being merged in the preliminary decree the question of its non-survival to or against the surviving parties alone upon the death of a party or survival upon the death of the sole plff. or defdt do not arise. The suit is continued for a final decree but the same, of necessity, is to be on the basis of already settled rights and liabilities under the preliminary decree. It shall always remain a question as to what the decision would have been if Sulaiman J. were to consider this aspect of the matter.

26. Be that as it may, having regard to the preponderance of authorities which are almost unanimous and based on compelling reasons as referred to above, I am of the opinion that the view which is being followed consistently in the Indian High Courts is sound and deserve to be followed in this Court.

<u>27. The end result of the discussion is that it is incontestable that once a preliminary decree is passed by a court it has no jurisdiction either to pass an order dismissing the suit or to record that the suit has abated as the heirs of one or more of the original and necessary parties had not been substituted within the statutory period. After the passing of the preliminary decree there is no further 'right to sue' in the plff in respect of his original cause of action and the suit cannot abate in terms of rules 3 and 4 of Order XXII. Rules 3 and 4 of Order XXII are not, therefore, applicable to cases of the kind under consideration but rule 10 govern such cases.</u>

28. I, therefore, hold that the view taken by the learned. Subordinate Judge in the instant case is correct and the question formulated in the beginning should be answered in the affirmative.

In the result, the rule is discharged but without any order as to costs.

End.

parties:
Momtaj Begum and others ----- Plaintiff-Petitioners
Vs
Arju Miah and others ----- Defendant-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Khondker Musa Khaled J: On an application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, this rule was issued calling upon the defendant opposite-party Nos. 1-12 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 27-4-2010 passed by the learned Joint district Judge, First Court, Noakhali allowing Misc. case no 44 of 2009 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure arising out of Title Suit No. 31 of 2005, should may deem fit and proper.

2. At the time of issuance of the Rule, operation of the impugned judgment and order was also stayed.

3. The that the present petitioners as plaintiffs filed the Partition Suit no. 31 of 2005 in the Court of Joint District Judge, Noakhali for partition of the suit land. Summons on all the defendants of the Partition Suit were duly served and the defendant Nos. 12-27 appeared jointly and filed a written statement and ultimately they prayed for a separate saham. The defendants 53-62 also appeared and filed a written statement claiming their separate saham and the defendant no. 1 also entered appearance in this suit. Ultimately the suit was fixed for preemptory hearing and the plaintiffs were present on several dates fixed for hearing, but the suit could not be taken up for hearing as the Court was busy in hearing other cases. Ultimately, the suit was fixed for preemptory hearing on 15-5-2008 and the Tadbirker of the plaintiffs was sick on that date and, as such, an adjournment petition was filed on behalf of the plaintiffs, on that date only set of defendant (defendant Nos. 53-62) was present by filing hajira. But the learned Judge of the trial Court was pleased to reject the adjournment petition of the plaintiffs as condition precedent (CP) costs awarded earlier, was not paid by the plaintiffs and consequently the suit was dismissed for default under order XVII rule 1(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure vide an order 15-5-2008. Thereafter on 3-6-2008, the plaintiffs filed an application under the newly amended order XVII, rule 1(7) read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure by depositing statutory compensatory costs of Taka 2,000 along with the previous awarded CP cost vide Chalan and prayed for revival of the suit on setting-aside the order of dismissal. The copies of the said revival application was also served on the learned Advocates for all the set of defendants, who entered appearance in the suit.

4. After hearing the parties, the learned Joint District judges was pleased to allow the application of revival under order XVII, rule 1(7) of the Code of Civil Procedure and the suit was revived by an order dated 3-6-2008. All the three set of the defendants had knowledge about the revival of the suit. Thereafter, next date for hearing was fixed on 24-6-2008 and the plaintiffs and contesting defendants 53-62 adduced evidence in support of their respective cases and the. learned Judge of the trial Court ultimately decreed the suit of the plaintiffs in part on contest against the defendants 53-62 and ex-parte against the rest on 9-3-2009. The defendants 53-62 also got saham. Though the defendants 12-27 field a joint written statement, they did not turn up to contest the suit and after dismissal of the suit by the aforesaid judgment, only defendants 12-19 filed Misc. case no. 44 of 2009 under order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for setting-aside the decree passed against them ex-parte and restoration of the suit.

5. The plaintiffs-opposite-party Nos. 1-13 submitted a written objection opposing the application for restoration and after hearing the learned Joint District Judge allowed the Misc. case vide the impugned judgment and order dated 27-4-2010.

6. Being aggrieved, the plaintiff-petitioners preferred this revisional application and obtained the instant Rule and stay order as stated earlier.

7. Mr. Abul Kalam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioners submits that the plaintiffs failed to pay CP cost awarded on an earlier date and again they filed an adjournment petition on the subsequent date which was rejected and consequently the Partition suit was dismissed for default on 15-5-2008 under Order XVII, rule 1(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. On that date, the opposite-parties (defendants 12-19) were not at all present in the Court. Though defendants filed a joint written statement along with other defendants, but none of those defendants of the same group appeared by filing hajira. Only defendants 53-62 were present on the said date of dismissing the suit for default. However, the plaintiffs field an application for revival of the suit within 20 days by depositing compensatory costs together with CP. Case on serving copy of the same to all the defendants through their Advocates and got the suit revived on setting-aside the order of dismissal by an order dated 3-6-2008. It is contended that the related chapter containing the rules imposing restriction on adjournments, does not provide any scope to issue notices after revival of the suit under order XVII, rule 1(7) of the Code. Since defendants 12-19(petitioners of the Misc. case) had knowledge about revival application on getting copy of the same, no further notice was necessary. Moreover, there is no legal requirement to issue further notice after revival of the suit under the said newly inserted provision of the code of Civil Procedure. The defendants 12-19 (Petitioners of the Misc. case) cannot also claim notice in the proceeding as of right like a proceeding under order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is submitted that they had no reason to abstain from contesting Partition Suit, though the defendants 53-62 appeared on the date of dismissal for default, received compensatory costs and thereafter contested the suit after revival. These opposite-parties, being absent defendants on that date, filed Misc. case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was not legally maintainable, but the learned Judge of the trial Court allowed the Misc. case illegally. He submits further that the. application under Order IX, rule 13 of the code of Civil Procedure has no manner of application in the instant case. In fact, service of summons was made as usual in the suit and those defendants also appeared. In such a situation, there was no legal requirement for serving fresh notice upon the defendants 12-19. It is further contended by the learned Advocate that the suit was contested of the defendants 53-62 and they got separate saham, but they were not made parties in the Misc. case in spite of the fact that their interest has been affected by the impugned judgment and order. So, the learned Judge has committed gross illegality in allowing Misc. case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, the impugned judgment and order cannot legally be sustained he added.

8. Mr. Md. Saidul Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite-parties (defendants 12-19) submits, in reply, that the defendants 12-19 had no opportunity to know about the restoration of the suit which was done in their absence. So, these defendants were entitled to get notice of revival of the suit as of right and for the sake of equitable justice. It is contended that those defendants knew about the dismissal of the suit, and they were not aware of the subsequent revival and, as such, could not come to contest the suit at the time of trial. The learned Advocate submits that though there is no specific provision of serve notice after revival under Order XVII, but notice was necessary in the line of the provisions of the Order IX of the Code of Civil Procedure as the order of revival was made behind the back of these opposite-parties (defendants 12-19). Referring to the case of Siddique (Md) vs Yeakuti Begum reported in 49 DLR 402, the learned Advocate submits that even if the suit is dismissed for default under Order IX, rule 2 of the. Code of Civil Procedure, the notice on the absent defendants afresh is necessary after restoration of the suit under, rule 4 of the said Order. Equity and justice demand for issuance of notice after such revival of the suit even if no specific provision is available. It is contended that there was sufficient reason which prevented these defendants from appearing before the trial Court after the revival as they were not an all aware of the subsequent proceedings of the suit, and, as such, the decree passed against them exparte has rightly been set-aside by the impugned judgment, which does not call for interference.

9. We have perused the certified copies to the impugned judgment and order, order of dismissal dated 15-5-2008, order of revival dated 3-6-2008, judgment and decree dated 9-3-2009, which has been set-aside by the impugned judgment, and the revisional application along with the documents annexed therewith.

10. Admittedly, the opposite-parties (defendants 12-19) appeared in the original suit on getting regular summons and they also filed a joint written statement with the defendants 20-27. The suit was fixed for peremptory hearing on 15-5-2008, on which date, these defendants 12-19 (petitioners of the Misc. case) were absent in the court, but the contesting defendants 53-62 were present by filing hajira. On that date, the petitioner-plaintiffs filed adjournment petition without paying the CP costs of Taka 200 and, as such, the court was pleased to reject time prayer of the plaintiffs and dismissed the suit for default in paying CP cost under Order XVII rule 1(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Subsequently on 3-6-2008, the suit was revived on payment of statutory compensation of Taka  2,000 along with the previous CP costs under order XVII, rule 1(7) of the code of Civil Procedure. It is admitted position of fact that no fresh notice was served on any of the defendant s after revival of the suit and that the suit was contested by defendants 59-62 after revival of the suit and contested judgment was passed against them and the suit was decreed ex-parte against the rest. The absent defendants 12-19 filed Misc. case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that they were not served with notice after revival of the suit and, as such, they were prevented by sufficient cause from appearing before the Court, when the suit was called for hearing after revival.

11. Now the pertinent legal question involved in this case is whether the defendants 12-19 (opposite-parties) were legally entitled to get any notice after revival of the suit in accordance with the provision of Order XVII, rule 1(7) of the Code. It is evident from the said provision that there is nothing in the relevant order and Rules requiring service of notice after revival of the suit. The relevant order XVII, rule 1(3) and XVII, rule 1(7) may be quoted below for ready reference;

12. Order XVII rule 1(3)—"Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rules (1) and (2) the Court shall not grant more than six adjournments in a suit before peremptory hearing at the instance of either party to the suit, and any adjournment granted to a party beyond the aforesaid limit shall make such party liable to pay a cost of not less than two hundred taka and not more than one thousand taka to the other party, within time to be specified by it ; non-compliance with which by the plaintiff shall render the suit liable to be dismissed and by the defendant shall render the suit liable to be disposed of ex-parte;

Provided that the court shall not grant more than three adjournments to a party even with cost under this rule."

13. Order XVII, rule 1(7)—

"A suit dismissed or disposed of ex-parte under sub-rule (3) or (4) shall not be revival for hearing unless the party, for whose non-compliance the suit was dismissed or disposed of ex-parte, makes within thirty days of such dismissal or ex-parte disposal, an application together with cost of two thousand taka into Court for such revival ; and upon such application being made, the suit shall be revived for hearing without any further proceeding ; and cost deposited into Court shall be paid to the other party."

14. It is evident from the above quoted provisions of law that nothing has been mentioned as to necessity of issuing any notice after revival of the suit when it was so dismissed for non-payment of cots in compliance with the court's order. It may be mentioned that the aforesaid new provisions were inserted in the order no. XVII which relates to adjournment and this chapter is not a part of the provisions relating to dismissal, ex parte disposal and subsequent restoration as contemplated under Order IX of the Code of Civil Procedure. Though a reference has been made to the provisions of Order IX in rule 2 of the order XVII, it relates to the mode of actions to be taken in case of dismissal for default or ex-parte disposal etc. this Rule is not new having relatively with the new amendments. The Order IX of the Code is not relevant for the purpose of revival of the suit under Rule 1(7) of the Order XVII which speaks continuation of the proceeding if money is paid within time. On such payment, the Court has no option but to revive the suit without any interruption. Adjournments are restricted by the said new provision only to reduce delay in disposal of suit. In this process, there is no need of initiating Mice. Case like an application under Order IX, rule 9, rule 13 etc. which is almost a separate proceeding for restoration of the suit after disposal of the suit for default or ex-parte decree. But the procedure for revival of a suit under the newly amended provision of Order XVII are made for passing revival order in the same proceeding of the suit. As such, an application for revival under this order is necessary to be made after serving copy to all the parties to serve the purpose of notice like any other application. As such, the question of issuing separate notices does not arise. Compensatory cost is however necessary to be paid to the parties present on the date of dismissal order.

15. In the instant case, the defendants 59-62 were present in the Court and they also received compensatory costs in accordance with law. It appears from the Annexure-B(2) that the copy of the application made under order XVII, rule 1 (7) for revival was duly served on all three set of defendants on 3-16-2008 who entered appearance in the suit through their engaged Advocates. It appears that one set of defendants who was present on the date of dismissal, contested the suit after revival be adducing witnesses. The defendants 12-19 and some other defendants did not appear during whole period. When summons were duly served previously and the defendants 12-19 knew about the suit and did not turn up for hearing on the date of dismissal for default, the question of issuing further notices on them does not arise at all.

16. Notice is necessary only when the defendants remain un-aware of the pending proceeding against them. Since copy of the revival application was duly served on the defendants, they cannot plead ignorance of the fact of the revival. Even if defendants 12-19 were found present in the Court on the date of dismissal for default, they could say that due to knowledge about dismissal order, they did not turn up for hearing on the subsequent dates. But in this case those defendants were absent on that date. So, they cannot ask for fresh notice after revival when they were not aware of the dismissal. The defendant 12-19 appear to have maintained silence throughout the whole trial period and after about a year, when contested judgment against another set of defendants was passed, immediately thereafter they came to the Court with the Misc. case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure to nullify the whole proceeding and final adjudication in a contested judgment and decree against others taking advantage of ex-parte disposal against them.

<u>17. It may be mentioned here that the suit was not dismissed for default under Order IX, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure and legitimacy of getting notice after restoration is not available under Order XVII, rule 1 (7) of the Code of Civil Procedure where restoration procedure was maintained with the knowledge of the parties. So, there is no scope to issue any further notice under the new provision unless the Court is fully satisfied that the party was eager to contest, but could not get any information about the revival. In the present case, admittedly copy of the application for revival was served on their engaged Advocate. In any view of the matter, the cited case of 49 DLR 402 is not at all applicable in the case.</u>

18. It appears from the impugned judgment that the learned trial Judge has made the following observation and findings:—

“নথি পর্যালোচনা দেখা যায় যে, মূল মামলা খারিজের পর পূর্নবহালের বিষয় আইনজীবিকে অবহিত করিলেও নোটিশের মাধ্যমে বিবাদী প্রার্থীকে জানানো হয় নাই। যেহেতু প্রার্থী বিবাদী মূল মামলা খারিজের পরে পূনরবহালের বিষয় যথাযথভাবে নোটিশের মাধ্যমে অবহিত ছিল না ফলে বিবাদী প্রার্থী মূল মামলা প্রতিদ্বন্ধিতার সুযোগ পান নাই। এমতাবস্থায় ন্যায় বিচারের স্বার্থে প্রার্থীপক্ষের প্রার্থনা মঞ্জুর করা যায় ফলে বাদীপক্ষ প্রার্থীতমতে প্রতিকার পাইতে হকদার। মামলা প্রমাণিত হইয়াছে।”

19. Thus, the learned Judge was satisfied about giving proper information of the revival order, but allowed the case due to non-issuance of formal notice, though there is no such legal requirement.

<u>20. Purpose of serving notice is nothing, but to give information to the parties about the proceeding, so that they can appear if they like. The said purpose appears to have been served by giving information through their engaged lawyer. But the learned Judge of the trial Court even after admitting about getting information of revival misdirected himself by saying that notice was necessary to be served in the suit after its revival. Since there is no legal requirement to issue any notice after revival and it is evident before the trial Court that information of revival was duly given, the finding and decision arrived at by the learned Court below appears to be erroneous.</u>

21. In view of the aforesaid circumstances and legal position of the case, we are led to hold that no notice was required to proceed with the suit after revival order passed under Order XVII, rule 1(7) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Moreover, the defendants 12-19 were aware of the proceeding and there was no sufficient cause to prevent them from appearing before the court when the trial was held after revival of the suit. Rather it appears that the impugned judgment and order has prejudiced the plaintiffs and defendants 53-62 for setting-aside their contested decree.

22. It may be mentioned here that the defendants 53-62, who also got saham in the decree, were not also made party in the Misc. case filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, though their interest has been affected by the impugned judgment. So, the Misc. case was also bad for defect of the parties as well. Therefore, the trial Court appears to have committed error of law owing to misreading of evidence resulting an error in the impugned judgment and order which amounts to failure of justice, and as such, interference is necessary.

23. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 27-4-2010 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Noakhali allowing Misc. case No. 44 of 2009 is set-aside and the consequently the said Misc. Case is dismissed. The stay order passed in connection with the Rule stands vacated.

Send a copy of the judgment and order to the Court below immediately.

End.
