Mr. Mahbubey Alam also failed to show with reference to the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, that those concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the Courts below are the result of misreading or non-consideration of any material evidence or the misconstruction of the documents particularly the agreements entered into between the developer company and the deceased defendant No. 3, so we see no scope of interference with those findings of facts.

19. The High Court Division rejected the objection raised by the appellants (petitioners herein) that the suit was bad for defect of party as Mr. Nesarul Islam, the subsequent purchaser, was not made a party in the suit on the clear finding that "Admittedly no registered kabala was executed for sale of the suit flat No. 4 /B to Nesarul Islam" and since there was no document on record to show that the suit flat was sold to Nesarul Islam, he was not a necessary party in the suit. Therefore, there was no defect of party in framing the suit. Mr. Mahbubey Alam could not also refer to any registered document on record to dislodge the said finding of the High Court Division. In this regard, Mr. Mahmudul Islam has rightly referred to the evidence of DW2 (he was examined as the attorney of defendant Nos. 4 and 5) in his cross-examination to the effect  c-“………নেসারুল ইসলাম এর কাছে নাঃ ফ্ল্যাট রেজিষ্ট্রী দলিল মূলে দেওয়া হয় নাই। তার সাথে বিক্রয়ের বায়না হয় কিনা আমার জানা নাই। মিউটেশন হয় নাই।” And these evidence of DW2 show that the learned Joint District Judge and the High Court Division took the correct view as to objection of the defect of party in framing the suit.

20. In view of the above, the only point remains for consideration by this Division is whether the plaintiff was entitled to get the decree for specific performance of contract in respect of the suit flat against defendant No. 3 and on his death against defendant Nos. 4 and 5, though defendant No. 3 did not sign the tripartite agreement. The learned Joint District Judge answered the point in the positive with the finding as under:—

“ যেহেতু বাদিনীর সহিত ২নং বিবাদী ৪ বি নং ফ্ল্যাটটি বিক্রয়ের চুক্তি হইয়াছে এবং যেহেতু ৩নং বিবাদী ল্যান্ড ওনার এর সহিত ১-২নং বিবাদী ডেভোলাপার এর স্বীকৃত চুক্তি মোতাবেক ৪-বি নং ফ্লাটটি ২নং বিবাদীর অংশভুক্ত ফ্ল্যাট সেহেতু ঐ ফ্লাট পাইতে বাদিনী আইনতঃ হকদার।”

21. In coming to the said conclusion, the learned Joint District Judge considered the provisions of sections 12(c) and 27 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned Judges of the High Court Division also took similar view.

22. Now let us see whether the Courts below were correct in taking the above view.

23. In deciding the point, we are to remember that the concept of undertaking construction on one's land by a developer company is a new development in our country, and it is still developing, and definitely when the Specific Relief Act was enacted in 1877 none even conceived of this kind of transaction. In this kind of transaction like the instant case, the land owner first enters into an agreement with a developer company to undertake construction works on his land on the terms and conditions as stipulated therein and also gives a power of attorney to the developer to undertake all necessary steps and works for undertaking such construction on his land. As usual the developer company which invests its capital or money in undertaking the construction work on the land of the owner is given the right to forward sell the flats which fall in his share as per terms of the agreement and by virtue of the said right, the developer company forward sells or enters into agreement with the buyers for sale of the flats within his share and a stipulation is also made in the contract between the developer and the owner of the land to sign the contract of such forward sale along with the prospective buyer which is called a tripartite agreement. And now this kind of transaction is known as real estate business. It is also to be noted that in this kind of deal or transaction, the entire financial investment is made by the developer. Same thing happened in the instant case. This will be clear if we consider the preambles and the terms of the 3(three) contracts executed between the land owner and the developer company, defendant No. 1.

24. The first contract between the land owner, (deceased defendant No. 3) and the developer company (defendant No. 1) was signed on 18-10-2001, the first paragraph of the preamble of the said agreement reads as follows:

"WHEREAS the land owner has offered his land executioned and described in the scheduled for developer in order to construct a G+5 stored (sic) building. The developer has agreed to develop the same by constructing a G+5 storied building having with moderns amenities by spending his own money or with the help of advance money taken from buyers or by taking loan from Bank or Financial Institution. The developer shall sell flats to buyers after keeping 50% flats for the land owner."

Clauses 8 and 9 of the said agreement read as follows:

"08. That the developer will have the rights to register deed of conveyance to the purchasers of the 50% flats.

09. That the developer shall have the liberty to forward sell flats and obtain part payment as advance from intending buyers and execute deed of agreement showing undivided interest in the soil in favour of buyers and in that case a tripartite deed of agreement shall be executed to which the land owner would be one of the parties. Liabilities for advance money thus received shall be of the developers only."

25. This agreement was followed by another agreement executed on 18-8-2002 between defendant No. 3 and the developer-company making provision for constructing 2(two) more stories subject to the approval by the Cantonment Board. The first two paragraphs of the preamble of this agreement read as under:—

"WHEREAS, the Land Owner has offered his land executioned and described in the schedule for the developer in order to construct, at first, a Six storied building (Ten Flats) and after approval from the Cantonment Board, to construction additional two story i.e. Eight story flats building (Fourteen Flats). The Developer has agreed to develop the same by constructing at (sic) a Six storied building (Ten Flats) and after approval from the Cantonment Board to construct additional Two story i.e. Eight story flat building (Fourteen Flats) having modern amenities by spending his own money or with the help of advance money taken from buyers or by taking a loan from the Bank or a Financial Institution.

The Developer shall sell the first 5(five) flats to buyers and after approval from the Cantonment Board for Eight Story Construction, an additional 2(two) flats, i.e. Total 7(seven) Flats. The Developer will also hand over 5(five) flats to the Land Owner and after approval from the Cantonment Board for an Eight Story Construction, additional 2(two) flats i.e. Total 7 (seven) flats 50% parking space. The foundation for the Eight Storied building will now be made."

26. Clauses 7-10 of the agreement are as under:—

"7. That the Developer shall have the rights to register the Deed of Conveyance to the purchasers of the 50% Flats giving full possession of the 50% Flats and 50% of Parking Space to the Land Owner. Registration will be made showing undivided interest in the soil in favour of the buyers.

8. That the Developer shall have the liberty to forward sell Flats and obtains part-payments as advance from intending Buyers and execute a Tripartite Deed of

9. Agreement to which the Land Owner will be one of the parties. Liabilities for the advance money thus received shall be of the Developers only.

10.That the Developer would have the option to reallocate/cancel Flats of payment defaulters and offer choice to buyers willing and having cleared dues. "

And this deed was again followed by another deed dated 16-8-2004 under the style "SUPPLEMENTARY DEED OF AGREEMENT."

27. Paragraphs 1, 5 and 6 of the preamble of this supplementary agreement read as under:

"AND WHEREAS the LAND OWNER has mutually agreed to make changes in the original DEED OF AGREEMENT dated 18-8-2002 and the parties made this Supplementary Deed of Agreement

WHEREAS the land Owner has offered his land executioner and described in the scheduled for the developer in order to construct a six-storied building (Ten Flats). The developer has agreed to develop the same by constructing a six-storied building (Ten Flats) having modern amenities by spending his own money or with the help of advance money taken from buyers or by taking loan from Bank or Financial Institution.

The developer shall sell 5(five) flats to buyer and the developer will hand over 5(five) Flats with 50% Parking Space to the Land Owner after Completing the construction of the Flats in all respects before handing over the 5(five) Flats to the buyers."

28. Clauses 1, 3, 6, 9, 10, 11, and 12 of this agreement run thus: "

01. That since the Developer have already started constructing the building after signing the Agreement dated 18th August, 2002, it is further stipulated that the Developer will construction 10 (ten) flats of about 2050 sft. Apt. Area each on the scheduled land within February, 2005, failing which a penalty of Tk. 50,000/- (Taka Fifty Thousand) per month to be paid to the Land Owner by the Developer until the complete hand over of his share of the Flats.

03. That the Land Owner have already delivered possession of the vacant Land to the Developer for the construction of the Building after signing the Deed of Agreement dated 18th August, 2002.

06. That the Developer have already got the Plan Approved for constructing the proposed Six Storied apartment building from the Dhaka Cantonment Board and arrange the funds from his own resources, and from the prospective buyers if necessary or by taking loan from the Bank or Financial Institution. In taking money from the Bank or Financial Institution, or an Individual, the Developer will not mortgage the Flats/Apartments or the Landed Property on which the Developer will construct the proposed Apartment Building.

09. That the Land Owner shall execute and register Deed of Conveyance of 5 (five) Flats of Developer's share in favour of Developer or his selected Purchaser after receiving the possession of 5 (five) Flats and 50% of Parking Space from the Developer as per clauses and schedule stated in the Deed of Agreement.

10. That the Developer shall have the liberty to forward sell Flats and obtains (sic) part-payments as advance from intending Buyers and also receive full payment against the cost of the flat on or before giving full possession of the flats to the purchaser. The Developer shall also execute a Tripartite Deed of Agreement to which the Land Owner will be one of the parties; Liabilities for the money thus received by the Developer against the cost of the flats shall be of the Developers only. The Land Owner will have no responsibility of giving possession of the flats to the purchasers. In executing this clause, the Developer shall act in a way in which the interest of the land Owner i.e. receiving possession of 5 (five) flats and 50% parking space as stated in clause 09 and completion of the Building in all respects are maintained.

11. That the Developer would hand over 5 (five) Flats to the Land Owner in the following manners i.e. 1st floor 2(two), Flats, 5th Floor, 2(two) Flat and 2nd Floor. North side 1 (one) flat as per measurements. The Developer will construct a small room, present kitchen size (250 sft.) on the top floor (roof) for the use of the Land Owner (for servants) and a cover for keeping a car after the demolishing of the existing garage and servant quarters. The Developer will also hand over 50% of the Parking Space-as per the design-on the ground floor to the Land Owner.

12. That Ownership of the 5 (five) Flats of Developer's share shall be on the basis of Sale Deed. As soon as the purchasers of the flat pays full payment of the price of the Apartment to the Developer and the Developer complete the construction of the six storied building including the Parking Space in all respects and hand over manner. Land Owner would have no liabilities of any manner."

29. It is also to be noted that defendant Nos. 4 and 5 never denied the execution of the three agreements by their predecessor, deceased defendant No. 3 with the developer company. Rather DW2 in his examination-in-chief as well as in cross-examination by the plaintiff clearly admitted execution of the said three agreements by deceased defendant No. 3. Relevant portion of the evidence of DW2 is as follows:—

“ ………৩নং বিবাদী ১৮-১০-২০০১ ইং তাং ১৮-৮-২০০২ইং ১৬-৮-২০০৪ ইং তারিখ তিনটি চুক্তি করেছিল ডেভেলপার এর সাথে।”

30. The major difference between the first 2(two) agreements and the last agreement (supplementary agreement) was that in the last agreement the parties, i.e. the developer and the land owner (defendant No. 3) made an amicable partition between them of the flats to be constructed on the suit land and as per the said partition, the suit flat fell in the share of the developer, defendant No. 1 of which defendant No. 2 is the Chairman. It is also significant that the agreement to sell the suit flat by the developer to the plaintiff was entered into on 19-8-2004, i.e. after the execution of the supplementary agreement on 16-8-2004 and defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in their written statement categorically admitted the fact of entering into agreement with the plaintiff (Exhibit-8) for selling the suit flat which fell in their share. It is also very pertinent to state that defendant Nos. 4 and 5 in their written statement clearly admitted the fact of selling the four other flats by the developer to the other sellers, namely: defendant No. 9-Md. Saiful Islam, lshtiaque Ahmed, Abdullahil Rakib and Mozammel Hossain and no question was also raised by them about the signing of the tripartite agreement by deceased defendant No. 3 while selling 4(four) flats to them. Defendant Nos. 4 and 5 raised the dispute only about the sale of the suit flat. The paragraphs of the preambles of 3(three) agreements and the clauses as quoted hereinbefore clearly show that the land owner undertook to sign the agreement to be executed in between the developer and the purchaser to be called as tripartite agreement. It is also noteworthy to mention that the terms of the agreements clearly show that the land owner had/has no stake whatsoever in selling the flats by the developer to the buyers and that he would have no choice but to sign the agreement which would be executed and signed by the developer with the buyer. The terms of the agreements further show that the land owner gave unqualified power and authority to the developer to forward sell the flats of its share and to receive part payment as advance money against such sale of the flats from the buyers including the power to register the deed of conveyance and also to enter into agreement for such sale. But, the facts as emerged from the pleading show that defendant No. 3 preferred not to sign the agreement entered into between the plaintiff and the developer and in the suit defendant Nos. 4 and 5 took the plea that since defendant No. 3 did not sign the tripartite agreement, they were not bound by the agreement executed between defendant No. 2 and the plaintiff on 19-8-2004; in other words, defendant No. 3 not being party to the agreement, the same could not be specifically enforced against defendant Nos. 4 and 5 who are the heirs of defendant No. 3(since dead).

31. Now, the question is when defendant No. 3 in three written agreements specifically undertook to sign the tripartite agreement to be executed between the developer and the buyer, could he, and in his absence, defendant Nos. 4 and 5, take the plea that since defendant No. 3 did not sign the tripartite agreement specific performance of contract entered into between the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 1 and 2 could not be enforced against them. Our answer is No.  Because in that case, the purchaser-plaintiff who having seen the agreements executed between the land owner and the developer, on good faith, entered into agreement with the developer to purchase the suit flat and paid her good money for the purpose, shall be defrauded. Further, reading the clauses of 3(three) agreements executed between the land owner and the developer as quoted herein-before, it appears to us that the land owner having allowed the developer to forward sell of the flats of their share to the buyers by entering into agreement and accepting part payment as advance, was duty bound to sign the tripartite agreement. We are also of the view that since the land owner in clear terms undertook in the agreements executed between him and the developer to sign the tripartite agreement, he was estopped from taking such plea within the meaning of section 115 of the Evidence Act, because, he by signing the 3 (three) agreements with the developer in the terms as quoted hereinbefore caused a belief in the mind of the plaintiff, a buyer that he would put his signature in the tripartite agreement as a matter of course. The plea of defendant Nos. 4 and 5 also sounds to us a bit strange and self contradictory as, though they admitted the fact of sale of the other flats by the developer to four persons (names have been mentioned hereinbefore), they took a completely reverse plea in respect of the suit flat. It is also to be noted that defendant Nos. 4 and 5 clearly admitted the fact of getting the flats which fell in their share. One thing we must point out here is that in support of the case of defendant Nos. 4 and 5 that defendant No. 2 having failed to undertake the construction work of the project 'Heritage' had abandoned the project, the defendants failed to file a single scrap of paper to show that either they or the other purchasers from the developer ever made any correspondence with the developer company and gave any notice to them asking them to complete the construction of the project. And this in fact substantiates the case of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 that defendant No. 2 never executed any deed of agreement in favour of defendant No. 9 and other flat purchasers and any power of attorney giving them any power to complete the rest work of the project 'Heritage'. It is also very important to state that in the 1st and the last agreement executed between the land owner and the developer there were provisions for penalty at the rate of taka 50,000 per month to be paid to the land owner by the developer in case the developer failed to hand over the flats to him within the time stipulated therein. Therefore, defendant No. 3 had no reason or cause to disengage the developer from undertaking the remaining work of the project and then to take step to complete the works by engaging others as alleged by defendant Nos. 4 and 5. The plea that since defendant No. 3 did not sign the tripartite agreement, defendant Nos. 4 and 5 are not bound by the contract entered into between the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 1 and 2, does not also appear to us bonafide. If such plea is given countenance to, then, the intending buyers from the builder construction companies shall be put into unnecessary harassment and suffering which shall have also a negative impact upon the real estate business.

32. In the context, we feel it necessary to consider clauses (a)(b)(c)(d)(e) and (f) of the interpretation clause of the Contract Act as given in section 2 thereof in order to see whether mere non-signing of the tripartite agreement shall absolve defendant No. 3 and in his absence defendant Nos. 4 and 5 from being bound by the agreement which was signed by the two other parties, namely, the developer and the plaintiff.

33. Clauses (a)-(f) of the said interpretation clause read as under:—

(a) When one person signifies to another his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other to such act or abstinence, he is said to make a proposal:

(b) When the person to whom the proposal is made signifies his assent thereto, the proposal is said to be accepted. A proposal, when accepted becomes a promise:

(c) The person making the proposal is called the "promisor," and the person accepting the proposal is called the "promise".

(d) When, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains, from doing or promises to do or to abstain from doing something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise:

(e) Every promise and every set of promises, forming the consideration for each other, is an agreement:

(f) Promises which form the consideration or part of the consideration for each other are called reciprocal promises:

<u>34. From a combined reading of the above clauses of section 2 of the Contract Act read with the paragraphs of the preambles and the terms of 3(three) agreements as discussed above, it is abundantly clear that defendant No. 3 entered into an agreement with defendant Nos. 1 and 2 to sign the tripartite agreement without any reservation, whatsoever, in case the developer forward sells its share of the flats of the project 'Heritage'. As already stated hereinbefore, in paragraphs 21(ga) of the written statement defendant Nos. 4 and 5 categorically admitted that flat Nos. 2/ A, 3/A, 3/B, 4/A and 4-B fell in the share of the developer. So, defendant No. 2 did not commit any wrong or illegality in entering into contract with the plaintiff to sell the suit flat. In this regard, we may also refer to section 10 of the Contract Act. This section has clearly spelt out that all agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract for a lawful object and are not "hereby expressly declared to be void." "Hear" refers to second part of the section (second part of the section is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case). Now if we flashback to the preambles and the clauses of the agreements as entered into between the developer-company and defendant No. 3 as quoted hereinbefore and consider those along with clauses (a)(b)(c)(d)(e) and (f) of section 2 and section 10 of the Contract Act, it would prima facie appear that, the land owner of his own accord agreed to sign the agreement to be executed between the developer and the buyers of the flats which fell in the share of the developer, therefore, the plea of defendant Nos. 4 and 5 that their predecessor defendant No. 3 not being a signatory to the tripartite agreement the same cannot be enforced against them is not legally sustainable.</u>

35. It is very significant to state that defendant Nos. 4 and 5 never took the plea that defendant No. 3 rescinded or cancelled the contract executed with the developer-company. It is also very pertinent to state that in para-graph-20 of the last agreement (the supplementary agreement), it has been specifically stipulated that "any dispute or differences arising between the parties of this Deed with regards to the construction shall be referred to Military Estate Officer (MEO) Dhaka Cantonment, Dhaka and has them settled once for all." But, the land owner (deceased defendant No. 3) never resorted to the said arbitration clause, though the case of defendant Nos. 4 and 5 was that as the developer could not complete the work of the project satisfactorily they had abandoned the project and then defendant No. 3 completed rest work of the project by engaging his own men including the other flats' buyers from the developer-company. Rather it is the plaintiff who approached the Cantonment Board by filing an application on 20-12-2006 complaining that though the developer signed the tripartite agreement in respect of the sale of the suit flat, the land owner did not sign the same as admitted by defendant Nos. 10 and 11 in their written statement. The plea of defendant Nos. 4 and 5 that defendant No. 2 voluntarily executed an agreement on 15-2-2005 in favour of the other flat owners to complete the remaining works of the project 'Heritage' by expressing his inability to finish the work is purely question of fact and the plea has been disbelieved by the Courts below by giving reasons with reference to the evidence as already discussed hereinbefore (we do not discuss it here to avoid repetition). More interesting part of the case is that defendant Nos. 4 and 5 in their written statement categorically admitted the fact of sale of other four flats by the developer to four buyers (except the suit flat) and also receipt of taka 1,36,03,000 from them and thus admitted the fact of ownership of the developer about 5 (five) flats including the suit flat and also their right to transfer those flats then how defendant No. 3 and after his death defendant Nos. 4 and 5 could deny their liability to execute and register the kabala in respect of the suit flat? We also failed to understand how defendant No. 3 and other flat buyers from the developer of the project in question could claim to sell the suit flat when admittedly the same fell in the share of the developer and defendant No. 2 as its Chairman entered into an agreement with the plaintiff to sell the same. Such a case of defendant Nos. 4 and 5, sounds to us absolutely illogical as well as unconscionable. And moreso, when the agreements entered into between the land owner and the developer had remained in force till date.

<u>36. Chapter 11 of the Specific Relief Act has dealt with "Of the Specific Performance for Contracts". Section 12 of the Act has dealt with the contracts which may, in the discretion of the Court be enforced in the discretion of the Court except as otherwise provided in the Chapter. In the context, we are concerned with clause (a) of section 12. From a reading of clause (a) and the main section it is clear that when the act agreed to be done is in the performance wholly or partly, of a trust that can be specifically enforced. In the instant case, defendant No. 1 developer having the right to forward sell the suit flat entered into an agreement vide Exhibit-'8' with the plaintiff by signing the same and the plaintiff having paid the part payment of the contracted money which has also been admitted by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in their written statement, the act agreed to be done was partly performed and was in the nature of a trust, the land owner having agreed in unequivocal term to sign the tripartite agreement in case the developer forward sells out the flats of its share could not have a different identity other than a party with the developer and could not keep himself away by not signing the agreement. And defendant Nos. 4 and 5 being the heirs of defendant No. 3, specific performance of the contract, can very much be enforced against them within the meaning of section 27 of the Specific Relief Act. Therefore, the Court below rightly decreed the suit. It may be stated that breach of agreement to sell a flat to be constructed on the suit land cannot be adequately compensated by money as explained by the legislature in the explanation appended to the section and therefore, clauses (b) (c) and (d) to section 12 are also attracted in the instant case.</u>

37. In view of the above, the High Court Division did not commit any illegality in concurring with the decision of the learned Joint District Judge in decreeing the suit.

<u>38. From the statements made in the plaint and the written statement of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and the evidence on record one thing is clear that after 80% of the works of the project 'Heritage' particularly, the suit flat was completed the land owner somehow disengaged the developer from completing the remaining work of the project and then it was done by him through his men. So, defendant Nos. 4 and 5 are entitled to get the cost incurred in completing the 20% works of suit flat from the developer company which escaped the notice of the learned Joint District Judge as well as the High Court Division. In this regard, it may be stated that though in paragraph-5 of the plaint, the plaintiff specifically stated that 80% works of the project was completed when she was giving pressure upon the developer to get the signature of defendant No. 3 in the agreement dated 19-8-2004, defendant Nos. 4 and 5 after quoting the said portion of the plaint in their written statement simply denied the same in a general way without stating their version of the progress of the work. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 also in their written statement asserted that they completed more than 80% work of the project and these assertions of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were also not denied by defendant Nos. 4 and 5 in their written statement. Defendant Nos. 4 and 5 have also not stated how much cost was incurred for the completion of the remaining 20% works of the suit flat (we are not concerned about the other flats of the project). It is also noteworthy that in paragraph 21 of the written statement where actual facts have been stated defendant Nos. 4 and 5 have not stated at what stage of the work of the project the developer had allegedly abandoned the same. Be that as it may, assessment of cost is basically a question of fact and this is neither desirable nor possible for this Division. If, so advised, defendant Nos. 4 and 5 may demand the amount of 20% of the cost incurred by them in completing the work of the suit flat from the developer by giving notice in writing within one month from the date of receipt of this judgment by furnishing accounts of such cost and if any dispute arises as to the quantum of cost between them, then the parties may resolve the matter by resorting to clause 20 of the supplementary agreement dated 16-8-2004.</u>

With the above observations, this petition is dismissed.

End.

full_judgment:
Sultan Hussain Khan; J.:- These four appeals have arisen out of two suits instituted by the consignee for recovery of money for goods short delivered and are directed against the decrees passed in them.

2. The plaintiff in both the suits imparted two consignments of drugs and medicines from U.S.A. The two consignments comprised of 27 cartons and 30 cartons of drugs and medicines. Both the consignments were carried from U.S.A. to Dacca by the defendant No. 2 Air India International in their air-crafts. The aforesaid two consignments reached Dacca on 27.12.72 and 6.2.73 respectively and were delivered to their agent, defendant No.1, Bangladesh Biman. Defendant No.1 was the ground handling agent of the defendant No. 2. The plaintiff after obtaining delivery order from the defendant No. 2 and compliance of all customs formalities approached the defendant No. 1 for delivery of the consignments but the plaintiff was given delivery of only two cartons of drugs and medicines out of 27 cartons of first consignment on 2.2.72. Similarly the plaintiff having approached the defendant No. 1 for delivery of the remaining consignment after compliance of customs formalities was given delivery of only 12 cartons out of 30 cartons on 10.2.73. These short deliveries were how-ever endorsed on import applications by the concerned officers. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant No. 1 asked the plaintiff to take delivery of the remaining cartons out of the two consignments later on and the plaintiff accordingly made repeated approaches to the defendant No. 1 at many times for delivery but the defendant ultimately failed to give delivery of the cartons. The plaintiff alleged that due to negligence, misconduct and misfeasance of the employ the defendant No. 1 who has been acting as agent of the defendant No. 2 at Dacca Airport the plaintiff suffered the losses arising out of short delivery of 25 cartons and 18 cartons out of the two consignments of drugs and medicines'. The plaintiff claimed a sum of Taka 36,480j- for loss of 25 cartons of drugs and medicines in Money Suit No. 27 of 1973 and Taka 21150f- for loss of 18 cartons out of the second consignment bf drugs and medicines in Money Suit No. 28 of 1973. The defendants repudiated the claims and hence the plaintiff instituted these two suits. 

3. In both the suits all material facts and pleadings are identical and hence both were heard analogously. In both the suits defendants No. 1 filed written statements and contested the suit. The defendants No. 2 also filed separate written statements in the suits to contest them. Defendant No. 3, 6 .and .7 jointly filed written statements in both the suits and contested them. Similarly defendant Nos. 4 and 5 jointly filed written statements to contest the suits. Defendant Nos. 4 and 5 are Collector of Customs and Superintendent Air Freight section of the Customs Department respectively. They have denied their liability for loss of the cartons and further asserted that custodian of the goods in question was Bangladesh Biman and not the customs authorities and as such they were not liable to pay compensation to the plaintiff. 

4. The defendant No. 1, inter alia, contended in its written statements in both the suits that the consignments arrived at Dacca Airport by Air India International on 27.12.1972 and 6.2.1972 respectively and those were duly off loaded by this defendant and the same was given to the customs air freight unit at the airport ; according to customs regulation relating to international cargo, the consignments were, however, kept in the airport apron as directed by the customs authorities and under the charge of Airport Manager, Civil Aviation Department of Bangladesh. This defendant further alleged that when the plaintiff approached them for deli-very of the consignments they asked the plaintiff to approach the customs air freight unit, hereinafter referred to as A.F.0 and the customs officials accordingly autlioriud delivery in writing and this defendant went to the airport apron to make delivery but only found there two cartons out of 27 cartons of the first consignment and 12 cartons out of 30 cartons of the second consignment and the same was delivered to the plaintiff. The remaining cartons of the two consignments could not be traced out in-spite of thorough search in the airport apron. This defendant denied their liability an account of the loss of the cartons and that the losses were not caused due to their negligence or misconduct. This defendant further alleged that the suit was bad' for defect of notice to this defendant and that the principal of this defendant having been impleaded in the suit, it is not a necessary party in the suits and that in presence of the principal no decree can be passed against the agent for alleged loss and the short delivery of the cartons. 

5. The defendant No. 2, Air India Inter-national contended in their written statements in both the suits, besides taking legal objection as to limitation, estoppel and waiver etc. that the notice of loss was not given to this defendant within the time in accordance with the provision of Rule 26 of the Carriage of Goods by Air (International Convention) Act, 1966. They asserted that they made over the consignments to the defendant No. I and the Airport Customs authorities and thus they have no responsibility for the loss of the cartons as alleged by the plaintiffs. It was alleged by this defendant that by its letter dated 21st March, 1973 the defendant No. 1 admitted receipt of the consignments from the defendant No. 2 and that the defendant No. 1 kept the consignments on the Airport apron in front of their cargo space since the A.F.U. of customs refused to accept the consignment as they had no ware housing facilities. They alleged that the defendant No. 1 and the customs authorities at Dacca Airport are responsible for the loss of the cartons. They alleged that they had no responsibility after the consignments were offloaded or landed in Dacca and handed over to the defendant No. 1 and the customs authorities with intimation, to the consignee. They pleaded that they have no negligence or misconduct, and defendant No. 1 and the customs authorities are responsible for the same, and that they had no responsibility for the loss. 

6. The de Andant Nos. 3, 6 and 7, namely, Government of Bangladesh, Director General Civil Aviation and Airport manager, Civil Aviation Department respectively, filed joint written statements to contest the suits. They contended that as they have no ground facilities at Dacca Airport defendant No. 2 handed over the consignment to the defendant No. 1, the Bangladesh Biman for keeping the consignments in their godown. They also pleaded that Bangladesh Biman or Civil Aviation authorities had no responsibility for the consignments since they were not parties to the contract of carriage be-tween the plaintiff and defendant No.2. 

7. The learned Subordinate Judge after framing appropriate issues and hearing the suits decreed them in full. These four appeals have been filed by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 Bangladesh Biman and Air India International respectively two appeals by each of them against the decrees in two suits. 

8. Mr. S. M. Nurul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant No 1 in F. A No. 71 and 71 of 1976 has submitted that the trial court committed wrong in holding that Bangladesh Biman as agent of the Air India International was responsible for the loss of 43 cartons out of the two consignments inasmuch as that the two consignments reached Dacca Airport and was placed in the custody of air freight unit of customs at Dacca Airport by the defendant No. 1. According to Mr. Alam, the possession and control of the consignments having been given to the customs authorities at Dacca Airport in fact and under law as well, the defendant No. 1 is not responsible for loss of the cartons out of the two consignments imported by the plaintiff. According to Mr. Nurul Alam, Bangladesh Biman was merely a ground handling agent of defendant No. 2 Air India International who carried the consignments from U.S.A. to Dacca. He has further submitted that under law in accordance. with the provisions of section 74 of Customs Act, 1969, Bangladesh Biman Ole defendant No. 1) had no control and possession over the consignment and the customs unit at the Airport was the custodian of the consignments as soon as those arrived and landed at Dacca Airport and that the responsibility for the loss of the cartons ought to have been held by the learned Subordinate Judge to be upon the customs authorities. Elaborating his point the learned Advocate for defendant No. 1 has submitted that in view of the provisions of sections 42, 64, 6, 6, 74 of the Customs Act, 1969, the responsibility for the losses cannot be placed upon the defendant No. 1. He has strenuously submitted that under Customs Act, 1969 possession of the imported cargo passed on to the Customs authorities as soon as these were landed at Dacca Airport, and the consignments cannot be kept in the custody of Bangladesh Biman. He has submitted that there is no evidence that Bangladesh Biman was given permission to take the goods into their custody. According to him the evidence adduced by the customs authorities that the custody of the consignments were never with them cannot displace their legal possession of the consignments after those were landed at Dacca Airport and off-loaded from the aircraft. The possession and control of the consignments passed on to the customs authorities who gave sanction for delivery after they completed several formalities for clearance of the consignments. He has next submitted that defendant No. 1 being admittedly an agent of defendant No. 2 and the principal having been impleaded in the suit no decree can be passed for loss of the cartons against the agent. In this connection he has also submitted that at the trial the defendant No. 2 made no allegation of misconduct or negligence on the part of defendant No. 1 and hence no decree ought to have been passed against them. 

9. Mr. Hafizullah the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of defendant No. 2 in F.A. Nos. 89 and 90 of 1976 has submitted that the carrier having delivered the consignments in full to defendant No. 1 they have no responsibility for loss of 37 cartons out of them. He has also submitted that the carrier having fully landed the goods and made them over to their agent, the defendant No. 1, they cannot be held liable for the alleged loss of the cartons. The liability for the alleged loss ought to have been held by the learned Subordinate Judge to be the personal liability of the agent. He however has supported the contention of Mr. Nurul Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of defendant No. I that the customs authorities were in control of the consignments after those were landed in Dacca Airport. He nonetheless submitted that they delivered the consignments to defendant No. 1 their local agent and as such in any view they cannot be held liable for the alleged loss of the cartons. He has: also submitted that the suit was bad for absence of proper notice of claim under section 26 of carriage by Air (International Convenlim) Act, 1966. 

10. It is not in dispute that two consignments of drugs and medicines were imported by the plaintiff from U.S.A. The first consignment comprises of 27 cartons and the second consignments comprises of 30 cartons. The loss of 25 cartoons out of the first consignment and 12 cartons out of second consignment is not in dispute. Only two cartons out of the 1st consignment was delivered to the plaintiff on 2.2.73 and 12 cartons out of second consignment were delivered on 10.2.73. The loss and short delivery of the consignments were endorsed on the import applications. The plaintiff claimed Taka 36,480f- in Money Suit No. 27 of 1973 for loss of 25 cartons of medicines and drugs and Taka 21,150/- in Money Suit No. 28 of 1973 for loss of 12 cartons of 'drugs and medicines. The plaintiff has claimed these compensations on the basis of market value of the drugs and medicines short delivered to them. It is in evidence and not disputed by defendant No. 1 that they handled the consignments. It is in their written statements that “the consignment was duly offloaded by this defendant and the same was given to customs airfreight unit at the Airport ". They have also stated in the written statement that the consignments were kept in Airfreight Apron as directed by the customs authority and under the charge of Airport Manager. It is also in evidence of D.W. 1 for defendant No. 1 that Bangladesh Biman is the agent of Air India and they offloaded the consignments and those were taken to the customs. On the question of custody and delivery of the consignments P.W.1 the Manager of the plaintiff has stated that they approached Bangladesh Biman (defendant No. 1) for clearance of the goods but they were given delivery of 2 cartons out of 27 cartons of first consignment and 12 cartons out of 30 cartons of the second consignment. It is in his evidence that the plaintiff approached Bangladesh Biman for the remaining cartons but they were not given the same though the defendant No. 1 asked them to 'come later on and that they approached defendant No. 2 several times for the remaining cartons but without any result. P.W.I further stated that the plaintiff lodged complaints to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 for loss of the cartons but they repudiated their claims and did not settle it. In cross-examination by the defendant No. 1 this witness denied the suggestion that Bangladesh Biman did not make delivery of the cartons to them. This witness also denied in cross-examination that the goods were delivered to them by the customs or that the customs authority in turn received the goods from the defendant No. 1 and kept them in their custody. He asserted in his evidence that the goods were kept in the custody of defendant No. 1. D.W.I deposing for defendant No. 1 Bangladesh Biman has deposed that the consignments were off-loaded and were given to the customs unit at Dacca Airport and that the goods were kept on the airport apron on the direction of the customs authorities. This witness denied that the goods were kept in their custody and the delivery was made by them. This witness, however, stated that they were the agents of defendant No. 2 for the purpose of unloading' and to make over the consignments to the customs unit at the Airport. In cross-examination he, however, could not show anything on paper that the defendant No. 1 after offloading the consignments gave them to the customs unit at the Airport. D.W.2 on behalf of the defendant No. 2 has stated that defendant No. 1 is their grounds-handling agent and that after offloading the consignments those were handed over to the customs unit at the Airport. In this connection, it may mentioned that in the written statements defendant No. 2 has stated that they handed over the consignments to defendant No. 1 and the customs authorities. In cross-examination this witness stated that the responsibility of the defendant No. 1 as agent of defendant No. 2 is loading and unloading and delivery through" customs unit at the Airport. D.W. 3 on behalf of defendant No. 4, the Collector of Customs, has stated that the goods were never given to their custody and they did not receive the consignments. They assessed duties on papers and afterwards checked the goods as to whether the goods were correct in terms of the documents. They denied their responsibility for loss of cartons. 

11. The defendant No. 1 and 2 have produced oral evidence to assert that the consignments were given to the customs authorities who kept them in their custody but there is no evidence on paper that after offloading of the consignments by defendant No. 1, those were handed over to defendant No. 5, the customs Airfreight at Dacca Airport. It is in evidence that defendant No. 1 offloaded the consignments on different dates. The defendant No. 2 has stated in their written statements and in their evidence that the goods were unloaded by defendant No. 1. It is stated in paragraph 10 of the written statements of defendant No. 2 that they handed over the goods to defendant No. 1 an d to customs unit at the Airports. There is no further evidence from' the side of defendant No. l excepting 'their oral assertion that the consignments were actually given to the custody of the customs unit at the Airport. It also appears from the two letter s, Ext. 14 and 15 (Kha) from the defendan t No. 1 addressed to defendant No. 2, that the customs A.F.U. refused to accept e import cargo as they had no adequate warehousing facilities, and consequently international cargo was piled up on the apron in. front of their cargo area and that the responsibility of looking after this cargo was as matter of fact upon them for which they were not prepared. From this evidence it is clear that the customs authorities at Dacca' Airport never accepted consignments for keeping them in their custody Mr. Nurul Main on the other hand has sub-mitted that the custody of the consignments were with the customs authorities as per endorsement in Exts. 6 and 6 kha the import applications to show that the goods were in custody of the customs. He has referred to the endorsements made in those applications by an officer on 2.2.73 and 10.2.73 td show that the goods were not in their custody. These two endorsements dated 2.2.73 and 10.2.73 do not show that the goods were kept in the custody of the Customs though these endorsements no doubt appear to be by certain customs officials. From both .the endorsements it appear that the consignee produced two cartons on. 2.2. 73 and 12 cartons on 10.2.73 for exanimation by the customs officials. From these endorsements it does not appear that the consignments wens kept in the custody of the Customs. On consideration of evidence adduced by the parties we are of the view that the consignments were not handed over to the customs unit at Dacca Airport and that physical possession and custody of the consignments remained with the defendant No. 1, the agent of defendant No. 2. 

12. Mr. Nurul Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant appellant has next submitted that under law the custody of the consignments passed on to the customs unit of the Airport who were in legal control and custody of them. He has referred to the provisions of section 74 of the Customs Act, 1969, which runs as follows:-
"74. Discharge of goods by conveyance other than vessels: when on arrival of a conveyance other than a vessel at a land customs-station or customs-airport the person-in-charge of such conveyance has delivered the import manifest under section 44 and the documents required under section 48, he shall forthwith take the conveyance or cause it to be taken to the examination station at the land customs-station or customs-airport and remove or cause to be removed all good carried in such conveyance to the customs-house in the presence of the appropriate officer or some person duly authorised by him in that behalf".
It is true that on arrival of the imported cargo at the Airport, it is to be offloaded in presence of the customs and removed to the customs house at the airport. The aforesaid provisions relate to the control and/or removal of the goods to the customs house for customs purposes. But the provisions of Customs Act, 1969, however, create no legal obligation on the part of the customs authority to keep all the imported cargo in their custody at the Airport until delivery is effected after completion of customs formalities. There is no provision in law that the possession and custody of imported goods pass on to the customs authority after their off-loading from an Aircraft. The customs authorities as observed earlier exercise control over movement of the imported goods until these are cleared after completion of customs formalities, and that clearance of goods for home consumption must be made upon an order of clearance by the customs authority. So in view of this legal position it cannot be said that the legal custody of the consignments passed on to the customs authorities after those were landed at Dacca airport. We have already found on evidence that the consignments were not given to the customs authorities and the custody of the consignments was never with them. In view of this finding the defendant No. 1 as agent of defendant No. 2 became responsible for the goods till its delivery to the 'consignee and is also liable for loss of the cartons from their custody. 

13. Rule 18 of Carriage. By Air (International Convention) Act IX of 1966 creates initial statutory liability upon the carrier in case of loss of goods during the carriage which includes the period during which the goods are in charge of the carrier. To appreciate the provisions of the Rule it is set out below:—
"18—(l) The carrier is liable for damage sustained in the event of the destruction or loss of, or of damage to, any registered luggage or any goods, if the occurrence which caused the damage so sustained took place during the carriage by air. 
(2) The carriage by air within the meaning of the preceding sub-rule comprises the period during which the luggage or goods are in charge of the carrier, whether in an aerodrome or on board an aircraft or in the case of a landing outside an aerodrome, in any place whatsoever.
From a reading of the provisions of the aforesaid Rule we are of the view that the carrier is prima facie liable for loss of goods if the loss took place during the carriage, and that the period of carriage comprises the period during which the goods are in charge of the carrier. The delivery of the consignments in the instant case to the defendant No. 1, the agent of the carrier, is no delivery to the consignee. Hence both the carrier and their agent are liable for the loss of the cartons as baileys. It has been argued by the learned Advocate for the defendant No. 1 that since their principal, the defendant No. 2 has not made any allegations of negligence and misconduct they cannot be held liable for loss of the cartons. D.W. 2 on behalf of defendant No. 2 has deposed that the consignments were made over by the defendant No. 1 to the customs. We have held that the cartons were lost while those were in custody of the defendant No. 1. In view of the loss of the cartons initial liability for the loss lies upon the carrier and its agent and a presumption of negligence has arisen therefor. Nothing has been shown by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 to rebut the presumptions. On the contrary, defendant Nos. 1 and 2 have pleaded that the consignments were in custody of the customs or rather they disowned its custody. Hence there is ho scope of pleading that the carrier or its agent took all precautions to protect the consignments as a prudent man until its delivery to the consignee. 

14. Mr. Hafizullah, the learned Advocate on behzrf of defendant No. 2 appellant, has submitted that his client, Air India Inter-national has no liability after the goods were off-loaded or landed at Dacca Airport in good order and condition. He has submitted that the carrier incurs no liability after it has handed over the consignments to defendant No. 1. He has submitted that after the contract of affreighment ended the carrier cannot be held liable. In our view after the contract of affreighment ends on offloading of the consignment the carrier incurs a new liability as a bailee or an involuntary warehouseman, if the goods continue to remain in its custody or in the custody of its agent and that the carrier or its agent is bound to take reasonable care of the goods. This view finds support in the case of Abdur Rahman Abdul Gani vs. Mackennonl Mackenzie & Co & another. (1) In this view and on consideration of the evidence on record we hold that defendant No. 1 and 2 are liable for loss of the cartons out of the two consignments and they are liable to pay compensation therefor, and the learned Subordinate Judge rightly found that the carrier and its agent are responsible for the loss. 

15. With regard to the objection as to the defect in the notice sent by the plaintiff before filing of the suit, it appears to us that provisions under section 26 of Carriage by Air (International Convention) Act IX of 1966 do not apply to loss of cargo and short delivery of the same by the carrier or his agent to the consignee. Rule 26 lays down that in case of damage of goods complaint to they carrier for recovery of such damage must be made normally with. 14 days from the date of receipt of the goods and in case of delay of delivery of the goods the complaint is to be made within 21 days from the date on which the goods were placed at the disposal of the consignee. From a reading of the provisions of Rules 18,22 and 26 we are of the view that words 'loss' and 'damage' have been distinctly used and meant in the aforesaid Act to convey different meanings. The meaning of the word damage in Rule 26 distinguished from the word 'loss' used in Rules 18 and 22 would mean harm or injury to goods as such and not damage by loss of goods. This interpretation appears to be harmonious and compatibles with the other relevant provisions of the Act. Conceding that the provisions of Rule 26 are applicable, it also appears that notice of loss of cartons having been made within 21 days, the suit cannot be held to be bad on account of defect in the notices (Exts. 1 and 1 (ka)) of complaint of such loss. We, therefore, find no substance in the contentions of the learned Advocate for the appellant on this ground. On the question of the liability of the defendant No. 1 as agent of defendant No. 2 Mr. Nurul Alain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant No. 1 appellant has submitted that the principal having been impleaded in the suit the agent cannot be held liable for the alleged loss of the cartons. In the facts and circumstances of the cases it has been found that the consignments were in custody of defendant No. 1, the agent of defendant No. 2. Once the custody of the consignments have been proved to the with the defendant No. 1 the carrier as well as their agent are liable for loss of the cartons since the carrier and its agent has failed to displace the presumptions of negligence and to prove how the consignments were dealt with after their landing at Dacca Airport. We have already observed that Rule 18 has created an initial statutory liability for loss of, the consignments from the Airport which could be rebutted by them. In our considered view there is no escape from the conclusion that the defendant Nos. 2 and 1 are both responsible as carrier and its agent respectively for loss of the cartons and the learned Subordinate Judge rightly decreed the suits against them. The decisions refer-red to by the learned Advocate for the defendant No. 1, reported in 19 D.L.R. page 75 and 21 D.L.R. (S.C.). 245 are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. 

16. For the reasons stated herein above, we do not find any substance in these appeals. These four appeals are, accordingly, dismissed. The judgment and decree passed by the learned trial court are affirmed. In view of the facts of this case we award one set of costs to the plaintiff to be borne equally by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. 

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 30-6-2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos.2178 and 2179 of 1991)
full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: The litigation relates to a property which belonged to one Paresh Nath Dey, defendant No. 1, (the defendant) who is said to have entered into an agreement for sale of the same with late Hasan Ali Driver, the predecessor-in-interest of the appellants on 15th January, 1964. Paresh Chandra Nath subsequently instituted Money Suit No. 6 of 1965 against Hasan Ali Driver in respect of the same property claiming him as tenant for recovery of arrear rents. According to the plaintiffs, the defendant Paresh filed a compromise petition on 7th June, 1971 with Hasan Ali Driver in the suit acknowledging the previous contract and agreed to execute a sale deed. The suit was accordingly dismissed on the basis of compromise and thereafter, as the defendant Paresh did not execute the sale deed as promised, the plaintiffs instituted the suit for specific performance against the defendant treating the compromise petition as novation of the contract.

2. Defendant Nos.  3 and 4 (the contesting defendants) after being added at their instance contested the suit. Their claim is that the defendant Paresh entered into an oral agreement with their father on 7th February, 1962 in respect of the suit property and subsequently the agreement was reduced into writing on 25th April, 1970 and possession was delivered to them. Thereafter as the defendant Paresh did not execute the sale deed, they instituted Title Suit No. 73 of 1971 for specific performance, in which, the defendant Paresh filed a solenama on 2nd August, 1971 and the suit was accordingly decreed on compromise and got the sale deed executed and registered through court on 22nd October, 1971. They are bonafide purchasers for value without notice to the plaintiffs contract and that the defendant Paresh having no subsisting interest in the suit property, the suit for specific performance is not maintain-able against them.

3. The trial court decreed the suit against the contesting defendants and ex-parte against the defendant Paresh directing them to execute and register a sale deed. On appeal by these contesting defendants, the court of appeal below modified decree of the trial court and decreed the suit in respect of 8 annas, 9 gandas, 2 karas and 6 krantis share excluding the share of the defendant Nos. 5-8, who are also the heirs of Hasan All Driver and directed the defendants including Paresh to execute and register the sale deed in respect of the plaintiffs share out of the suit property. Defendant Nos. 3 and 4 thereafter took a revision petition in the High Court Division. A Single Bench of the High Court Division set-aside the judgments of the courts below and dismissed the suit. Plaintiffs thereupon obtained leave from this Division.

4. It was urged on behalf of the appellants that the High Court Division exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the courts below without reversing the findings of facts, such as, the genuineness of the plaintiffs agreement dated 5th January, 1965 and the delivery of possession of the property pursuant to such agreement in favour of their predecessor and that the High Court Division erred in considering an inadmissible evidence, exhibit-M, a written statement filed by Hasan Ali Driver in the earlier suit admitting that he had entered into a portion of the suit property as tenant under the defendant Paresh.

5. The basis of the plaintiffs claim is the compromise petition filed by their predecessor with Paresh Nath Dey in Money Suit No. 3 of 1964 on 7th June, 1971 admitting the execution of the contract for sale earlier in January, 1964 and that as per terms of the solenama, the defendant Paresh received Taka 2,000 towards the consideration money and promised to execute a sale deed within 1(one) month from date. The court of appeal below believed the plain-tiffs claim for specific performance of the subsequent contract holding that the trial court on a proper appreciation of the materials on record rightly believed that there was novation of the contract and payment of balance consideration money and that there was no cogent ground to interfere with the same. The court of appeal below though suspected the claim of the con-testing defendants that Paresh Nath filed solenama in their suit for specific performance on the reasoning that it was not a believable story that a member of Hindu community would file solenama during the war of liberation, on the other breath, believed the plaintiffs claim of filing solenama by Paresh Nath during the same period in his suit. The court of appeal also found that the contesting defendants got possession on 25th April, 1970. This finding negates the earlier finding of the court of appeal below. The court of appeal below apparently made self contradictory findings. If the contesting defendants did not get possession on the basis of the contract, then how they, got possession in respect of a portion of the suit property is not clear to us- the plaintiffs did not give any explanation in this regard. Taking these facts into consideration the question is whether the findings of the court of appeal below have been legally interfered with by the High Court Division exercising its revisional jurisdiction.

6. Mr Mahmudul Islam, while supporting the judgment of the High Court Division argued that the defendant Paresh having instituted Money Suit No. 3 of 1969 claiming Hasan All Driver as his tenant and disputing the alleged execution of contract for sale on 15th January, 1964 and since Hasan Ali Driver had filed written statement in that suit on 22nd August, 1965, he had notice that the performance of the contract was refused by Paresh Nath and therefore, the suit for specific performance for enforcement of the original contract said to have been executed in 1964 having not been filed within 3 years of refusal, the said contract was barred by operation of law. Mr Mahmudul Islam contended that Hasan Ali Driver had constructive knowledge about the refusal by Paresh Nath to execute the sale deed in pursuance of the contract. In the facts of the given case there cannot be novation of the contract which will be enforceable by law. Mr Islam added that the limitation for filing the suit for specific performance reckoned on 12th August, 1965, if there be any, and his claim was barred by operation of law on 12th August, 1969. I find force in the contention of the learned counsel.

7. The determination of the question raised on behalf of the plaintiffs as to whether the High Court Division has exceeded its revisional jurisdiction depends upon the construction of the novation of the contract which was said to have been executed by the parties in the money suit by filing a compromise petition. This, in my opinion, is a pure question of law for the plaintiffs are seeking specific performance on the basis of the subsequent contract in continuation of the previous contract as will be evident from their pleadings. The courts below while decreeing the suit did not consider a vital question as to whether this new contract is legally enforceable against the contesting defendants in view of plea taken in their pleadings that Paresh Nath had refused to perform claiming that the first contract was forged by filing money suit in 1965 against Hasan Ali Driver claiming him as tenant under him in respect of a portion of the suit property and this refusal constituted the cause of action for filing suit for specific performance but he did not file suit within three years of such refusal. In the context of the matter, the High Court Division held that the question of novation did not arise in this case since the previous contract executed in 1964 was evidently barred by limitation in 1969, inasmuch as, Hasan Ali Driver had constructive knowledge about the refusal. After the expiry' of three years, there was no enforceability of the previous contract as being barred by law, the High Court Division observed, the question of novation of the said contract in 1971 did not arise at all.

8. As regards possession, the High Court Division held that Hasan Ali Driver having admitted that he had entered into a portion of the suit property as tenant, the court of appeal below erred in law in believing the plaintiffs possession in pursuance of the execution of the deed of contract. This finding is absolutely correct and I find no cogent ground to differ with such finding. More so, as observed, above, the court of appeal below also found the possession of the contesting defendants in a portion of the suit property. This possession supports their claim that they got possession in pursuance of the contract. As regards the plaintiffs claim of novation of the contract, the High Court Division rightly held that it is not a believable story that a member of Hindu Community would file compromise petition with Hasan Ali Driver during the period of war of liberation in June, 1971, and that too, in his suit for recovery of the arrear of rents.

9. Similarly the claim of the defendants that they got compromise decree against Paresh Nath Dey during the period of war of liberation is also doubtful. But then, the fact, remains, rightly or wrongly, they got a decree in a suit for specific performance and the said decree was acted upon and the said decree has not been challenged by any one till now. The High Court Division has further held that the manner of execution of the novation of contract as claimed by the plaintiffs has created doubt about the existence of a genuine contract and that the plaintiffs have failed to prove the filing of solenama, the part payment of the consideration money and the delivery of possession pursuant to the novation of the contract. The High Court Division further held that in view of the dubious conduct of the plaintiffs predecessor, they are not entitled to a discretionary relief for specific performance since they have not come in court with clean hands. The High Court Division has also noticed section 62 of the Contract Act and has held that the plaintiffs claim for novation of the contract is contrary to law, inasmuch as the previous contract having been barred by limitation, the question of novation does not arise at all.

<u>10. This section appears in Chapter under the heading "contracts which need not be performed" Section 62 provides that "if the parties to a contract agree to substitute a new contract for it, or to rescind or alter, the original contract need not be performed". When a party seeks relief for specific performance of the novation of contract, the Court is required to consider section 62 and to examine whether or not there was really existence of the novation of contract. The courts below though held that there was novation of contract but totally ignored the question as to whether in the facts of the given case, there was novation of the contract which could be enforceable against the contesting defendants. The courts below presumed that in view of submission of solenama in the money suit filed by Paresh Nath as claimed by the plaintiffs, there was novation of contract which was acknowledged by Paresh Nath by filing a solenama.</u>

11. The question of novation arises if there is existence of a subsisting enforceable contract between the parties. In terms of the law, a new contract is substituted for it, the consideration mutually being the discharge of the old contract Novation is a substitution of a contract which rescinded or extinguished the previous contract.

In this connection Mr Mahmudul Islam has referred the case of Vishram Arjun vs Irukulla Shankariah, AIR 1957 Andra Pradesh 784. In that case it was observed "Substitution of a new contract is the core of novation. It's essential feature is that a right under the original contract is relinquished and new rights referable to new contract are created. The substituted con-tract therefore must be a valid and enforceable contract to be effective as-novation'. If the new agreement or contract suffers from legal flaw such as want of registration, stamps etc., on account of which it becomes unenforceable, the original contract will not be extinguished and the rights and liabilities of the parties will be determined on that basis."

12. Similar views have been taken in the State of Bihar vs Ram Ballabh Das Jalan, AIR 1960 Patna, 400. It was observed "ordinarily under the common law novation is brought about by introduction of new parties or alteration between the same parties by introduction of new terms. It is not consistent with the original debtor remaining liable in any form on the terms of the old contract. The right against the original debtor on such contract must be extinguished and there must be present substitution of another contract for the original contract."

13. Novation would occur when the contract is rescinded or extinguished the previous contract, such that the terms of "the two contracts should be so inconsistent that they cannot stand together or render it impossible the performance of the performer. In Lata Construction vs Dr Rameshchandra Ramniklal Shah, AIR 2000 SC 380, it was observed "One of the essential requirements of 'novation'; as contemplated by section 62 is that there should be complete substitution of a new contract in place of the old. It is in that situation that the original contract need not be performed. Substitution of a new contract in place of the old contract which would have the effect of rescinding or completely altering the terms of the original contract, has to be by agreement between the parties. A substituted contract should rescind or alter or extinguish the previous contract. But if the terms of the two contracts are inconsistent and they cannot stand together, the subsequent contract cannot be said to be in substitution of the earlier contract".

<u>14. After execution of a new contract, this substituted contract gives new cause of action and obligates the earlier ones. If there is no intention to rescind the prior contract altogether, there is no substitution and the original con-tract is still enforceable but this is not the case of the plaintiffs. Their case is that by filing solenama the parties have entered into a fresh contract and as per terms of the contract, the plaintiffs paid Tk. 2,000. On the other hand, the definite case of the contesting defendants is that they had entered into a written contract with Paresh Nath on 25th April, 1970. So apparently the execution of the defendants contract is prior to the date of plaintiffs contract said to have been executed on 7th June, 1971. If that be the position, the said contract is not enforceable against the contesting defendants in view of section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act. Learned counsel for the plaintiffs failed to meet those findings rather finds it difficult to assail those findings. The Court of appeal below has not diverted its attention in that regard.</u>

15. This provision provides, except as otherwise provided by this chapter, Specific Performance of a Contract may been forced against "(b) any other person claiming under him by a title arising subsequently to the contract, except a transferee for value who has. paid his money in good faith and without notice to the original contract". So a plaintiff may seek a decree for specific performance against a subsequent purchaser if he claims title, 'arising subsequently to the contract but he is not entitled to a decree against a transferee who is a bonafide purchaser without notice to the original contract. Similarly, he is not entitled to a decree for specific performance against a person who has acquired right or interest in respect of the same property prior to the contract. Though the plaintiffs claimed that the present defendants are subsequent purchasers with prior notice of the plaintiff's contract but they failed to substantiate their claim in view of the fact that the contesting defendants got a decree in pursuance of their contract which was earlier in point of time.

16. In Abdul Huq vs Yehia Khan, AIR 1924 Patna 81, an agreement was executed on 24thAugust, 1916 and the suit was filed on 25th September, 1916. The defendant Nos. 1-4 sold the properties to defendant No. 7 who was thereafter added as a party in the suit. The trial Court found that there was a valid pre-existing contract and that the defendant. No. 7 purchased the property with notice to the prior contract but was of opinion that the defendant No. 7 as co-sharer had a right of pre-emption. The trial court declined to give the plaintiff a decree for Specific Performance of Contract. On construction of section 27(b), the Patna High Court held that the operation of section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act is confined to cases where the contracts are in the first instance enforceable as against the parties to the contract. The liability of a person claiming under a party to the contract rests upon the antecedent liability of a party to the contract and arises by reason of the fact that as transferee he takes subject to the transferor's preexisting contractual obligation; and where there is no pre-existing contractual obligation, it seems that the case entirely fails as against the transferee. The plaintiff cannot enforce a contract as against a transferee unless the transferee has notice of the original contract. The notice of the original contract must mean notice of an existing obligation under the contract; and where the contract is itself unenforceable; it seems that it is impossible to maintain the view that the contract can be enforced as against a subsequent transferee.

17. In Samptram vs Bawo Lal, AIR 1955 Allahabad 24, there was an agreement for sale on 25th June, 1952. On 17th July, 1952 the owner entered into an another contract with the plaintiff Bawo Lal to sell the same property. On 25th September, 1952 the owner executed a sale deed in favour of Sampathram and Ram Gopal, the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 and thereafter the plaintiffs filed the suit on 26th September, 1952. The suit was decreed by the trial Court. On appeal from the said judgment by Sampathram, the Allahabad High Court held the agreement in favour of "Sampathram and Ram Gopal being of a prior date namely 25-6-1952 the plaintiff can claim no equities against Sampathram or Ram Gopal and cannot, therefore, enforce his agreement of a subsequent date as against".

The Allahabad High Court took notice of section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act and refused to maintain the decree for specific performance.

18. There is no doubt that the earlier contract executed by Hasan Ali Driver with Paresh Nath was barred by operation of law and therefore, legally there could not be novation of the said contract since the previous contract was unenforceable on the alleged date of novation. The second contract was said to have been executed after the execution of the contesting defendant's contract on 25th April, 1970. In view of the above admitted position, the plaintiffs are not legally entitled to a decree for specific performance against the contesting defendants. In view of the above the High Court Division legally interfered with the judgments of the courts below on a proper construction of section 62.

19. The submission that the High Court Division exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact is devoid of substance. The courts below have not adverted to the legal aspects of the matter and upon superficial consideration of the materials on record decreed the suit. The second contract was not enforceable against the contesting defendants. The courts below fell in an error in decreeing the suit for specific performance.

20. The High Court Division also considered exhibit-2A, the compromise petition filed in Money Suit No. 3 of 1969 and rightly held "evidently it plaintiffs agreement was executed after the defendant's deed of agreement. So, the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 get preference, even if both the agreement are considered genuine". The plaintiffs contract is not legally enforceable against the contesting defendants in view of section 21(b) of the Specific Relief Act. Thus we find no merit in the contention of Mr TR Khan that since the defendants are claiming title to the suit property subsequent to the plaintiffs contract, the onus, lies upon them to prove that they are not bonafide purchasers for value without notice to the previous contract. We do not dispute the statement of law argued in Zulfikar Mahmud vs National University and others, 60 DLR (AD) 40 referred by Mr Khan.

<u>21. The plaintiffs are claiming specific performance on the basis of the contract which was executed subsequently. There is no doubt that whoever claims or has taken a plea that he is a subsequent purchaser of the property without notice to the previous contract for sale, the onus lies upon him to prove such fact. Mere denial in the written statement that he has no notice of the previous contract will not defeat the decree for specific performance. Mr Khan has failed to notice that the plaintiffs claim is not founded on the contract said to have been executed on 15th January, 1964. Even if they claimed that there was a prior contract that contract did not exist by reason of Hasan Ali Driver's knowledge about the refusal by Paresh Nath Dey to honour the contract. He had constructive knowledge about the refusal by the defendant in December, 1965.</u>

22. Therefore, even if it is assumed that there was a contract the said contract ceased to exist by operation of law. Therefore, the plaintiffs claim that their contract is earlier than that of the defendant has no basis at all. Their contract is barred in view of refusal by Paresh Nath. The High Court Division, in the premises, is perfectly justified in holding that the plaintiffs are not legally entitled to a decree for specific performance of contract. There is no merit in these appeals.

23. The appeals are, therefore, dismissed without, however, no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
B.K. Das, Advocate ----- for appellant 
A. Hasib with Mokhtar Hossain, Advocate ----- for respondent
parties:
Abdul Mujib Chowdhury
Vs.
