Syed Abdul Mutalib & Others
full_judgment:
M. H. Rahman, J.:- This appeal is directed against the judgment of the court of appeal below decreeing the plaintiff's suit for partition in preliminary form. The plaintiffs' case is that they purchased /10/- annas share of the suit land on 25.5.1963 and the defendant purchased the remaining share subsequently on 7.6.63. Joint possession was given to the plaintiffs and the defendant. It was stipulated that the defendant would enjoy their share in the southern part and the plaintiff’s would enjoy their share in the southern portion. There was a misguiding stipulation in the purchase-document to the effect that plaintiffs would get 30 cubits from the north in their /10/- annas share and the defendant would get/6/- annas share in the north without specifying dimensions in cubits. This was done by the defendant on whom the plaintiffs relied for negotiation, execution and registration of the kabala. When the defendant demanded specific possession of his share in the northern side the plaintiffs could not agree to the demand as the southern side of the 1st schedule land was far less in area and dimension than the northern side. Thereafter the defendant brought Title Suit No. 339 of 1964 in the 1st Court of Sadar, Munsif, Sylhet. On transfer to the Additional Court of the Munsif the suit was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 74 of 1965. The defendant got an ex-parte decree for specific possession in accordance with the description given by him in that suit. There was a rehearing of the matter and the suit was restored to its original file and number. The plaintiffs had two tenants, Israil Ali and Syed Mahibul Islam, in their northern rooms. As plaintiff No. 1 was in Karachi his mother, plaintiff' No. 2, used to depend on Syed Mahibul Islam. Defendant No. 1 in collusion with Syed Mahibul Islam filed a solenama purported to have been executed by plaintiff No. 2 and by his two tenants though in fact neither plaintiff No. 2 nor Israel All executed the same. The plaintiffs further contended that they did not empower their lawyer to execute the Solenama. The Compromise decree was put to execution in Title Execution Case No. 7 of 1967 in the 1st Munsif Court, Sylhet. When the defendant was about take delivery of possession through a lawyer Commissioner plaintiff No. 2 brought Title Suit No. 122 of 1967 for a declaration that the alleged compromise decree was null and void, but the suit was dismissed on 31.8.67. Thereafter the defendant proceeded with the execution case and got delivery of possession on 8.9.67 in the northern portion of the suit premises in excess of his due share. Thereafter the plaintiffs demanded on 6.1.63 partition of the suit property by metes and bounds, but the defendant did not agree.

2. The defendant contested the suit denying the material allegations in the plaint. He contended that the suit was not maintainable and it was barred by estoppel, waiver acquiescence and under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It was also asserted the suit was hit by the final decision of Title Suit No. 74 of 1965 and Title Suit No. 122 of 1967 and that plaintiffs could not got any decree without setting aside the decree passed in the former title suit No. 74 of 1965 on the basis of which of the delivery of possession was obtained through court. Further case of the defendant is that the plaintiffs purchased specific land in the southern portion denoted by specific measurement, leaving out the land to the north, and as the plaintiffs purchased earlier the question of joint possession did not arise. Besides, Title Suit No. 314 of 1965 filed by the plaintiff was allowed to be dismissed for non-prosecution; and that the appeal against the decree of dismissal of Title Suit No. 122 of 1967 was also dismissed.

3. The trial court found that before the Advocate Commissioner both sides were found to-have admitted the southern boundary of the suit holding to be the pucca wall of the jail quarters but at a later stage, Syed Abdul Marine, the husband of plaintiff No. 2 appeared to have contended that the southern boundary of the holding to be a pillarover 2-3/4 cubits to the north of the pucca wall. The learned Advocate Commissioner accepted the pucca wall as the southern boundary of the suit holding. The trial court noticed that the plaintiffs filed Misc. Case No. 27 of 1967 under section 47 of the Code, but the same was dismissed for non-prosecution on 28.10.67. It observed that plaintiffs and defendants purchased some-specific share of the suit holding described by boundaries, and measured in terms of cubits, and what-ever ambiguity there was about it was set at rest by the subsequent litigations between the parties. Hence it was held that plaintiffs suit was barred by res judicata under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and estoppel, acquiescence and waiver. The trial court also held that the plaintiffs and defendant were not co-sharers in the suit holding as they purchased specific separate share in the land and as they were in exclusive possession of their respective shares.

4. The court of appeal below reversed the decision of the trial court and decreed the suit in preliminary form. It found that the suit was not hit by res judicata as the question of partition was not a point at issue in Title Suit No 74 of 1965. It held that plaintiffs and the defendant intended to purchase /10/-annas and -6/- annas share and there was no evidence on record that there were actual measurements at the time of incorporating the stipulation as to measurement by cubits in the schedules to the respective kabalas. The court of appeal below found that the stipulations were incorporated in the documents for convenience of possession of the parties without intending any final partition.

5. Mr. B.K. Das, the learned Advocate for the appellants, has not challenged the appellate court's finding that the suit was not barred by resjudicata. He has, however, conceded that the suit was hit under section 47 of the Code. Mr. Das has also urged that as by the Solenama the defendant gave up his claim of Rs. 1000/- against the present plaintiffs the latter's subsequent suit ought to be held as barred by estoppel as the defendant acted to his detriment by the terms of the solenama.

6. Mr. Das has relied on Amir Uddln v. Mr. Khairi and another (1) and Rajendra Prassad and others v. Jai Prakash Pandey and others (2) and Syed All Mridha v. Hamfda Khatoon & others, (3)

7. In all the three cases there was a compromise between the parties to the suit and the decree was passed in terms of the com-promise and put to execution.

8. Title suit No. 74 of 1965 between the plaintiffs and the defendant and others were concluded by the compromise by which the parties admitted their respective title and agreed to demarcate their respective shares in the properties in question and the compromise was put to execution: In A.I.R. 1928, Lahore, 938, it was held that where in the execution of a decree possession was alleged to have been given in a property not covered by the decree the suit for recovery of the excess land was barred under section 47 of the Code, and the appropriate remedy to recover the ex-ecess property was by way of an application under section 47. In A. I. R. 1957 (Patna) 700, where the plaintiffs' property was wrongly sold in execution it was held that the suit for declaration of title and delivery of possession with regard to the land wrongly sold in execution was barred under section 47. In 26 D.L.R. 279, a contractual obligation created on the basis of a solenama was considered as a question of adjustment within the meaning of section 47 of the Code and a separate suit for specific performance of that obligation was held to be hit by section 47. In that case on the prayer of the plaintiff appellants the matter was remanded to the trial court and the plaint filed in the suit was directed to be treated as an application under section 47.

<u>9. It appears that there was no clear evidence that plaintiffs and defendant were given distinct possession in the suit property by the vender. The descriptions as to the respective shares of the plaintiff and the defendant and as to measurement of the land caused misgivings in the minds of the parties. The series of litigations between the parties were ultimately concluded by the compromise decree. After execution of the compromise decree it is clear that the suit property ceased to be a partible property and the suit for partition was not available to the plaintiffs. Again as the defendants gave up Rs. 1000/- as consideration for the compromise the present suit which is in effect directed against that compromise must be held as hit by the principle of estoppel.</u>

10. It appears from the plaint that the cause of action arose on 8.9.67 when the defendants got delivery of possession.

<u>11. There is no doubt that the plaintiffs' grievance that the defendant get more land than his due share arose from the execution of the compromise decree and any prayer for correction or adjustment of the execution of the decree should determined by the executing court and not by way of a separate suit. Finding his difficulties Mr. Hasib the learned Advocate for the respondent has prayed that the plaint should be converted into an application under section 47 of the Code and be sent down for disposal by the executing court. The Court of the Munsif, Sadar, Sylhet was the executing court. The suit was, however, fined before the second court of the Subordinate Judge, Sylhet. Hence, the suit cannot be converted to an application under section 47 of the Code. In view of the above I allow the appeal. The judgment and decree of court of appeal below are hereby set aside and those of the trial court are affirmed.</u>

There will be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Yasin with A. Baqui, Advocates ------ For the Appellant. 
M.H. Khandker with A.F. Mohammad Ali, Advocates ------ For Shantiranjan Karmakar, Advocate ------ For Respondents 1-5.
parties:
Osmanuddin ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Subal Chandra Mondal and ors ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
Abdul Wadud Chowdhury, J: This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against the judgment and decree dated 28-2-77 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd  Court, Dacca in Title Suit No.40 of 1972 and arises out of a suit for specific performance of contract.

2. The plaintiff's case was to the effect that he had his homestead and lands at Mohakhali under P.S. Tejgaon, Dacca but these having been acquired he was in the lookout for some other agricultural lands. The lands of some of his co-villagers were also requisitioned and they settled in different villages, namely, Amback, Konabari, Mouchak, Arabari etc., in the vicinity of the area of the defendants. The plaintiff gave out his intention to purchase some agricultural lands including homestead. One of his co-villagers took him to the defendants who were willing to transfer their homestead and other lands including agricultural implements, livestock and cattle etc. as they wanted to leave the country. Talk of sale between the plaintiff and the defendants was finalized in the middle part of February, 1971 and the consideration was fixed at Tk. 40,000/-. A deed of agreement was executed on 15-2-1971 by the defendants in favour of the plaintiff on receipt of Tk. 9,000/- as earnest money. The defendants delivered vacant possession of the agricultural lands to the plaintiff retaining in their possession the homestead and it was decided that the defendants would cultivate the lands as Bargadars. It was stipulated in the deed of agreement that the sale deed would be completed within one month. The title deed of the defendants in connection with the suit land was handed over to the plaintiff at the time of the execution of the deed of agreement. Thereafter, the plaintiff obtained nationality certificate of the defendants and stamp papers were also purchased by the plaintiff. It was decided that the kabala would be executed and registered on 15th March, 1971 on which date the plaintiff would pay the balance consideration money. The plaintiff raised a tin chapra on the western bank of the river on the south of the defendants homestead and managed installation of a pump machine there. In the meantime country wide non-cooperation movement was launched in the early part of March, 1971 and there was total dislocation of communication etc. The plaintiff approached the defendants and requested them to execute and register the sale deed in his favour on receipt of balance consideration money. Though the defendants showed their willingness they delayed the execution and registration on the plea of general strike. Thereafter, total dislocation, chaos and confusion prevailed all over the country due to military crack-down on 25th March, 1971. The plaintiff kept contact with the defendants, but the defendants delayed the execution and registration of the document. In the meantime the defendants paid 20 mds of paddy as barga crops to the plaintiff. This dilatory tactics adopted by the defendants aroused suspicion in plaintiff's mind. He, therefore, issued an Advocate's notice upon the defendants on 19-6-71. On receipt of the notice the defendants agreed to execute the sale deed but delayed the performance on the plea of prevailing circumstances in the country. After liberation of the country the plaintiff again approached the defendants but this time the defendants showed a different attitude. All attempts made to persuade the defendants failed. The cause of action for the suit first arose on 15-2-71, the date of execution of the agreement and lastly on 1-6-72 when the defendants admitted their liability to execute and register the sale deed but failed to do so. As the defendants did not execute the document on receipt of the balance consideration money the plaintiff has filed the present suit.

3. The suit was contested by defendants 1 of 5 by filing a joint written-statement. Their contention is that the claim of the plaintiff is false, fraudulent, malafide and illegal. The alleged agreement is void ab-initio as it was obtained by the plaintiff by mis-representation, undue influence fraud and against the free will of the defendants. It was further contended by them that the time was the essence of contract. It was agreed upon between the parties that if the plaintiff did not take the kabala within one month, the earnest money will be forfeited and the agreement will come to an end. As the plaintiff did not take the kabala on payment of the balance consideration money within the stipulated period of one month inspite of repeated demands by the defendants, the plaintiff was not entitled to any relief whatsoever. It was further contended that the real price of the suit land was not less than Tk. 60,000/- even in 1377 B.S. In the last part of 1377 B.S. the remour started that it would not be safe for Hindus to stay in the then East Pakistan. As a result thereof, the Hindus of the locality got panicky and became anxious to leave for India after selling away their properties. Out of the 19 Hindu families, 16 sold their properties and one after another left for India within few months. As a result, the defendants got all the more panicky. At that time the plaintiff proposed to purchase the suit land for consideration of Tk. 36,000/- and the defendants agreed to sell their properties in presence of some witnesses. There was a condition for the sale that if the defendants or their heirs returned and paid back the consideration money in full within 10 years from the date of sale, the plaintiff or his heirs would reconvey the land to them. The plaintiff agreed to that and assured that the transaction will be completed within a week. He informed them that he will come back again on the 2nd of Falgoon, 1377 B.S. and will inform the defendants the exact date when he will pay the consideration money and get the kabala executed and registered. On the 2nd Falgoon, 1377 B.S. the plaintiff along with 2 strangers came, one of whom was introduced as a deed writer. The plaintiff paid Tk. 5,000/- to the defendants and produced a document already written beforehand and asked the defendants to sign the same. The defendants raised objection as to the recital in the agreement of payment of Tk. 9000/- as baina instead of Tk. 5,000/- and as to the recital of the period of one month's time for completion of the transaction and also with regard to the omission of the term of reconveyance as agreed upon. The plaintiff told them that in any case the defendants will get Tk. 31,000/- as balance money. So writing of Tk. 9,000/- is immaterial. As regards the period and writing of period of one month the plaintiff said this period is required for procuring nationality certificate and for purchasing stamps. As regards reconveyance of the suit land the plaintiff said that a separate deed of agreement would be executed at the time of registration of the kabala. On such assurance, the defendant No. 4 put his thumb impression and other defendants put their signatures in the so-called bainapatra in presence of Sadhu Charan Sarkar. The defendants did never deliver possession of the suit land to the plaintiff. The plaintiff has inserted the same in the deed of agreement afterwards in collusion with the scribe. The defendants also denied the story of cultivation of the suit land as bargadar of the plaintiff and payment of 20 mds of paddy as borga crop to the plaintiff. On the 2nd Falgoon of 1377 B.S. the defendants requested the plaintiff complete the transaction within the next few days. The plaintiff did not turn up within 8/10 days. When the defendant No. 1 saw the plaintiff, he requested him to complete the transaction without further delay. But the plaintiff deferred the matter from time to time on various pretext and thus one month's time as stipulated by the parties expired due to the default of the plaintiff alone. Even after that default by the plaintiff, the defendants requested the plaintiff several times to complete the transaction on payment of balance consideration. The plaintiff approached the defendants and asked for refund of the earnest money amounting to Tk. 5,000/- saying that he would not purchase the suit land. The defendants agreed to pay the same in 5 yearly equal installments and the plaintiff also agreed and went away. Again the plaintiff met the defendants in Baishak 1379 B.S. and asked them to pay back the said sum at a time without delay. The defendants expressed their in ability to repay the earnest money at a time. After sometime the defendants received summons of the suit. The defendants contend that the plaintiff's suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge held that the plaintiff's case that there was an agreement by which defendants 1 to 5 agreed to sell the disputed property to the plaintiff and that the consideration money was fixed at Tk. 40,000/- out of which Tk. 9,000/- was paid as advance, was true. He rejected the defence contention that the consideration was fixed Tk. 36,000/- and advance paid was Tk. 5,000/-. He also held that time was not the essence of the contract. He, however, held that the situation prevailing at that time made the defendants panicky and out of that fear they entered into an agreement to sell the properties. But before the kabala was registered and the transaction was completed non-co-operation movement started and the country was victimised by military crack-down and as such the very purpose for which the defendants wanted to sell the properties, that is crossing the border and going to India, was frustrated. Thereafter, the country was liberated on 16th December, 1971 and the question of leaving the country by the defendants thereafter did not arise at all. He also found that the defendants have no other properties except the suit land and if they are compelled to perform the contract, they will have no land left and they will be put to great hardship. In that view of the matter, the learned Subordinate Judge refused to grant the relief of specific performance of contract to the plaintiff on equitable grounds. He further held that earnest money amounting to Tk. 9,000/- was lying with the defendants since 15-2-1971 and the value of the money has risen more than 4 times and as such for the ends of justice he passed a decree against the defendants for Tk. 36,000/-, that is 4 times the money he has paid as advance for the loss he has sustained by this money being withheld for such a long time. As against the said judgment and decree the plaintiff has preferred an appeal. The defendants also preferred a cross-objection.

5. The plaintiff's case is that after coming to a finding that the plaintiff's case was true, the learned Subordinate judge should not have dismissed the suit of the plaintiff on the ground of hardship, because of the fact, at the relevant time there was no hardship on the part of the defendants and they entered into a contract knowing fully well about the facts and circumstances prevailing in the country and in that view, it was urged that a decree for specific performance of contract ought to have been passed. As against the finding the learned Subordinate Judge as to the validity of the contract as also the money decree that has been passed a cross-objection has been filed by the defendants, who contended that the plaintiff's suit was not maintainable in view of the fact that the time was the essence of contract as also for the reason that the plaintiff's story of payment of Tk. 9,000/- or that the contract was for Tk. 40,000/- have not been substantiated. It has also been urged by the cross-objectors that the deed of agreement contained interpolations by addition of certain sentences inserting the story of delivery of possession in favour of the plaintiff and in view of this fraud the learned Advocate for the cross-objectors submits that the plaintiff has not come with clean hands and as such his suit should have been dismissed in toto. In view of the fact that the appeal and the cross-objection are with regard to the same transaction, we take up both the appeal and the cross-objection together and dispose them of by this judgment.

<u>6. So far as the question rose by the appellant that the court should not consider the ground of hardship in view of the fact that the hardship must relate to the circumstances at the time of the agreement of which the defendants did not foresee. The learned Advocate submits that the condition of the country at that time was well known to the defendants and as such it could not be said they did not foresee the hardship, and therefore, the learned Judge erred in law in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff on this ground. The learned Subordinate Judge has discussed this point and has come to the finding that the condition of the country at the relevant time was known by both the plaintiff and the defendants and the defendants were under panic because of the fact that there was a rumour that the lives of the Hindus were not safe in the then East Pakistan. It is also in evidence that some of the Hindu families of the village of the defendants also left after selling their home and hearth for India. In that view of the matter, we find that the learned Subordinate Judge was not wrong in refusing the specific performance to the plaintiff. The condition of the country at that time was such that the defendants lost their mental balance and were eager to leave the country at any cost to save their lives. In that view of the matter, we do not find any substance in this appeal.</u>

<u>7. So far as the cross-objection is concerned Mr. M.H. Khandker the learned Advocate has raised several points. He has urged that time is the essence of the contract because in the deed of agreement it was clearly stated that the document was to be executed within one month and the document having not been executed within one month the plaintiff was not entitled to enforce the performance of the said agreement. He has drawn our attention to the deposition of the plaintiff and referred the relevant portion of the agreement by the defendants to prove that the kabala was to be executed within one month failing which the advance money will be forfeited and this one month having expired it should be taken that the time was the essence of contract and as such the plaintiff was not entitled to any relief as he came to court long after the expiry of the said period. Mr. Khandker has referred to several decisions to substantiate his case that time was essence of contract in the facts and circumstances of the case. But in view of the admission in the written statement to the effect. that the defendants requested the plaintiff to take suit property on payment of the consideration money even after the expiry of that period of one month would show that the parties did not consider the stipulation in the agreement to the effect that the kabala was to the executed within one month, otherwise, the advance money be forfeited to be the essence of the contract. As a matter of fact the parties did not adhere to the same but kept it open even after the expiry of the period mentioned in the agreement. In that view of the matter we do not think it necessary to refer to those decisions referred to by Mr. Khandker. It also transpires from the evidence of the parties that the time was not essence of contract. Defendant No. 1 has stated that they approached the plaintiff several times to have the kabala executed and registered. The condition of the country at that time also must be taken into consideration. It is also in evidence of the plaintiff that he approached the defendants, but the defendants did not dare to come out because of the circumstances prevailing in the country. At that time there was general strike and everything came to a standstill. In that view it was not possible to have the kabala executed and registered within one month. The parties by their conduct having extended the time it could not be said that time was the essence of the contract. With regard to the question of fraud and interpolation of the document as argued by Mr. Khandker, he submitted that in view of the fact that the question of delivery of possession has been inserted in the document subsequently, the plaintiff was not entitled to any relief on the basis of such a fraudulent kabala. We are not concerned with the question of delivery of possession of the plaintiff here. He has made out a case that the defendants wanted to sell property at Tk. 40,000/- out of which they took an advance of Tk. 9,000/- and executed a deed of agreement in favour of the plaintiff. The defendants have admitted that they executed the document due to hard pressure and the condition prevailing in the country at that time. On evidence the court below has accepted the plaintiff's case of consideration money being Tk. 40,000/- out of which an advance of Tk. 9,000/- was paid. The court has on the ground of hardship refused the specific performance of contract and rejected the prayer of the plaintiff for the specific performance. So far as the refund of consideration is concerned the court has held that in view of the fact that the time was not essence of contract the question of fraud does not arise, and the defendants received Tk. 9,000/- in 1971 and did not refund the same until now and as such he was liable to refund the same to the plaintiff. He has, however, considered that the value of the money has gone down more than 4 times. He therefore passed a decree against the defendants to refund 4 times the advanced amount to the plaintiff. We do not find any illegality in this order of the learned Subordinate Judge.</u>

8. The question of delivery of possession was not material in this case. This document has been admitted by the defendants. Their only case that the question of delivery of possession was subsequently inserted. The plaintiff contended that the same was written in the same sitting with consultation of both the parties. As to the evidence with regard to this point the P. Ws. have categorically stated that this was written in the same sitting with the consent of both the parties. The defendants have denied this contention but the witnesses who deposed in their favour were interested witness, and as such the learned Subordinate Judge was right in rejecting the same.

9. In that view of the matter we do not find any substance in this cross-objection as well. Both the appeal and the cross-objection are, therefore, dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Md Fazlul Karim, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record—For the Appellants. 
Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate (Probir Neogi, Advocate with him) instructed by Abu Siddique, Advocate-on-Record—For Respondent Nos. 1(a) - 1(g) 
Not represented—Respondent Nos.2-12.
parties:
Md. Tahedul Islam and others  ------ Appellants.
Vs.
Md. Mojibar Rahman and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated June 24, 1996 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.809 of 1991)
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This is defendants appeal by leave against the judgment dated June 24, 1996 of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.809 of 1991 making the Rule absolute and thereupon setting aside the judgment and decree dated 29-8-1990 of the Court of District Judge, Gaibandha in Title Appeal No. 45 of 1988 whereby the appellate Court sent the suit back to the trial Court for disposal of the same in the light of the discussion and direction made in the judgment. The revisional application was filed against the judgment and decree of the appellate Court reversing the judgment and decree dated February 28, 1988 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Gaibandha in Other Class Suit No. 324 of 1986 decreeing the same.

2. The suit was filed seeking declaration of title in respect of the land described in schedule 'Ka' attached to the plaint and the structure therein. The subject matter of the suit is 1/2 decimal of land.

3. The suit was filed stating, inter alia, that the land measuring 1 decimal was taken on lease by the plaintiff and his maternal uncle Rahim Boksha Bepari by the kabuliyat dated April 12, 1939, that after amicable partition plaintiff got 1/2 decimal of land as described in schedule `ka' to the plaint, that plaintiff sold the land got by amicable partition as well as the structure therein to Shafion Nessa by the kabala dated January 3, 1941 who re-transferred the land to him by the kabala dated December 16, 1946 and since then plaintiff is possessing the land and carrying on business in the shop. Rahim Boksha Bepari sold his share to the extent of 1/2 decimal of land to Haji Jalilur Rahman, the predecessor of the defendant Nos.1-10 and after his death his heirs defendant Nos. 1-10 are possessing the land purchased by Haji Jalilur Rahman from Rahim Boksha Bepari, that RS Khatian in respect of the 1/2 decimal of land has been prepared in the name of the plaintiff and he is paying rent, that Haji Jalilur Rahman filed Other Class Suit No.844 of 1975 in the Court of Munsif, (now Assistant Judge) 2nd Court, Gaibandha seeking rectification of the RS record but the same was dismissed on February 14, 1977, that upon suppression of the said fact defendant Nos.1-10 filed petition before the Revenue Officer, Gobindaganj and the Revenue Officer by the order dated July 28, 1986 cancelled the RS record which stood in the name of the plaintiff. The said action of the Revenue Officer having had clouded plaintiff's title he was constrained to file the suit seeking relief as stated hereinbefore.

4. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos.1-10 by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint. It is their case that their predecessor Haji Jalilur Rahman by the kabala dated May 7, 1941 purchased 1 decimal of land from Rahim Boksha Bepari and his brother, that although CS record was prepared in the name of Rahim Boksha Bepari but as the land was acquired with the money of Rahim Boksha's brother, as such Rahim Boksha Bepari and his brother executed the deed in favour of Haji Jalilur Rahman, that Rahim Boksha Bepari let out land in suit with the structure to the plaintiff who is his nephew at the monthly rent of Rs.1½, that the kabuliyat dated 12-4-1939 executed by plaintiff and Rahim Boksha Bepari in respect of the land in suit is fictitious, that plaintiff never took settlement of the land in suit and, as such, the transaction between the plaintiff and Shafion Nessa was fictitious, that plaintiff taking advantage of monthly tenancy got the RS record prepared in his name and managed to pay rent, that when the defendants noticed the said fact they filed petition before the Revenue Officer for cancellation of the RS record mutating the name of the plaintiff and the Revenue Officer corrected the RS record in the name of the defendants, that Haji Jalilur Rahman by the Heba deed dated October 20, 1975 transferred the land to the defendant Nos. 1-10.

5. The trial Court on consideration of the materials on record decreed the suit with the finding that no paper has been filed by the defendants to establish that plaintiff is their tenant, that the documents showing transfer and re-transfer of the land in suit by the plaintiff and Shafion Nessa being documents more than 30 years old can be considered genuine, that defendants did not file paper to show that Rahim Boksha Bepari was the owner of the entire land i.e. 1 decimal of land, that the defendants also claimed that Haji Jalilur Rahman transferred the land to them by Heba deed but the document has not been filed in the Court, that defendants predecessor filed suit seeking correction of the SA record but the same was dismissed and upon suppression of the said fact the defendants got the khatian prepared in the name of the plaintiff cancelled and that the order of the Revenue Officer dated July 28, 1986 cancelling the khatian that stood in the name of the plaintiff was not sustainable in law, that the plaintiff has right, title and interest in the land in suit and in the shop standing therein.

6. The defendants went on appeal. Before the appellate Court the defendants filed 2 documents, namely, Heba deed dated October 20, 1975 and the kabuliyat dated December 17, 1927. The appellate Court upon taking the said two documents into consideration observed that the trial Court while decreeing the suit did not make any decision in any respect as regard the documents namely, kabuliyat and the Heba deed. It is pertinent to mention that the defendants did not file the Heba deed dated October 20, 1977 and the kabuliyat dated December 17, 1927 before the trial Court and this being the position there was no occasion for the trial Court to make any comment on those two documents. It may also be mentioned that defendants did not take any step to dislodge the genuineness of the kabuliyat dated April 12, 1939 by which the plaintiff and his maternal uncle Rahim Boksha Bepari took settlement in equal share 1 decimal of land as described in the schedule attached to the plaint.

7. The appellate Court was of the view that although CS khatian was prepared in the name of Rahim Boksha Bepari but about the same the trial Court did not make any decision either way, that the trial Court was in error in arriving at the finding that plaintiff was not the tenant of the defendants since in arriving at the said finding the trial Court did not consider the documents i.e. CS khatian, kabuliyat and other papers, that trial Court was in error in granting relief sought by the plaintiff without considering the documents filed by the parties as stated hereinbefore.

8. Before the appellate Court, the defendant Nos. 1-10 filed two documents, namely, Heba deed and the kabuliyat of 1927 and the said Court held since defendants documents namely, Heba deed, the kabuliyat and the CS khatian prepared in the name of Rahim Boksha Bepari, RS Khatian and other papers, were not discussed extensively and properly by the trial Court, as such, for proper adjudication of the dispute of the parties it would be legal and proper to remand the suit to the trial Court and thereupon, upon allowing the appeal, sent back the suit to the trial Court for disposal taking into consideration the documents filed before the appellate Court and the other materials already on record as well as in the light of the observations made by the appellate Court.

9. The plaintiff then moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute upon observing that the trial Court on consideration of the evidence was quite correct in arriving at the finding that the plaintiff has right, title, interest and possession in the land in suit and the defendants failed to show that the plaintiff is their tenant in the land in suit. The High Court Division further observed that plaintiff in support of his case that he and Rahim Boksha Bepari took settlement of 1 decimal of land brought on record the kabuliyat dated April 12, 1939 (Exhibit 6), the RS Khatian (Exhibit 1) and the 'dakhilas' (Exhibit 2) and also the fact that he as owner transferred the land in 1941 to Shafion Nessa and he re-purchased the same in 1946 from her and that as against the said evidence brought on record by the plaintiff the defendants in support of their claim that plaintiff is their tenant in the land in suit did not produce any documentary evidence nor any reliable evidence except the evidence of DW 1 who is one of the defendants and that the defendants did not produce any evidence to show that Rahim Boksha Bepari was the owner of the entire land i.e. 1 decimal of land as in the schedule 'ka' to the plaint. The High Court Division observed that although defendants claimed that they have got the land by Heba-bil-ewaz deed but the same was not produced before the trial Court and that defendants predecessor filed Title Suit No.448 of 1975 against the plaintiff seeking declaration that he is the owner of 1 decimal of land of CS plot No.482 listed in CS Khatian No.259 but the same was dismissed, that the findings and the decisions arrived at by the trial Court are based on due consideration of the evidence on record and, as such, the appellate Court was not correct in observing that the trial Court decreed the suit without considering the documents relating to the land in suit produced by the parties. The High Court Division observed that DW 1 in his evidence categorically stated that the defendants have no paper to show that the plaintiff is their tenant and that he (DW 1) is not aware on what basis plaintiff is possessing the land in suit. The High Court Division also observed that from the materials on record it is seen that the defendants failed to adduce any evidence in support of their case that plaintiff is their tenant in the land in suit and the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiff has been able to establish that he has right, title and interest in the land in suit is based on due consideration of the evidence and the appellate Court in reversing the judgment of the trial Court did not consider the evidence both oral and documentary. The High Court Division further observed that the lower appellate Court sent back the case on remand for the purpose of adjudication of the same taking into consideration the document filed before it without arriving at a decision as to whether at all those documents have any relevancy in disposing of the suit and that the evidence already on record is not sufficient for adjudication of the dispute between the parties.

10. Leave was granted to consider the contention that the trial Court disbelieved the case of the defendants only on the consideration that they did not produce any document in support of their claim that Rahim Boksha Bepari was the 16 annas owner of the land in suit and also could not prove that they had become owners of the land in suit by the Heba-bil-ewaz deed, but the defendants having had produced the aforesaid documents namely, kabuliyat dated July 17, 1927 executed by Rahim Boksha Bepari in favour of the landlord and the Heba-bil-ewaz deed dated October 20, 1975 and in the written statement having had contended in respect of the said documents (in the written statement there was averment only in respect of the Heba-bil-ewaz deed) the High Court Division while reversing the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court sending the suit back on remand to the trial Court for conclusive determination of the suit with reference to the said documents along with other documents which were already filed in the case on misconception of the provision of Order XLI, rule 27 and Order XLI, rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure set aside the order of remand and thereupon affirmed the judgment of the trial Court. It was also the contention that the High Court Division was in error in depriving the defendants to produce the basic document in Court for consideration of their case i.e. Heba-bil-ewaz deed, by which they got ownership of the land in suit.

11. The learned Counsel for the appellant submits that because of production of the kabuliyat of the year 1927 executed by Rahim Boksha Bepari alone as serious contention as to title of the plaintiff arose and that in the context of the two kabuliyats, one of 1927 and other of 1939 as there was necessity of reconciliation of the contention of the parties, as such, order of remand made keeping in view the question of ends of justice was quite legal and, as such, the High Court Division was in error in setting aside the judgment of the appellate Court, that because of the CS khatian which was prepared in the name of Rahim Boksha Bepari in the context of the kabuliyat of 1927 and consequent thereupon kabulayat of 1939 being a malafide fact giving rise to serious contention and conflict as to the title of the parties and, as such, there having had necessity of reconciliation of the contest between the parties by allowing them to lead evidence in support of their respective claim, particularly the claim of the defendants, the appellate Court was quite correct in making the order of remand of the suit to the trial Court for disposal of the same upon taking into consideration the documents filed before the appellate Court. It has been submitted by the learned Counsel for the appellant that the suit i.e. Suit No.488 of 1975, was filed by the plaintiff for illegal gain. The learned Counsel for the appellant also submitted that the entry in the CS khatian unless annulled the plaintiff is not entitled to the relief sought in the suit.

12. The learned Counsel for the respondent has submitted since there was no pleading of the defendants as to the kabuliyat of 1927, the trial Court was not required to decide about the same or, in other words, the Court was not required to decide a matter which was beyond the pleading, that the document of the year 1927 was for 10 years and there was specific averment in the document of 1927 that establish that on the expiry of the said period land shall go back to the landlord and the lessee shall have no claim in respect of the land, that a document would not be admitted in evidence which would have no bearing on the decision and, as such, since the document of 1927 was for 10 years and that after the expiry of fixed period the land having had gone back to the landlord and thereupon Rahim Boksha Bepari, in whose name kabuliyat of 1927 stood and the plaintiff having had taken lease in 1939 of the land in suit jointly having equal share, the document of 1927 had no relevancy in deciding the contention of the parties in respect of the land in suit in the context of the later document i. e. kabuliyat of 1939, and that being so the appellate Court was quite in error in sending back the suit to the trial Court for disposal of the same taking into consideration the kabuliyat of 1927, that since the kabuliyat of 1927 has no relevancy for the disposal of the suit and consequently, the Heba-bil-ewaz deed on the basis of which the defendants are claiming the entire land in suit, i.e. 1 decimal of land, is also not relevant for the disposal of the suit and, as such, the appellate Court was in error in making the order of remand for adjudication of the suit taking the said documents into consideration, that additional evidence would be allowed by the appellate Court only when the same has relevancy to the subject matter of the suit and shall have effect on the result of the suit and that as the documents, i.e. kabuliyat of 1927 and the Heba-bil-ewaz deed of October 20, 1975, have no relevancy to the subject matter of the suit and thus shall have no effect on the result of the suit, the appellate Court was in error in accepting the said 2 documents as additional evidence and thereupon sending back the suit to the trial Court for adjudication taking into consideration the said documents.

13. The moot question in the appeal is, how far the appellate Court was free from error in allowing the defendants' prayer for acceptance of the kabuliyat of 1927 and the Heba-bil-ewaz of 1975 or, in other words, in allowing the defendants to produce those documents as additional evidence without considering how far those documents in the background of the kabuliyat of 1939, genuineness whereof was not questioned by the defendants, was relevant for the disposal of the suit and that the documents filed by the defendants have any bearing on the result of the suit.

14. The provision of law relating to production of additional evidence at the appellate stage is in Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The general provision of law is that parties to an appeal shall not be entitled to produce additional evidence, whether oral or documentary, before the appellate Court except in a case where the Court from whose decree the appeal has been filed refused to admit evidence which ought to have been admitted in evidence or when the appellate Court requires any document to be produced or any witness to be examined to enable it to pronounce the judgment, or for any other substantial cause, then the appellate Court may allow such evidence or document to be produced, or witness to be examined. In the instant case, condition i.e. refusal by the trial Court for admission of evidence which ought to have been admitted, is absent. Now there remains the other condition i.e. whether the Court requires the document as filed by the defendants for the purpose of enabling it to pronounce the judgment or for any other substantial cause.

15. The provision of Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure came up for consideration in the case of Parsothh and others vs Lal Mohar and others reported in 58 Indian Appeals, 254 wherein it has been observed the provisions of "Order XLI, rule 27, are clearly not intended to allow a litigant who has been unsuccessful in the lower Court to patch up the weak parts of his case and fill up omissions in the appellate Court. Linder rule 27(1)(b) it is only where the appellate Court "requires" it (i.e. finds it needful) that additional evidence can be admitted. It may be required to enable the Court to pronounce judgment, or for any other substantial cause, but in either case, it must be the Court that requires it". This is the plain grammatical reading of the sub-clause. The legitimate occasion for the exercise of this discretion is not whenever before the appeal is heard a party applies to adduce fresh evidence, but "when on examining the evidence as it stands, some inherent lacuna or defect becomes apparent". It may well be that the defect may be pointed out by a party, or that a party may move the Court to supply the defect, but the requirement must be the requirement of the Court upon its appreciation of the evidence as it stands. Wherever the Court adopts this procedure it is bound by rule 27(2) to record its reasons for so doing, and under rule 29 must specify the points to which the evidence is to be confined and record on its proceedings the points so specified".

16. In the case of Cecil Waldron Andrew vs Helen Andrew reported in 9 DLR (PC) 682 it has been observed " that fresh evidence on appeal will not be permitted unless two conditions are satisfied. The first is that the new evidence was not available to the party seeking to use it at the trial or that reasonable diligence would not have made it so available. The second condition is that the fresh evidence, if true, would have had, or would have been likely to have had, a determining influence on the Court below".

17. In the case of Messrs Muhammad Siddiq Muhammad Umar and another vs Australasia Bank Ltd reported in PLD 1966 (SC) 684 = 18 DLR (SC) 430 it has been observed "The rules of procedure are not made "for the purpose of hindering justice" and, as Such, we should not give such a restricted interpretation to the provisions of rule 27 of Order XLI of the Code of Civil Procedure as would, in effect, amount to tying down the hands of the appellate Court and stand in the way of doing complete justice in a cause. The rule merely prescribes that the requirement must be a genuine one and that the need for the additional evidence must be felt by the Court itself after it has examined the evidence already on the record and come to the conclusion that there is apparently some inherent lacuna or defect which hinders the due administration of justice. If it comes to this conclusion, then it has the power to call for additional evidence subject to the condition that it must record its reasons for doing so in order that a higher Court may be able to ascertain that the need was not merely imaginary but based upon factual grounds".

18. In the case of Sunil Krishna Banik and others vs Kailash Chandra Saha and others reported in 1984 BLD (AD) 320 = 36 DLR (AD) 220, (same case has been reported in 36 DLR (AD) 220), it has been observed "Clause (b) of Rule 27(1) appears to have conferred discretion on the appellate Court to allow additional evidence in order "to enable it to pronounce judgment, or for any other substantial cause". This discretion is not subject to any other limitation or restriction excepting what is indicated by the words used therein. To do justice is the special preserve or domain of a court of law and this has been stressed by the words used in clause (b) as aforesaid. It is true that such admission should not be encouraged. Power to admit additional evidence should, therefore, be sparingly used".

19. In the case of Mohammad Ali Akhand vs Bahatan Nessa and others reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 50 = 3 BLC (AD) 177 it has been observed "this power can be exercised only where the court requires further evidence for one of the two causes specified in the rule". It has been viewed by this Division that a party at the appellate stage would not be allowed to adduce additional evidence if allowing or production of additional evidence would amount to give the party an opportunity "to fish out evidence in order to prove their case" and to fill up the lacuna.

20. The consistent view is that additional evidence can be allowed by the Court on two occasions as in Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure. We have already observed that the first occasion or situation for admission of additional evidence is absent in the instant case.

<u>21. The law is settled now that additional evidence as in Order XLI, rule 27(1)(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure can only be produced when the Court feels the necessity thereof. The Court before allowing a party to produce additional evidence is required to "record the reason for its admission". There is another aspect which the Court is required to consider while allowing the party to produce additional evidence that the evidence so intended to be produced as additional evidence would have "a determining influence on the courts below" or, in other words, the evidence so intended to be produced as additional evidence has the relevancy and that would have effect on the result of the suit.</u>

22. The document i.e. kabuliyat dated 17-12-1927 is at page 60 of the additional paper book filed by the defendants. The learned Counsel for the respondent upon referring to the kabuliyat dated 17-12-1927 has submitted that the same was for 10 years and that also referred to an averment in the said kabuliyat which “মেয়াদ অন্তে উক্ত জমি জমার সহিত আমার কোন স্বত্ব সম্পর্ক থাকিবে না উহা সকল প্রকার খাস দখলে পাইয়া অন্যত্র পত্তন করিতে পারিবেন তাহাতে নিবেদন আপত্তি করিতে পারিব না” In the background of the said averment in the kabuliyat dated 17-12-1927, which the defendants intended to produce before the appellate Court as additional evidence and the said Court allowed the prayer, it is evident that after the expiry of the period for which Rahim Boksha Bepari took lease by the kabuliyat dated 17-12-1927, the plaintiff and Rahim Boksha Bepari took fresh lease of the land by the kabuliyat dated 12-4-1939.

23. The learned Counsel for the respondent submits that since the kabuliyat dated 17-12-1927 by efflux of time became non-effective and that Rahim Boksha Bepari who took lease of the land in suit by the aforesaid kabuliyat having had taken fresh lease of the land along with the plaintiff by the kabuliyat dated 12-4-1939, the kabuliyat of the year 1927 as has no relevancy to the subject matter of the suit and that also as would have no effect or bearing on the result of the suit, the appellate Court without considering the vital aspect of the matter of admission of additional evidence in the background of the facts of the case was in serious error in allowing the defendants to introduce the kabuliyat of the year 1927 as additional evidence and thus, the appellate Court was in error in accepting the said kabuliyat as additional evidence although the same has no relevancy as well as bearing on the subject matter of the suit.

<u>24. The defendants, on the basis of Heba-bil-ewaz deed dated October 20, 1975 executed by Haji Jalilur Rahman, father of the defendants, are claiming the land in suit. It is the defendants' case that Haji Jalilur Rahman purchased the land in suit from Rahim Boksha Bepari by the kabala dated May 7, 1941. It has already been seen that on the aforesaid date Rahim Boksha Bepari had interest only in 1/2, decimal of land out of the land taken lease by him and the plaintiff by the kabuliyat dated 12-4-1939. Haji Jalilur Rahman, the predecessor of the defendant Nos.1-10, having had acquired 1/2 decimal of land from Rahim Boksha Bepari on the basis of the kabala dated May 7, 1941, the defendants by the Heba-bil-Ewaz deed dated October 20, 1975 can only claim 1/2 decimal of land wherein Haji Jalilur Rahman had interest at the time of making the Heba-bil-Ewaz deed. The plaintiff has filed the suit claiming 1/2 decimal of land and the suit was decreed by the trial Court in respect thereof. The defendants tried to establish in the trial Court that their predecessor Haji Jalilur Rahman acquired the entire suit land i.e. 1 decimal, from Rahim Boksha Bepari and that they have got the land in suit from Haji Jalilur Rahman by Heba-bil-Ewaz deed. There was no averment about the mode of acquiring of title by Rahim Boksha Bepari in the entire land. The defendants in their pleading only mentioned about their acquisition of title by the heba of October 20, 1975 but the same was not produced before the trial Court. The defendants , predecessor Haji Jalilur Rahman acquired interest in the land in suit to the extent of 1/2 decimal of land from Rahim Boksha Bepari who along with the plaintiff took lease of 1 decimal of land by the kabuliyat dated 12-4-1939. This being the position the documents i.e. kabuliyat of the year 1927 and the Heba-bil-Ewaz of October 20, 1975, produced by the defendants before the appellate Court as additional evidence had no relevancy to the subject matter of the suit and bearing on the result of the suit. The kabuliyat of the year 1927 was in no way relevant for the purpose of adjudication of the suit since after the expiry of the period for which land of the said kabuliyat was leased out to Rahim Boksha Bepari the same went back to the landlord and thereupon Rahim Boksha Bepari along with the plaintiff took fresh lease of the land in suit in equal share in the year on April 12, 1939. So, in the year 1941 when Haji Jalilur Rahman made purchase from Rahim Boksha Bepari, at that time Rahim Boksha Bepari had title only to the extent of 1/2 decimal of the land in suit and that in the year 1941 Rahim Boksha Bepari legally could have transferred 1/2 decimal of land out of the entire land in suit, i.e. 1 decimal of land, to Haji Jalilur Rahman. This being the position, introduction of the kabuliyat of 1927 and the Heba-bil-Ewaz of the year 1975 by the defendants to substantiate their claim of acquiring entire land in suit is in no way relevant for the purpose of adjudication of the suit or, in other words, for the determination of the interest of the plaintiff in respect of the land claimed by him.</u>

25. The learned Counsel for the appellants submitted that because of the production of the kabuliyat of the year 1927 a serious contention regarding the title of the plaintiff has arisen and that the land in suit having been recorded in the CS khatian in the name of Rahim Boksha Bepari, which has a presumptive value, as such, for the purpose of resolution of the conflict so has arisen there is necessity of the documents filed by the defendants as additional evidence for effective adjudication of the suit and that also for ends of justice, the documents need. be admitted as additional evidence.

26. In the background of the said submission the learned Counsel has referred us to the case of Sunil Krishna Banik and others vs Kailash Chandra Saha and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 220 (same case has also been reported in 1984 BLD (AD) 320). We are in full agreement with the principle of law enunciated in the reported case, but the fact is that in the instant case the documents which have been produced by the defendants as additional evidence and the Court allowed the defendants to produce the same as additional evidence, the same, in the background of the facts and circumstance as stated hereinabove, had no relevancy to the subject matter of the suit and that would in no way have any bearing on the result of the suit.

<u>27. We have already mentioned that the kabuliyat of the year 1927 was for limited period and that after the expiry of that limited period the land which was the subject matter of kabuliyat of 1927 was taken lease by Rahim Boksha Bepari and the plaintiff jointly in equal share. The land so taken lease jointly by Rahim Boksha Bepari and the plaintiff in the year 1939 is the subject matter of the suit. We have also mentioned hereinbefore that by the Heba-bil-Ewaz of October 20, 1975 the defendants have acquired only the interest which Haji Jalilur Rahman acquired from Rahim Boksha Bepari on May 7, 1941 i.e. Haji Jalilur Rahman by purchase from Rahim Boksha Bepari acquired interest in 1/2 decimal of land of the kabuliyat of April 12, 1939 which is in the name of Rahim Boksha Bepari and the plaintiff. This being the position the appellate Court was in serious error in allowing the defendants to produce the said two documents as additional evidence and thereupon accepting the said documents as additional evidence and that in sending back the suit to the trial Court for fresh adjudication in the light of the documents which have no relevancy to the subject matter of the suit and would have no bearing on the result of the suit. In that state of the matter, the High Court Division was not in error in interfering with the judgment of the appellate Court and thereupon restoring the judgment of the trial Court.</u>

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed. There is no order as to cost.

End.

N I Bhuiyan, Advocate-on-Record—For Respondent. Nos. 1 and 2. 
Not represented—Respondent Nos. 3-12.
