full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: The appeal by the plaintiff is against the judgment dated August 27, 1996 of the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 211 of 1996 allowing the same. The appeal was filed against the order dated November 5, 1995 of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka in Title Suit No. 135 of 1995 allowing the application filed by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 herein under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and section 6 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 seeking rejection of the plaint of Title Suit No. 135 of 1995.

2. The genesis of Title Suit No. 135 of the 1995 is that the respondent No. 2 filed Artha Rin Adalat Case No. 55 of 1990/82 of 1982 before the Court of Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Rangpur impleading the appellant as the sole defendant seeking decree for an amount of Taka 57,074 and other ancillary reliefs. The said suit was decreed in 1990 and the respondent No. 2 put the decree into execution by initiating Money Execution Case No. 96 of 1991 and got the mortgaged property sold in auction.

3. Thereafter the appellant filed Title Suit No. 135 of 1995 in the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka impleading the Uttara Bank Ltd Head Office, Dhaka, Uttara Bank Ltd Branch at Central Road, Rangpur, the auction purchaser and several others as defendants seeking the following reliefs amongst others:

“(ক) ২নং বাদী কর্তৃক রংপুর ২য় সাবজজ আদালত ও ১ম অর্থঋণ আদালতে স্থাপনকৃত মানি মোকদ্দমা নং-৫৫/৯০ এবং তৎ উপজাত ২৫-১০-১৯৯- এবং ৩০-১০-১৯৯০ ইং তারিখে একতরফা রায় ও ডিক্রি এবং মা্নি ডিক্রি জারী মোকদ্দমা নং-৯৬/৯১ ও তৎ উপজাত ১৭-৬-১৯৯২ইং তারিখে নিলাম বিক্রয় কার্য্যক্রম অবৈধ, বেআইনী যোগসাজসী ও বাদীর উপর কার্য্যকর নহে মর্মে ঘোষণা ও ডিক্রি দিতে,

(খ) অত্র বাদী বিবাদী ব্যাংকের নিকট হইতে বিবাদী কথিত মতে কোন ঋণ গ্রহণ করে নাই এবং কোন বন্ধকী দলিল ও কাগজ পত্রাদি সহি স্বাক্ষর করে নাই। বিবাদীগন যোগসাজসী ও ষড়যন্ত্র মুলকভাবে জালিয়াতির মাধ্যমে উহা সুজন করিয়াছে ফলে উহার দরুন অত্র বাদী বিবাদীগনের নিকট কোন দায় দেনা ইত্যাদি সৃষ্টি হয় নাই মর্মে ঘোষনা ও ডিক্রি দিতে,

(গ) রংপুর ২য় সাবজজ ও প্রথম অর্থঋণ আদালতে দাখিলী মানি ডিক্রি জারী মোকদ্দমা নং-৯৬/৯১ উপজাত নিলাম বিক্রয়ের মাধ্যমে অত্র বাদীগন স্বত্ত্ব দখলীয় ও ৪-১১নং মোকাবেলা বিবাদীগনের নিকট বিক্রিত সম্পতিতে বিবাদীগনের কোন স্বত্ব স্বার্থ অধিকার ইত্যাদি উপজাত হয় নাই মর্মে ঘোষণা ও ডিক্রি দিতে,

(ঘ) বাদীর পক্ষে বিবাদীগণের বিরুদ্ধে মোকদ্দমা খরচের ডিক্রি দিতে”

Schedule attached to the plaint is as follows:

“তপসিল “ক”

জেলা রংপুর সাব রেজিষ্ট্রি রংপুর জে এল নং-৯১ মৌজা রাধা বল্লভ খতিয়ান পুরাতন নং-৩৯৭/১, দাগ নং-১৪০, ভূমির পরিমাণ ০.৩৫ শতাংশ।

“তপসিল “খ”

জেলা রংপুর সাব রেজিষ্ট্রি রংপুর থানা-কোতয়ালী মৌজা রাধাবল্লভ জে, এল নং-৯২ এস, এ খতিয়ান নং-১৭৪০ আর এস খতিয়ান নং-১৬২২, দাগ নং-১৫৬৩, ভূমির পরিমাণ ০.১৭ শতাংশ

4. In due course defendant Nos.1 and 2 i.e. Uttara Bank, Head Office, Dhaka and the Uttara Bank, Branch at Rangpur, entered appearance and filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and section 6 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 with the prayer for rejection of the plaint stating that decree was passed by the Court in Rangpur and that the decree was also put into execution in Rangpur and that the property which was sold in auction is located in Rangpur town within the jurisdiction of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Rangpur and hence, the plaint of the suit so filed in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is liable to be rejected. It was also the contention of the Bank that the plaintiff who was defendant in Suit No. 55 of 1990 did not file any appeal against the decree passed in the said suit and, as such, he is not entitled to challenge the decree passed in Artha Rin Adalat Case No. 55 of 1990/82 of 1982, that no cause of action arose within the jurisdiction of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka where defendant No. 1 i.e. the Uttara Bank Corporate Office, 90, Motijheel, Commercial Area, Dhaka, is located, that no transaction between the Uttara Bank Branch at Rangpur and the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 135 of 1995 took place within the jurisdiction of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. The application filed seeking rejection of the plaint was opposed by the plaintiff. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed the application for rejection of the plaint observing that plaintiff's suit is barred by the provision of section 6 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 and that the property which has been sold in auction is in Rangpur town and, as such, is within the jurisdiction of the Court in Rangpur and hence the suit filed by the plaintiff cannot be proceeded before the Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka and thereupon, rejected the plaint.

5. As against the order of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka the plaintiff i.e. appellant herein, went on appeal before the High Court Division. The High Court Division upon observing that of the defendants in Title Suit No. 135 of 1995 only defendant No. 1, Uttara Bank, has its Head Office at Dhaka but the said defendant No. 1 was not a party in the Artha Rin Adalat Case No. 55 of 1990/82 of 1982 filed at Rangpur and in that background the High Court Division observed that Uttara Bank Limited, Head Office, Dhaka was impleaded as defendant No. 1 "only to institute the suit at Dhaka challenging the decree passed by the Court at Rangpur" and thereupon held that Uttara Bank Limited, Head Office, Dhaka was an unnecessary party in Title Suit No. 135 of 1995 "since the appellant had challenged the ex-parte decree and the execution thereof obtained by the defendant No. 2 Uttara Bank Ltd, Central. Road Branch, Rangpur, the suit ought to have been filed at Rangpur." The High Court Division further held that the learned Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka should not have rejected the plaint rather ought to have returned the plaint for filing the same before the appropriate Court. On the aforesaid findings the High Court Division allowed the appeal and thereby restored the suit to its file and number and directed the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka to return the plaint to the filing learned Advocate in terms of Order VII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

6. The plaintiff thereupon, moved this Division and obtained leave to appeal.

7. Leave was granted to consider the contentions that the High Court Division was wrong in taking the view that the plaintiff-petitioner's suit was incompetent before the learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka as because the judgment and decree and the execution thereof impugned in Title Suit No. 135 of 1995 was passed and taken in the Court at Rangpur, though the defendant No. 1 namely, Messrs Uttara Bank Limited represented by its Managing Director, 90, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka, as a body corporate was the plaintiff in Artha Rin Case No. 55 of 1990 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, and Artha Rin Adalat, Rangpur and that the suit was maintainable under the provision of section 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure, that the direction to return the plaint is illegal and not sustainable in law and that the High Court Division ought to have considered the appeal on merit i.e. whether the plaint was legally rejected by the trial Court.

8. The Artha Rin Adalat Case No. 55 of 1990/82 of 1982 was filed before the Artha Rin Adalat, Rangpur by Uttara Bank, Branch at Central Road, PS Kotwali, Rangpur.

9. Title Suit No. 135 of 1995 of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is the off-shoot of Artha Rin Case No. 55 of 1990 and the decree passed therein as well as the Execution Case No. 96 of 1991 of the 2nd Court of Sub-ordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Rangpur. In the Artha Rin Adalat case respondent No. 2 was the plaintiff and the appellant was the sole defendant.

10. The appellant filed Title Suit No. 135 of 1995 in the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka seeking the reliefs as stated herein-before. The relief so sought in the title suit primarily for declarations that the decree passed in the Artha Rin Adalat case and the proceedings of the Execution case initiated in the light of the decree in the Artha Rin Adalat case are illegal, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiff, that the documents on the basis whereof decree in the Artha Rin Adalat case was obtained were collusive, forged, fabricated and that the signature appearing in the papers were not of the plaintiff and, as such, a decree may be passed that the plaintiff, i.e. appellant herein, did not owe any amount to the Bank, i.e. plaintiff of the Artha Rin Adalat case, and that auction purchasers in the Execution Case No. 96 of 1991 by their purchase have not acquired any right, title and interest in the land belonging to the appellant.

11. The contention of the appellant is that respondent No. 1 Uttara Bank Limited, Head Office at Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka is a corporate body and carries on business in different areas outside Dhaka and, as such, suit filed by the appellant in Dhaka was very much entertainable by the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka in the light of the provision of section 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Explanation-II thereto.

12. The provision of section 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as follows:

"20. Subject to the limitations aforesaid, every suit shall be instituted in a Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction—

(a) the defendant; or each of the defendants where are more than one, at the time of commencement of the suit, actually and voluntarily resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain; or

(b) any of the defendants, where there are more than one, at the time of the commencement of the suit, actually and voluntarily resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain, provided that in such case either the leave of the Court is given, or the defendants who do not reside, or carry on business, or personally work for gain, as aforesaid, acquiesce in such institution; or

(c) the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises.

Explanation I—Where a person has a permanent dwelling at one place and also a temporary residence at another place, he shall be deemed to reside at both places in respect of any cause of action arising at the place where he has such temporary residence.

Explanation II—A Corporation shall be deemed to carry on business at its sole or principal office in (Bangladesh) or, in respect of any cause of action arising at any place where it has also a subordinate office, at such place."

<u>13. It is seen from the plaint of the Title Suit No. 135 of 1995 that there are as many as 3 principal defendants and 9 proforma defendants. Suffice it to mention there is no provision in the Code of Civil Procedure to categorise the defendants in the suit as principal defendants and proforma defendants. In a suit parties who figure as the opposers of the relief sought in the suit are of one class i.e. defendants. There is no legal basis to attribute description to the opposers as the principal defendants and the proforma defendants. It appears that aforesaid categorisation is being made through relief directly is not sought against the parties who have been described as proforma defendants but plaintiff intends adjudication of the dispute between him and the parties who have been described as principal defendants in presence of the parties described as proforma defendant(s). Although there is no provision in law for such categorisation but the practice appears to be a long standing one and is being resorted to, off and on.</u>

14. The learned Counsel for the appellant submits that the suit filed by the appellant in the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka seeking relief against the decree obtained in the Artha Rin Adalat case and the execution case initiated on the basis of the decree obtained in Artha Rin Adalat case although of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Rangpur but plaintiff's suit having been filed impleading the Corporate Office or, in other words, Head Office of the Banking Company carrying on business through its Branch Offices, as in the instant case Branch at Rangpur town, the suit so filed because of the provision of clauses (a) and (b) of section 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) and Explanation II of section 20 of CPC is very much maintainable.

15. The undenied position is that the transaction, which is being claimed by the appellant as fraudulent, between the respondent No. 2 i.e. Messrs Uttara Bank Branch at Central Road, Rangpur having its Head Office at Dhaka and the appellant, took place, as claimed by the plaintiff of the Artha Rin Adalat case, at Rangpur. The respondent No. 2 filed the suit against the appellant at Rangpur and obtained decree and thereupon put the decree into execution in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Rangpur and that in execution of the decree the property of the appellant was put to auction and was purchased by the respondent No. 3 herein. So, all the transactions and the matters relating to that took place at Rangpur. It is true respondent No. 2 is the Branch Office of the respondent No. 1 and that the respondent No. 1 is carrying on business through its Branch Offices in different parts of Bangladesh, but the fact is transaction between the appellant and the respondent No. 2 and the matters thereafter touching there took place at Rangpur.

16. The learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that in view of the provision of section 20(b), CPC read with Explanation II to the said section, the appellant quite in accordance with law has filed the suit impleading the respondent No. 1 whose Head Office is at Dhaka and its Branch Office at Rangpur as defendant No. 2. The provision in explanation II to section 20 of CPC is that a Corporation would be deemed to carry on business at the place where Head Office—sole or principal office of the Corporation situates and that in case of question of cause of action it would be that the cause of action has arisen at the place where the Corporation has a subordinate office. In the background of the said provision of law the learned Counsel for the appellant submits that since the defendant No. 1 carries on business through its Branch Office at Rangpur the suit so filed could very much be proceeded in Dhaka. The learned Counsel continued that since the residence of the defendant No. 1 is at Dhaka and, as such, the question of arising cause of the suit is immaterial. It has also been submitted that provision of section 20, CPC does not contemplate a situation whether the later suit is the off-shoot of the previous suit in the background of the result whereof the later suit was filed or, in other words, section 20 of CPC does not contemplate a situation whether a particular suit is a primary one or is the product of primary suit or earlier suit.

17. As against the aforesaid contentions of the appellant, the learned Advocate-on-Record reiterated the grounds upon which the High Court Division allowing the appeal made order for return of the plaint for filing the same in the appropriate Court. The High Court Division has observed that defendant No. 1 i.e. Messrs Uttara Bank Head Office at Motijheel, Dhaka, has been impleaded in Title Suit No. 135 of 1995 only to institute a suit at Dhaka although the said defendant was an unnecessary party in the suit filed challenging legality of the decree obtained in earlier suit decreed at Rangpur and the proceedings of the execution case wherein the property of the appellant was sold and purchased by the respondent No. 3.

<u>18. On reading the pleading of the plaintiff we are of the view that the finding as regard impleading of respondent No. 1 in Title Suit No. 135 of 1995 appears to be correct. As it appears to us, that impleading of the defendant No. 1 in the Title Suit No. 135 of 1995 of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is a contrivance to file the suit in Dhaka against the proceedings of Title Suit No. 55 of 1990 of the Artha Rin Adalat, Rangpur and the execution case initiated in the light of the decree in the Artha Rin case.</u>

<u>19. The provision of clauses (a) and (b) of section 20, CPC and the Explanation II thereto contemplate that one can file a suit impleading a person in the category of the defendant amongst others against one who carries on business at the place where the suit has been filed or that in the case of a Corporation a suit can be filed impleading the Corporation in the category of defendant where its principal office locates or at a place where cause of action of the suit arises. The provision of clause (b) of section 20, CPC provides that where there are defendants more than one, if some of such defendants do not reside or carry on business or personally work for gain within the jurisdiction of the Court wherein suit has been filed in that case upon taking leave of the Court the suit can be proceeded against such category of defendants or that if such category of defendants "acquiesce in such institution." In the suit filed by the appellant defendant No. 3 (auction purchaser), it is seen, neither resides nor carries on business or personally works for gain within the jurisdiction of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, There is no material in the record showing obtaining of leave of the Court to proceed with the suit against the respondent No. 3 in Dhaka Court.</u>

<u>20. On reading the plaint it is seen that cause of action for filing the suit by the appellant has arisen because of the decree passed in Artha Rin Adalat Case No. 55 of 1990 and the execution taken on the basis of the said decree ending in sale of the property of the respondent No. 3. It may be mentioned decree in Artha Rin Adalat Case No. 55 of 1990 was passed by the Court of Subordinate Judge, Rangpur and the execution case on the basis of the decree passed in the Artha Rin Adalat Case No. 55 of 1990 was initiated in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Rangpur and the property of the appellant in the said execution proceeding sold situates in Rangpur. The respondent No. 2 filed the case against the appellant in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Rangpur alleging that the transaction i.e. loan, was obtained in Rangpur town by the appellant from the respondent No. 2. It is true that respondent No. 1 carries on business through its branch office at Rangpur but the fact remains that the transaction between the appellant and the respondent No. 2 took place in Rangpur. The appellant in his suit filed in the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka impugned the proceedings of the suit decreed by the Court at Rangpur and also the proceedings of the execution case was taken out on the basis of the aforesaid decree in the Court at Rangpur and the property of the appellant was put into auction sale located at Rangpur and was purchased by the respondent No.3 who resides at Rangpur. In such a situation we are of the view the appellant, taking recourse to the provision of section 20(a), CPC read with Explanation II to said section is not competent to file the suit in Dhaka, which is, in fact, the offshoot of the suit which was decreed at Rangpur, since for the purpose of establishing that the decree in Artha Rin Adalat Case No. 55 of 1990 was legally passed and that execution case taken out on the basis of the decree obtained in the Artha Rin Adalat Case and that property of the appellant sold in the execution case were legally done are to be established by the respondent No. 2 through the evidence, both oral and documentary, from Rangpur. So, considering the convenience of the respondent No. 2 in a situation like the instant one we are of the view the appellant is not competent to file the suit as filed in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka impleading the respondent No. 1 whose Head Office is at Dhaka and carries on business through its branches in Rangpur and other places. (see AIR 1992 SC 1514). In the case of Union of India and another vs Ladulal Jain reported in AIR 1963 SC, 1681 it has been held:</u>

<u>"The principle behind the provisions of clauses (a) and (b) of section 20 is that the suit be instituted at a place where the defendant would be able to defend the suit without undue trouble."</u>

<u>21. It may be mentioned the transaction, which the appellant is alleging fraudulent, in connection with which Artha Rin suit was filed, actually took place at Rangpur. There may be a case(s) where decree in a suit was obtained at a particular place, as in the instant case at Rangpur, and that execution was taken out at some other place, say Dhaka and pursuant to that, the judgment-debtor's property located at the place where the execution case has been initiated on the basis of the decree obtained at some other place, as in the instant case at Rangpur, is affected, in such a situation the judgment-debtor figuring as plaintiff can very much file a suit in the jurisdiction where the execution case has been initiated, seeking setting aside of the decree on the ground that the decree was obtained fraudulently and then the Court at such a place i.e where the execution cases has been initiated, would be competent to entertain a suit seeking declaration that the decree in the previous suit was obtained fraudulently and in all other cases the judgment-debtor is to file the suit seeking setting aside the decree passed in the previous suit in the jurisdiction of the Court which passed the decree. The proposition of law as stated above is holding the field from long back, at least from 1902. The suit by the appellant having not been filed at Rangpur in the background of the situation as stated hereinabove, the Court at Dhaka had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit and, in that state of the matter, the High Court Division has quite correctly passed the order for return of the plaint to the learned Advocate of the appellant for filing the same in the appropriate Court. The learned Counsel for the appellant in support of the contention that the suit filed by the appellant in the light of the provision of section 20, CPC can very much be prosecuted in Dhaka has relied upon the decision in the case of Messrs Anwar and Brothers vs Bangladesh Shipping Corporation reported in 1995 BLD 447 = 1 BLC 23. Facts of the said case, in short, are that the plaintiff filed the suit in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against the Bangladesh Shipping Corporation through its branch office at Dhaka for compensation due to late delivery of certain imported goods carried by the ship of the Corporation whose principal office is at Chittagong. Bangladesh Shipping Corporation, having its principal office at Chittagong, filed an application under Order VII, rule 10 read with section 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure contending that principal office of the Corporation at the relevant time was at Chittagong and that cause of action also arose at Chittagong where the goods were unloaded at the port the application so filed was allowed by the trial Court and made order for return of the plaint to the plaintiff. The plaintiff challenged legality of the order for returning the plaint before the High Court Division. While allowing the appeal the High Court Division has observed, upon taking into consideration the Explanation-II of section 20, CPC:</u>

<u>"We, therefore, hold that a plaintiff can sue a corporation either at the place of its principal or subordinate office, but in the latter case it must be found by the trial Court that the corporation can conveniently put up its defence through its subordinate office and thus it cannot be said that because of the expression "in respect of any cause of action arising at any place where it has also a subordinate office" in the Explanation II a suit cannot be instituted at the place of the subordinate office if no part of the cause of action arises at that place."</u>

22. Suffice it to say the observation made in the aforesaid case in the background of the facts of the said case has no manner of application to the facts and circumstances, as stated hereinbefore, of the instant case. In the background of facts of the case referred to by appellant the decision made therein, in our view, is not legally sound since evidence as regard the case of the parties would easily, readily, timely and conveniently be available at the place where the goods were delivered i.e. at the port city. Moreover mere cause of action wholly arose where the goods, said to have been delivered after inordinate delay. As has already been mentioned the intent and purport of the provisions of section 20, CPC are that suit is to be filed at a place where defendant would be able to defend the suit without undue trouble.

23. The appellant could have maintained his suit in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka if the decree passed in the suit filed at Rangpur would have affected the property of the appellant within the jurisdiction of Court at Dhaka and the decree was put into execution at Dhaka. The undisputed position is that decree passed in the Artha Rin Adalat case filed by the respondent No. 2 did not affect property of the appellant in different jurisdiction i.e. in the jurisdiction of Court at Dhaka. The situation being not like that as stated above, we are of the view that the High Court Division was not in error in making the order for return of the plaint to the learned Advocate of the appellant for presentation before the appropriate Court.

24. In the background of our discussions made hereinabove, we find no merit in the appeal.

25. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed.

There is no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Ranadhir Sen J: This appeal at the instance of defendants 16, 18 and 19 is directed against the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge in a suit for recovery of khas possession upon declaration that the suit properties were trust properties along with a prayer for accounting.

2. The plaintiff filed the suit as a pauper with leave of the Court under Order 33 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He claimed to be an administrator of the disputed properties appointed under the letter of ad-ministration granted in his favour by the learned District Judge.

3. The plaintiff case briefly stated is that one Girish Chandra Aich Chowdhury executed a will on 12-1-1911. One Ram Kumar was an elder cousin of the testator Girish. Girish Chandra Aich and Ram Kumar were in joint mess and property. Ram Kumar had no son. Girish Chandra Aich had three sons, Mohendra, Nabin and Nikunja. Mohendra was taken in adoption by Ram Kumar who died leaving Mohendra. Girish Chandra Aich bequeathed his entire properties in terms of the Will dated 12-1-1911. In terms of the said Will Mohendra, Nabin and Nikunja would get six annas live annas and five annas respectively in life interest and on their death their heirs would accordingly have life interest in the said shares. The beneficiaries under the Will were not given any right to transfer the property in any way. Mohendra was however appointed an executor named in the Will. After the death of Girish Chandra Aich in 1912 the beneficiaries started enjoyment of the properties in terms of the Will. Mohendra obtained a probate of the Will in 1926. Thereafter there was a partition amongst the beneficiaries in 1931. The beneficiaries under the Will made various transfers contrary to the provisions made in the Will. On the death of Mohendra the plaintiff, son of Nikunja prayed for a letter of administration. The learned Additional District Judge, however, granted the same in his favour after over-ruling the objections. An application was filed by the plaintiff before the learned Additional District Judge for recovery of khas possession of the properties which, according to him, were trust properties. The learned Additional District Judge, however, directed the plaintiff to seek remedy in a proper forum. Thereafter the instant suit was filed for the following reliefs:-

B. "That the properties described in the schedules below be declared trust property under the Will of late Girish Chandra Aich Chowdhury.

C. That the alienations made by the aforesaid Maliendra and Nikunja in favour of other defendants and the partition deed dated 3-11-31 be declared not to be binding on the estate and administrator of the estate of late Girish Chandra Aich Chowdhury.

D. That the decree for rendition of account regarding the Trust property be passed against defendants and the amounts found due be decreed against the defendants.

E. That a decree for khas possession of the suit property be passed against the defendants."

A further prayer was incorporated that defendants 8 to 18 should be ordered to remove at their own costs, the constructions made by their predecessor in any portion of the disputed lands within the time fixed by the Court in default, the plaintiff be authorised to remove the said constructions by way of execution and realise costs from the defendants.

4. The suit was contested by four sets of defendants, each filing separate written statement. The defendants 4 and 5 filed a written statement denying the general allegations made in the plaint and asserted their title to certain portion of schedule A(3) property as described in the plaint. These defendants contended that they were third parties purchasers for valuable consideration without notice of the alleged Will and Probate as such their purchased right cannot be affected in any way. A plea of bar under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act was also raised.

5. The defendant No. 19 filed a written statement disclaiming interest in the suit property. According to him he has been impleaded unnecessarily. He stated in paragraph 5 of the written statement that this defendant has got no claim or interest in any portion of the suit land. However defendant No. 19 raised an objection that the will was not given effect to before the probate and after the probate application Mohendra, plaintiff's father and uncle transferred bulk of properties to many persons who are in possession of the same for over two decades." Although defendants 16 and 18 are son and mother of the same family but written statements were filed separately. Defendant No. 18 claimed interest in schedule B properties and disclaimed any interest in oilier properties in suit. A bar of limitation was also pleaded by her. According to this defendant the Will was created for the object of protecting the properties from the hands of the creditors. Rant Kumar and Grirish Chandra were heavily indebted. These defendants further contended that after the death of Girish Chandra, plaintiff's father Nikunja and the executor Mohendra transferred bulk of the properties. She asserted that she purchased R.S. plot No. 382 of schedule (B) in mortgage execution sale. She has possessed the same since such purchase on payment of revenue to the Government by raising construction and making improvement thereon.

6. Defendant No. 16 has raised an objection that the suit was bad for misjoinder of parties. Schedule (B) properties being in possession of defendant Nos. 8 and 19, these defendants have got no connection with rest of the suit land. According to this defendant, the defendant No. 19 has got no possession and interest in schedule B land. The Will, if any, as alleged by the plaintiff was fraudulently and collusively created with a view to defraud the creditors. The clause restraining the legatees from transferring the properties was illegal and void. According to him, the bequest was absolute and complete by itself find the reservation clause is nothing but an attempt to protect the properties from their creditors. Girish had no right to make any provision regarding the properties inherited by Mohendra from his father. According to this defendant, the Will was never acted upon as will be evident from the partition deed executed by plaintiff's father and uncle sons and Mohendra after the probate was granted. This defendant claimed to be in possession of the properties in schedule (B) for over the statutory period of limitation by making construction upon the land and by excavating tank in a portion thereof.

7. The issues framed by the learned Subordinate Judge found due reflection of the contentions raised by the parties.

8. In support of the plaintiff's case the plaintiff alone was examined and Exhibits I to 7 were proved and marked as exhibits. Exhibit 1 is the letter of administration granted in favour of the plaintiff. Exhibit 2 is the certified copy of the Will. Exhibit 3 series are certain orders in the probate case. Exhibit 4 is the application for probate with Will in probate case No. 35 of 1926. Exhibit 5 is the certified copy of registered deed of partition executed by Mohendra and others dated 3-11-1931. Exhibit 6 series are copies of certain written statement filed in T.S. No 5 of 1958 and Exhibit 7 is the certified copy of the judgment passed by the said ease.

9. P.W. 1 in his evidence stated that his grandfather Girish Chandra Aids was the owner of the suit land and he made a Will Exhibit 2. The probate of the said Will was obtained. Ram Kumar had no interest in the suit land. Mohendra was the executor of the Will and he managed the properties in that capacity. Mohendra died in 1953 and thereafter he filed the application for letter of administration which was allowed and he was appointed an administrator in respect of the properties. The suit land being in possession of the defendants, he filed the suit for recovery of khan possession upon declaration that the properties were trust property. This witness stated that Mohendra or his father Nikunja had no right to transfer any land. According to him, the defendants were aware of the Will and the reservation made thereunder. The plaintiff characterised Exhibit 5 the partition deed as collusive. This witness further stated that he had no knowledge of the particulars of the properties or the persons in possession before his appointment as an administrator. He, however, denied the defence case that Girish Chandra, Ram Kumar, Mohendra and others were heavily indebted and that the Will was created to defeat the claim of the creditors. This witness further denied the defence claim of improvement of the suit land. In cross-examination he admitted that Mohendra left four sons. He further stated that he came to know about the Will in 1953 after the death of Mohendra. He, however, admitted that Girish Chandra Aids and Ram Kumar were in joint mess and property. R.S. operation, according to this witness, took place before his birth. P.W. 1 admitted that the defendants have their homestead and some pucca structures in certain portion of the suit land. He also admitted that he was an attesting witness to a settlement granted by his father defendant No. 1 in favour of one Dhirendra Nath Basu for live years. No other witness was examined on behalf of the plaintiff.

10. On behalf of the contesting defendants, defendant No. 19 Jogendra Lal Chowdhury was examined. He deposed for the defendants 16 and 18. This witness however, disclaimed any interest of his own in the suit land. He stated that he was a benamder of his maternal uncle in respect of the auction purchase. He denied any knowledge about the Will or the probate. According to him R.S. and P.S. khatians are correct. This witness, however, was claiming his presence at the time of the kabalas but he did not see any agreement.

11. On behalf of the contesting defendants 4 and 5 D.W.2 Sudhir Chandra De was examined. Defendant No. 4 was the uncle of this witness and defendant No. 5 was the wife of defendant No. 4 who is aged about 90 years. According to this witness defendant No. 4 and 5 purchased land and have possessed the same. The plaintiff and his father all along knew about the purchase by defendant Nos. 4 and 5. This witness was not present at the time of the kabalas. This witness admitted that the plaintiff did not know about these Kabalas. This is all the evidences on behalf of the contesting defendants.

12. An agreement dated 22-1-1962 was marked as Ext. A(1). Exhibit B(1) to B(5) are certain kabalas. Exhibit C I series are certain mortgage deeds. Exhibit D I series are the sale certificates. Exhibit E I series is the writ of delivery of possession. Exhibit Flseries are the copy of orders relating to delivery of possession. Exhibit GI is the copy of plaint in Title suit No. 99 of 1944. Exhibit HI is the certified copy of a patta. Exhibit 41) series are R.S. and P.S. khatians whereas. Exhibit J series are certain dakhilas. Exhibit K1 is the certified copy of demand notice Exhibit LI series are certain challans and Exhibit MI is the certified copy of the order sheet in certain title suits. These are all the documents put in evidence on behalf of the contesting defendants.

13. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the materials on record decreed the suit in full. The plaintiff title to the suit was declared and he was to get possession by evicting the defendants and removing the defendant construction and obstruction. The partition deed Exhibit 5 and the subsequent transfers by Mohendra and defendants 1 to 3 were declared to be not binding against the trust properties i.e. the suit lands. The learned Subordinate Judge however dismissed the plaintiffs claim for accounting. In reaching the aforesaid conclusion the learned Subordinate Judge found nothing wrong with issue No. 3, 4 and 10 and accordingly answered the same in favour of the plaintiff. While considering the question as to the bonafides of the Will executed by Girish Chandra, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge recorded a clear finding that the Will was a bonafide document and it was not created to defraud the creditors. Evidently, there was no evidence before the learned Subordinate Judge to indicate that Ram Kumar or Girish had any debts or Girish executed the Will in 1911 to defraud the claim of the creditors. While considering the question whether the Will was acted upon, the learned Subordinate Judge reached a concluding finding that the Will was acted upon. The learned subordinate Judge considered Exhibits 2, 3 and 4 and in the light of the evidence on record held that the application for probate was made by Mohendra and the probate was granted in his favour by a competent Court. The learned Subordinate Judge also noticed Exhibit 5 the deed of partition of the year 1931 purporting to partition the properties left by the Will. The learned Subordinate Judge noticed that the parties to the deed of partition admitted that they derived interest in terms of the Will. Accordingly he concluded that the Will was acted upon. Turning to the question whether a trust was created by the Will the learned Subordinate Judge was of the view that "a trust is obviously created according to Trust Act." The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have considered the recitals made in the Will in terms whereof the beneficiaries were to get the only usufruct of the properties and they had no right to transfer or to encumber the property in any way. Mohendra was appointed the first executor and he was entrusted with the duty to perform puja of the family deity from income of the property and to act in terms of the will.

14. The learned Subordinate Judge noticed that the defendants or their predecessors were no doubt transferees for valuable consideration from the plaintiff's father and uncle but was of the view that these transactions were hardly bonafide transfers. According to the learned Subordinate Judge the suit was not barred by limitation and the plaintiff was entitled to the relief claimed saved the relief for accounting. The learned Subordinate Judge negative the defence contention of adverse possession.

15. Defendants 4 and 5 did not prefer any appeal against the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge. Defendants 16, 18 and 19 have preferred this appeal. Out of the appellants, defendant No. 19 as indicated earlier is a disclaimer. The interest of defendant No. 18 Sorola Bala Chowdhury has devolved upon her son defendant No. 16 Narendra Lal Chowdhury on the death of Sorola Bala during the pendency of the appeal.

16. This appeal now therefore, is directed against the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge so far it relates to schedule (B) of the plaint. Keeping the said limitation in view Mr. Abdur Rab the learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal has taken us through the relevant materials on record to press the appeal Mr. Rab contends that the suit was bad for defect of parties since four sons of Mohendra have not been impleaded in the suit. It is in the evidence of P.W. 1 that Mohendra died leaving four sons.

17. Mr. S.S. Haider, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents contends that the sons of Mohendra have no subsisting interest and they are not in possession of any property in suit and as such their presence was neither necessary nor proper for disposal of the instant suit. On perusal of the materials on record there is nothing to indicate that the sons of Mohendra are in possession of any parcel of the suit property or that they claimed any interest therein either directly or through others. Therefore, their presence does not appear to be necessary and the suit does not fail on the ground of defect of parties for not impleading them. Thus the contention of Mr. Rab does not seem to be of any substance.

18. Mr. Rab has next contended that the clog to transfer as contained in the Will is hit by section 10 of the Transfer of Property Act and the Will to that extent is void. We may refer to section 10 of the Transfer of Property Act which runs as follows:-

"Where property is transferred subject to a condition or limitation absolutely restraining the transferee or any person claiming under him from parting with or disposing of his interest in the property the condition or limitation is void except in the case of a lease where the condition is for the benefit of the lessor or those claiming under him: Provided that property may be transferred to or for the benefit of a woman (not being a Hindu, Mohammedan or Buddhist) so that she shall not have power during her marriage to transfer or charge the same or her beneficial interest therein."

<u>19. It does not appear that disposition of the property by the Will was a transfer within the meaning of the Transfer of Property Act. Therefore, in our opinion, section 10 of the Transfer of Property Act has no part to play. The decision in the case of Seth Jassumal V. The Central Govt. Rehabilitation Department and others reported in 13 D.L.R. (S.C) 177 is distinguishable in facts and principles. It arose out of a reference. It rather assisted the plaintiff's case to this extent that a Will does not come within the ambit of Transfer of Property Act dealt under the Transfer of Property. Therefore, this contention of Mr. Rab does not stand on sound footing.</u>

20. Mr. Rab has next contended that the will did not create a trust and that the same was not acted upon. In this regard he has drawn our attention to the following provisions of the Trust Act. Section 3 of the Trust Act defines and interpretes the expressions used in the Act namely, "the person who reposes or declares the confidence is called the "author of the trust" the person who accepts the confidence is called the "trustee" the person for whose benefit the confidence is accepted is called the "beneficiary" the subject matter of the trust is called "trust property" or "trust money" the beneficial interest" or "interest" of the beneficiary is his right against the trustee as owner of the trust property;"

21. Section 4 speaks about the purpose for which a trust may be created. Section runs as follows:-

"A trust may be created for any lawful purpose. The purpose of a trust is lawful unless it is (a) forbidden by law, or (b) is of such a nature that, if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law, or (c) is fraudulent, or (d) involves or implies injury to the person or property of another, or (e) the Court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy.

Every trust of which the purpose is unlawful is void, And where a trust is created for two purposes, of which one is lawful and the other unlawful, and the two purposes cannot he separated, the whole trust is void."

Section 5 of the Trust Act runs as follows:-"No trust in relation to immovable property is valid unless declared by a non-testamentary instrument in writing signed by the author of the trust or the trustee and registered, or by the Will of the author of the trust or of the trustee."

Section 6 is also of some relevance and it runs as follows:-"

Subject to the provisions of section 5, a trust is created when the author of the trust indicates with reasonable certainty by any words or acts, (a) an intention on his part to create thereby a trust, (b) the purpose of the trust, (c) the beneficiary, and (d) the trust property, and (unless the trust is declared by will or the author of the trust is himself to be the trustee) transfers the trust property to the trustee."

Section 7 indicates that a trust may be created by every person competent to contract. Section 8 however speaks of the subject matter of a trust which must be property transferable to the beneficiary.

<u>22. Reading the aforesaid provisions, we may hold that a trust may be created by a Will. In the instant case the trust was created by the Will dated 12-1-1911 if the other requirements are found to be satisfied. Evidently, Girish Chandra Aich was a person competent to contract and as such there was no impediment in creating a trust by the Will. The subject matter of the trust is a property transferable to the beneficiary. It, therefore, satisfies this contention. We read in the will Exhibit 2 an intention of the testator who is otherwise qualified as the author of the trust and intention on his part to create a trust. The purpose is also well defined in the Will itself. The beneficiaries have been named and the duties and the confidence have been specifically spelled out in the Will itself. In such circumstances, we find it difficult to hold that no trust was created by the Will or that it was void. Mr. Haider pointed out that the amended section of section 1 of the Trust Act which runs as follows:-</u>

<u>"It extends to the whole of Bangladesh. But nothing herein contained affects the rules of Muhammadan Law as to waqf or the mutual relations of the members of an undivided family as determined by any customary or personal law, or applies to public or private religious or charitable endowments, or to trusts to distribute prizes taken in war among the captors; and nothing in the second chapter of this Act applies to trusts created before the said day."</u>

<u>Therefore, if we read the Will Exhibit 2 keeping in view the aforesaid requirements of the statute we may find that the testator has clearly depicted the situation prevailing at the time of execution of the Will and we may read his intention. We notice that Ram Kumar during his life time took loans by mortgaging ancestral properties and ultimately died. Girish Chandra Aich with his own income repaid loans and restored the properties and he also purchased many properties by his own efforts and money. Mohendra was a son of Girish but was taken in adoption by Ram Kumar, Girish Chandra Aich distributed the shares in six annas, five annas and five annas share of the usufructs of the properties in favour of Mohendra, Nabin and Nikunja respectively. He has clearly stipulated that the beneficiaries shall have life interest in the properties and they will enjoy the usufructs of the properties only but in no way shall be entitled to transfer, mortgage or encumber the same. These stipulations in our opinion are permissible in law and does not offend the provisions of section 10 of the Transfer of Property Act and as such the same cannot be termed void. This being the position the executor obtained the probate from a competent Court and went on discharging the duties as a trustee in respect of the trust property, which have been described in the schedule to the plaint. We notice certain other stipulations which indicate that a private family endowments was also made charging the income of the properties out of the usufructs for the purpose of Sheba puja. Girish Chandra Aich made a clear stipulation that "Mohendra shall not be entitled to claim any property as ancestral share. If he claims any property going outside of the provisions of this Will, then, he or his sons shall get nothing from this property acquired by me and wills my own money."</u>

<u>23. Reading the will as a whole we do not find any justification in support of the contention of Mr. Rab to strike down the same. Mr. Rab has referred to certain decisions in support of his contentions. A reference has been made to the case of Ram Ran Vijay Prasad Singh V. Province of Bihar reported in A.I.R. 1942 Patna 435 for the proposition that the essential characteristic of trust must be expressed with reasonable certainly. This case arose out of a reference under the Bihar Agricultural Income Tax Act. The Maharaja Sir Radha Prasad Singh made a declaration to spend certain sum of money for charitable and religious objects. It was contended that the said direction to spend the suns of Rs. 32,400/- meant to create a trust and as such was not exempted from the mischief of the Bihar Agricultural Income Tax Act. In the said Full Bench case it was held that the declaration was a mere pious wish and as such did not mean to create a trust for religious and charitable ground. It was however, noticed that the grantor or a testator need not use the word "trust" to create a valid trust. The facts appear to be distinguishable but in the instant case it may be said that Girish Chandra Aich did not spell out the word "trust" in the Will. The absence of the word "trust" in the Will did not vitiate the "trust" if the intention can be gathered and the requirements of a trust are established. Therefore this decision is of no active assistance to Mr. Rab.</u>

24. The learned Advocate has next relied upon a decision in the case of Thayamal V. Perumal Chetti and another reported in A.I.R. 1926 Madras 284. This case is evidently distinguishable in the facts of the instant case since the trustee did not assign the document. In the instant case we have indicated earlier that the will was duly executed by the testator and a probate thereof was granted. As such the requirements of section 6 of the Trust Act as quoted earlier have been satisfied. Therefore this decision is also of no help to Mr. Rab.

25. The next case relied upon by the learned Advocate relates to requirement of sections 5, 6 and 8. It is the case of Viscount Maugham, Lord Macmillan and Lord Wright Chambers V. Chambers and others reported in A.I.R. 1944 Privy Council 78. It has been noticed that the requirements of the statute must be satisfied in order to make a valid trust. We have earlier quoted the relevant provisions of the Trust Act to indicate that Exhibit 2, the Will satisfied the requirements of the relevant provisions of the statutes and as such created a valid trust. Therefore, this decision is also of no help to Mr. Rab. Similarly the case of Venkatachallapathi yer V. China Mona Chakaran paniIyer reported in A.I.R. 1922 (Madras) 83 does not help Mr. Rab for the proposition cavassed by him. We have read and construed Exhibit 2 in the light of the provisions of the Trust Act and in our opinion valid trust was created therein.

26. It has been next contended by Mr. Rab that the suit was barred by limitation. Mr. Rab referred to and relied upon section 10 of the Limitation Act which runs as follows:-

"Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, no suit against a person in whom property has become vested in trust for any specific purpose, or against his legal representatives or assigns (not being assigns for valuable consideration) for the purpose of following in his or their hands such property or the proceeds thereof or for an account of such property or proceeds, shall be barred by any length of time.

For the purpose of this section any property comprised in a Hindu, Muslim or Buddhist religious or charitable endowment shall be deemed to be property vested in trust for a specific purpose, and the manager of any such property shall be deemed to be the trustee thereof."

27. Reading this provisions as a whole it is evident that a suit against a person in whom the property has become vested in trust for certain specific purposes or his legal representatives or assigns shall not be barred by any length of time. By the amendment the second paragraph was added for the purpose of this section to comprehend "any property comprised in a Hindu, or Muslim or Buddhist religious or charitable endowment shall be deemed to be property vested in trust for a specific purpose." Therefore, the mischief of limitation generally in terms of section 10 did not bar the suit so far as the prayer for declaration is concerned. But Mr. Rab has specifically drawn our attention to the evidence of P.W.1 and the claim of contesting defendant 16. Mr. Rab has contended that it is only with regard to schedule (B) and more particularly with regard to the homestead and the tank that the suit is out of time since the plaintiff had knowledge of the transfer before 12 years from the date.

28. Mr. Halder has drawn our attention to a decision of a Single Bench of this Court in the case Afser Molla and another V. Abdul Aziz and others reported its 29 D.L.R. 416. In that case section 20 of the Trust Act and Article 148 of the Limitation Act were considered. In the instant case these provisions are not involved. This case therefore, is of no assistance to Mr. Haider. We have indicated earlier that defendant No. 16 group has been claiming title and possession on the basis of auction purchase for a period over 12 years. It has been admitted by P.W.1 that Defdts have their homestead and some pucca structures in certain portion of the suit lands. It is also in the evidence of P.W I that Mohendra died in 1953 and he came to know about the will after the death of Mohendra. The defence contention on the other hand is that they are in possession of their purchased land from the date of such purchase. It is difficult for us to rely upon the uncorroborated testimony of the plaintiffs that he had no knowledge as to the possession of the defendant No. 16 group in the homestead and the tank. In this view of the matter Mr. Rub has drawn our attention to Article 134 of the Limitation Act for the purpose of the suit. Article 134 provides for a suit within 12 years from the date the transfer becomes known to the plaintiff in order to recover possession of immoveable property conveyed or bequeathed in trust or mortgaged and afterwards transferred by the trustee or mortgagee for a valuable consideration. We have earlier held that the transfer was made by Mohendra a trustee under Exhibit 2 to the Will in contravention of certain terms. Therefore, such a suit for recovery of possession appears to be contemplated by the said Article. It is 12 years from the date of the transfer being known to the plaintiff. The plaintiff did not say in his evidence that the transfer of the homestead and the tank in favour of defendant No 18 and 16 as claimed by them was not known to him. It rather appears from his admission that the homestead of the defendants was known to him and to his knowledge, pucca structures in certain portions were built; if that is so, it was for the plaintiff to prove that he was within 12 years from his knowledge of the transfer. We find it difficult to rely upon his evidence that he had no knowledge of the transfer of the homestead and the tank as appearing in schedule B of the plaint. This homestead and the adjoining tank, in our opinion, cannot be recovered from the possession of defendant No. 16 group. In the circumstances we hold that the interest of defendant No. 16 as it now stands in the homestead and the tank remains unaffected and the suit is not liable to succeed to that extent for recovery of possession. We have no reason to disbelieve the long possession of defendant No. 16 group in the homestead and the tank and connected khatian and dakhilas supporting such claim. In this view of the matter we modify the decree of the learned Subordinate Judge to this extent. For the reasons stated above the appeal succeeds in part, namely, in respect of the homestead and the tank appertaining to Schedule (B) of the plaint as claimed by defendants Nos. 16 and 18. Barring the extent indicated above, the decree of the trial Court needs no interference.

29. In the result the appeal succeeds in part. The judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge are modified to the extent indicated above and the plaintiff's suit to the extent it relates to the homestead and the tank in occupation of defendant No. 16 and 18 stands dismissed.

30. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case we direct the parties to bear their own costs of this appeal.

End.

MI Farooqui with Sadekur Rahman Nazneen Nahar & Mahbub Ul-Islam, Advocates-For the Petitioners. 
Mahbubey Alam, Attorney-General Abdus Salam Mondal, Deputy Attorney-General, Bahauddin Ahmed Assistant Attorney-General & Mahfuza Begum Assistant Attorney-General-For the Opposite-Parties.
