full_judgment:
Nozrul Islam Chowdhury J: This Rule is directed an order dated 6-3-2001 passed by the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 36 of 2010 allowing an application for withdrawal of the suit under Order XXIII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure upon rejecting the application for transposition filed by the defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4.

2. Short facts necessary for the purpose of disposal of this rule are that the opposite-party No. 1 Bangladesh as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 36 of 2010 impleading the petitioners and others as defendants seeking a decree for declaration of its title and for partition. The petitioner entered appearance upon filling written statement thereafter issues were framed by the trial court and the suit was fixed for peremptory hearing. At that stage an application under Order XXIII, rule 1(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed by the plaintiff to withdraw the suit without any permission to sue afresh. Defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 who are the petitioners before us filed an application for transposition with a prayer for transposing them as plaintiff Nos. 1, 3 and 4 in the suit.

3. Both the said applications namely, the application under Order XXIII, rule (1) filed by the plaintiff and the application for transposition filed by the defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 were taken up for hearing by the learned Joint District Judge and after hearing both sides the learned Joint District by the impugned order dated 6-3-2011 allowed the application for withdrawal filed by the plaintiff and rejected the application for transposition filed by the defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4. While passing the impugned order the learned Joint District Judge also observed that the defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 i.e. the petitioners before this court are at liberty to bring a fresh suit.

4. Challenging the aforesaid order dated 6-3-2011 the defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 in that suit having felt aggrieved brought this application and obtained the present Rule.

5. Mr MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners has taken us through the entire materials including the impugned order and submits that the suit brought by the opposite-party No. 1 was in substance a suit for partition where the plaintiff prayed for a separate sham out of a piece of land as described in the plaint and that unlike any other suit. In a suit for partition the plaintiff and the defendants stand on the same footing and in the event of a prayer for a saham upon payment of court fees by any of the defendants his case has to be decided by the trial court for granting a sham as prayed for and in the position as aforesaid the trial Court acted illegally resulting an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in rejecting the prayer for transposition filed by the defendants in that suit as such, the impugned order is liable to be set-aside.

6. Mr MI Farooqui, submits further that the provision of Sub-rule (2) of rule 10 under Order I empowers the Court concerned to transpose the plaintiff into defendant and vice versa in the interest of justice and under the circumstances disclosed in the instant Rule dragging a party to a fresh suit as observed in the impugned order amounts to an error of law which has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. Since the Procedure Code specially the provision under Order I, rule 10 discourage multiplicity of the suit.

7. In substituting his submission the learned Advocate for the petitioner placed reliance in the case of Bhupendra Narayan Singh vs Rajeswar Prasad Bhakat reported in 58 Indian Appeal (PC) 228 and in the case of Nirode Chandra Banarjee vs Profulla Chandra Banarjee reported in 40 CLJ 538, Fayez Ahmed vs Kunchama Khatun reported in 12 DLR 712 and the case of Abdul Jalil Sheikh vs Rahima Khatun reported in 51 DLR 441.

8. Mr Farooqui also pointed out that the provision of Order XX, rule 18(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure makes room for the trial Court to decide right of the parties before granting a saham as prayed in a partition suit and in that view of the matter the transposition as prayed for by the petitioner has no occasion to cause prejudice to either party in any way, therefore, prayer for transposition ought to have been allowed by the trial Court and a contrary -New amounts to error of law which has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. It has also been pointed out by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that in the light of the judgment delivered in the case of Benoy Bhusan Bardhan being dead his heirs pronoy Bhusan Bardhan vs Sub-Divisional Officer, Brahmanbaria reported in 30 DLR (SC) 139 wherein it was held by the apex court to the effect; land in joint possession of which part in joint possession of real owner and part belongs to an enemy owner-Custodian cannot dispossess the real owner from the land. The only remedy to seek a partition so as to separate the enemy portion from the portion. (In the instant suit before us subject matter of the suit is in the nature of abandoned property though not enemy, property or vested property but the principles laid down in that case are same for this case). The government brought the instant suit for partition and rightly so, but at the concluding stage of the suit it is not known what prompted the plaintiff to withdraw from the same and that for this reason why the defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 filed the application for transposition and under the facts and circumstances involved in the instant case the said application ought to have been allowed by the trial court to determine the issue involved in the suit completely and effectually without dragging the parties to a separate suit opening the scope for multiplicity of the proceedings.

9. Mr. Mahabubey Alam, the learned Attorney-General, on the other hand, appearing for the opposite-party strenuously argued that the transposition is not permissible where the plaintiff and the defendants raised conflicting claim with a view to establish conflicting interest and with a view to substantiate his submission Mr Attorney-General placed reliance in the case of Malek Momtaz Ali vs Pakistan reported in PLD 1971 (Lahore) 395. It is also submitted by the learned Attorney-General that the instant suit being not a suit for partition simplicitor the contesting defendant are not entitled to an order of transposition in the category of the plaintiffs.

10. The learned Attorney-General has also given a written submission before us of which paragraph 2 reads as follows:—

"that in the plaint, Government having claimed 0.7831 acres of land of SA Plot Nos. 4236, 4237, 4223 and 4235 as abandoned property and having also prayed for a decree that recording of major portion of the said plots in Rs and Mahanagor Survey in the name of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is illegal and void and the Government having raised direct allegation against the defendant No. 1 and 2 and claim of the plaintiff being diametrically opposite to the defendant, as such defendant cannot be transposed as plaintiffs."

11. In paragraph 3 of the said written submission it has been disclosed as under:-

"that the plaintiff having made allegation against the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 for grabbing government property which are abandoned and, as such, specific allegation having been raised by the plaintiffs against the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 as such, the defendant cannot be transposed as plaintiff."

12. Mr Attorney-General, has also placed reliance in the case of Atash Ali vs Mst Gulap Banu an un-reported case where judgment was delivered in Civil Appeal No. 40 of 1990 by the Appellate Division and the case of Abdur Rahim vs Momtaz Begum reported in 32 BLD 64.

13. In view of the claim and counter claim made by the learned Advocate from both sides, we feel it proper to assess the submissions made by the learned Advocates one after another. In doing so we find that in the case of 58 Indian Appeal (PC) 228 an observation as made in that case to the effect:-

........the Court clearly had power at any stage of the proceedings to remedy the defect under Order I, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure by adding the proforma defendants as co-plaintiffs with the appellant. Such a course should in their Lordship opinion always be adopted where it is necessary for a complete adjudication upon the questions involved in the suit land to avoid multiplicity of proceedings."

Mr. Farooqui, place reliance in this part of the judgment as quoted above. The other case relied by Mr. Farooqui is the case reported in 40 CLJ 535.

14. Having gone through the said judgment it appears to us, that a celebrated Judge like Sir Ashutosh Mookerjee. Held that the Court has very wide powers under the Code of Civil Procedure, in respect of addition, or transfer, of parties. This discretionary power, should be exercised in such a way as to achieve the ends of substantial justice.

15. Mr Farooqui, also relied on in the case of 12 DLR 712 wherefrom we find that a Division bench of the High Court of East Pakistan has held:—

"Therefore, there is no doubt that a party cannot be transposed to the category of the plaintiff if the ends of justice require and the Court has got absolute power though it is a discretionary one to exercise that power where it is necessary, for ends of justice and to avoid multiplicity of suit."

16. The last decision relied upon by Mr. Farooqui, in the case of Abdul Jalil Sheikh vs Rahima Khatun reported in, 51 DLR 441. The recent judgment by a Division Bench of this Court. Having gone through the said judgment we find the ultimate decision arrived in that decision reads as under:-

"It appears that the suit is a suit for partition. The sole plaintiff who relinquished her share in the suit land has filed a compromise petition in Court allegedly in collusion with the defendant Nos. 13-16 and in view of the fact that these defendant petitioners claim share in the suit land through the admitted original owner Mollick Shah, they are entitled to be transposed in the category of the plaintiffs from defendants as prayed for."

17. To elucidate the aforesaid decisions for the purpose of deciding the applicability thereof in the instant case we find that in the instant case before us the plaintiff had prayed for a decree declaring its title in the suit land and .for correction of record of right and also for partition of its claimed land and in view of Order XX, rule 18 Sub-Rule (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure it is evident that while granting a saham to a particular property in a partition suit, it is also incumbent upon the Court concerned to decide the right, title in that particular property for the claimed saham. We have also quoted the written submissions advanced by the learned Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the opposite-party in this Rule. Wherefrom it is evident that claims and counter claims have been made by the parties over the same subject matter of the suit and that has to be decided finally and completely in between the parties and in doing so we find no reason for either party to be prejudiced on the final adjudication of the present suit. We have also pointed out earlier that the suit in substance a suit for partition and relying on the recent decision placed by the learned Attorney-General, we find that the view we have taken is also fortified by the judgment of Civil Appeal No. 40 of 1990 which reads as follows:—

"Generally in a suit for partition transposition of a plaintiff from the category of defendant and vice versa is allowed because of action in such a suit whether it be in respect of plaintiff or defendants remains the same."

18. The other case relied upon by the learned Attorney-General reported in 32 BLD 64. In that case it has been held by a Division Bench of this Court," the legal representative in a suit is not brought either on record under Order XXII, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure then they can be brought on record under Order I, rule 10, read with section 151 of the Code because failure to bring the parties on record as legal representative will prelude the applicant to get justice."

<u>19. An observation was also made in the judgment to the effect that the power of transposition as provided under Order I, rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure should be exercised for the ends of justice if it is required to transfer from one side to another. On the other hand, the refusal to do so prejudicially affected the aggrieved person by driving him to another suit.</u>

20. On a plain reading of the judgments relied upon by the learned Attorney-General we find that those judgments in no way help the opposite-party rather the case cited by him support the case of the petitioner, more particularly in view of the written submissions made by the learned Attorney-General we find that the question of title adverse to each other have been raised by the parties which should be resolved finally and completely in he proceeding of the instant suit at the instance of the defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 as prayed for by them before the trial Court upon transposing them from the category of the defendant to plaintiff.

21. Having considered the submissions made at length by both Mr. MI Farooqui and the learned Attorney-General, we find substance in the submission made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner while the submission made by the learned Attorney-General are not tenable particularly in view of the facts and circumstances and in view of the fact that the instant suit is one in substance a partition suit which should be allowed to proceed up to the finality deciding very many complicated issues raised by the parties in the meantime.

22. In view what has been stated above, we find substance in this Rule.

23. Accordingly, this rule is made absolute and the impugned order dated 6-3-2011 passed by the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 36 of 2010 is hereby set-aside and the defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 who were petitioners before us are hereby transposed to the category of plaintiffs while the plaintiff of the original suit is hereby transposed as defendant.

24. The trial Court is however directed to dispose of the suit as early as possible and till disposal of the suit the order of status quo granted by this Court shall continue. The learned Joint District Judge, is also directed to proceed with the suit in accordance with law specially with reference to the provision of Order XX, rule 18 sub-rule(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

End.

caseno: Civil Revision No.1769 of 2012 with Civil Revision No.1772 of 2012.
lawyer:
Md Ziaul Haque, Advocate with Rafiqul Islam Sohel, Advocate—For the Petitioners. 
Khair Ezaz Maswood, Advocate with AQM Shafiullah, Advocate with Ruhul Ameen, Advocate and Rokeya Akhter, Advocate—For the Opposite-Parties.
parties:
Rokeya Begum ------ Petitioner
vs
Advocate Abdul Awal and ors ------ Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
Sharif Uddin Chaklader J : Rokeya Begum as petitioner moved this Court under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure against the judgment and decree dated 30-11-2011 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Feni dismissing Title Appeal No.87 of 2009 affirming those dated 18-11-2009 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Feni Sadar, decreeing Title Suit No. 49 of 2002.

2. Plaintiff Abdul Awal on the following averments filed the suit for pre-emption under Mohammadan Law. It is his case that Bashirullah was the owner of the suit land of CS khatian No. 19 and SA khatian No.17, died leaving 3 sons, Siddique Ahmed, Sultan Ahmed and Khaiz Ahmed and 3 daughters, Firoza Khatun, Mamuna Khatun, Maksuda Khatun by his first wife and 2 daughters, Golnahar and Fatema Khatun by his 2 wife and 2nd wife Amena Khatun. Out of the heirs, Siddique Ahmed died leaving plaintiff, defendant Nos.5 and 6 as three sons, one daughter, defendant No.7 and wife, defendant No-8. Other heirs of Bashirullah also died leaving heirs as well. Plaintiff is a co-sharer by inheritance in the suit land. Plaintiff used to live in Dhaka. Plaintiff came to the village on 15-3-2002 and learned to know that the suit land has been transferred. Immediately plaintiff has performed the formalities of Talab-I-Ishad and Talab-i-Mowasibat in presence of witnesses and tendered price money to defendant No. l. But defendant No.1 did not pay any heed to this issue as such, plaintiff after obtaining certified copy on 17-4-2002 definitely came to know about the sale that defendant Nos.2-4 sold the suit land to defendant No.1 by Ewaz deed No.517 dated 28-1-1999. Plaintiff case is that exchange deed was made to overcome the right of pre-emption, filed the suit.

3. Petitioner as defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint and after taking all the preliminary objections as to maintainability of the suit, it is her case that Basirullah sold 44 decimals of land by deed No.4330 dated 23-9-1946 to the predecessor of defendant No. 1. Rustam Mia, Sultan Ahmed, son of Basirullah, sold to Rustam Mian 33 decimals of land by deed No.6227 dated 1-12-1957. SA khatian No. 17 rightly recorded his name along with others, as such, he was a co-sharer in the suit land. Rustom Mian died leaving Makbul Ahmed and 8 sons, one daughter, Hajera Begum. Makbul Ahmed died leaving 4 sons including defendant Nos. l and 4. The heirs of Basirullah were also co-sharer in the suit jote. Khaiz Ahmed, son of Basirullah died leaving wife, Halima Begum and Rokeya Begum and others as 3 daughters, Jamaluddin and others as 3 sons. In this way defendant Nos.2-4 became owners in the suit jote and they have transferred the suit plot to defendant No.1 by ewaj deed No.517 dated 28-1-1999. Defendant No.1 become the owner in that land and possessing the land to the knowledge of the plaintiff since transfer. Plaintiff is not entitled to claim pre-emption as he is no way co-sharer in the suit jote. Moreover, defendant No. 17 added after he has filed Miscellaneous Case No.62 of 2007. She has obtained a compromise decree in terms of solenama against the ewaj deed in question hence the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. Six issues were framed i.e. whether the suit is maintainable in its present form, whether the suit is bad for defect of parties, whether the suit is time barred, whether other formalities for pre-emption observed under Mohammadan law, whether the plaintiff is 1st Class co-sharer by inheritance in the suit jote, whether the plaintiff entitled to get a decree of pre-emption as prayed for?

5. In the suit plaintiff examined 4 witnesses and defendant No.1 examined including herself, Tofail Ahmed as DW 2, Hosen Ahmed as DW 3, Md Shahidullha as DW 4 and Haji Mozzamel Haq has deposed on behalf of defendant No. 17 as attorney. Plaintiff adduced exhibit-1 to exhibit-3 series and defendant Nos.1 and 17 exhibit-ka to exhibit-ga and exhibit-ka (1) to exhibit-ga (1).

6. Both the courts below decreed the suit concurrently. Mr Ziaul Haqgue, with Mr Rafiqul Islam Sohel, learned advocates appearing for the petitioner, submits that, both the Courts below committed gross illegality in not considering the suit land having been acquired by defendant No. 1 by previous Miscellaneous Case No. 62 of 2007 in pre-emption, this suit is not maintainable. Learned Advocate further submits that plaintiff had come to his village home before 15-3-2000 and he was also seen the shop made by the defendant No. 1 in the suit land but no discussion has been made to the said fact. Learned Advocate further submits that plaintiff did not perform all the formalities under Mohammadan Law, even there is no mention of tendering Taka 15,000 as suit value to the defendant No. 1 in the plaint as such the suit is not maintainable. Learned Advocate further submits that since the petitioner acquired the suit property in previously instituted Miscellaneous Case No.62 of 2007 by solenama in the aforesaid pre-emption case, the instant suit under Mohammadan Law is not maintainable.

7. On the question of maintainability of the suit, learned Advocate relied on the case of Nuri Miah vs Ambica Singh and another, 34 Indian Cases-869 and also the case of Md Arshad Hussain vs The State of Bihar and others, judgment dated 22-4-2011 passed in Letters Patent Appeal No.313 of 2010.

8. Learned Advocate also on admissibility of the earlier decision, relied on section 41 of the Evidence Act as well as on the case of Hazi Waziullah alias Waziullah Miah vs The Additional Deputy Commissioner, Revenue, Noakhali and Assistant Custodian of Vested and Non-Resident Property, 41 DLR (AD) 97. Learned Advocate also relied on the case of Attar Mia vs Mahmuda Khatun Chowdhury, 1 MLR (AD) 59 = 48 DLR (AD) 16. This judgment is on the question of partial pre-emption.

9. Mr Khair Ezaz Maswood along with Mr AQM Shafiullah, learned Advocates, appearing for the opposite parties, submits that concurring findings of fact if not perverse, under section 151(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure this Court has no jurisdiction to interfere with those findings. Learned Advocate on the question of two judgments on same subject matter submits that judgment passed under section 96 of the Sate Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not decree, it is order, other judgment passed on the instant suit, which being decree prevail over the judgment passed under State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and relied on the case of Mohammad Siddiq vs Ghasi Ram, AIR 1946 (Lahore) 322.

10. Rule of Civil Revision No. 1772 of 2012 was obtained by Abdul Malek alias Manu against judgment and decree dated 30-11-2011 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2n court, Feni in Title Appeal No.90 of 2009 affirming those dated 18-11-2009 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Feni Sadar, Feni decreeing Title Suit No.49 of 2002. In that suit plaintiff is same but defendant No.1, who is petitioner, is different. The facts disclosed by defendant No.1 of this suit is verbatim same as of defendant No. of the instant suit; as such, we do not proposed to write the similar fact once again. Issues were similar and witnesses examined are same.

11. Mr Rafiqul Islam Sohel, learned Advocate, appearing for the defendant-petitioner, submits that, Courts below concurrently failed to consider that defendant No.1 is a co-sharer by inheritance as such if any transfer made in favour of defendant No.1 then it is hit by provision of law. Learned Advocate referred to the case of Abdul Haque Miah vs Abdur Rashid, 1983 BLD (AD) 103 = 35 DLR (AD) 54. Learned Advocate next submits that transfer was made on 28-1-1999, suit has been filed on 9-6-2002, the suit having been filed long after period of limitation, is barred by limitation under Mohammadan Law, Mohammadan Law prescribed filing of suit within one year from the date of transfer. Learned Advocate further submits that pre-emptor-plaintiff having not been co-sharer, he has no locus standi to file the suit. Learned Advocate further submits that after purchase, khatian has been split up and jama has been separated, as such, suit for pre-emption ought not to be decreed.

12. Learned Advocate on determination of co-tenancy relied on the case of Fatema Bibi vs Sree Manik Lal Samaddar, 1996 BLD (AD) 129 = 50 DLR (AD) 97. Learned Advocate on separation of jama relied on the case of Male Mohammad vs Hafez Abul Kalam, 6 BLC (AD) 83 and the case of Abdul Momin alias Tara Mian vs Mahfizur Rahman, 1 ADC 515.

13. Let us proceed with our judgment.

14. On the question of defect of parties, Courts below concurrently found that plaintiff took all the step in getting the suit ready for hearing and defendant did not raise any objection specifically against defect of parties and did not supply any particulars of co-sharers, who are left out, found that the suit is not bad for defect of parties. On the question of limitation it appears that apparently the suit is barred by limitation as transfer was made on 28-1-1999 but the suit was filed on 9-6-2002. Section 245 of the Mohammadan Law prescribed period for filing suit is one year. It appears from the plaint that plaintiff went to village home, as for his profession he resides at Dhaka, on 15-3-2002. PWs. in chief as well as in their cross-examination stated that on 15-3-2002 there was admission of the plaintiff to pre-empt the case land. Courts below considered that it is on evidence that delivery of possession is made in 2002. As per section 245 of the Mohammadan Law the case is not barred by limitation as such it has been within the period of limitation i.e. within one year from the date of knowledge. On the vital question i.e. whether formalities of filing of the suit has been performed or not, Courts below found that plaintiff as per section 236 of Mullas Principles of Mohammadan Law per-formed both Talab-i-Mowasibat and Talab-i-Ishad. PWs. in their examination-in-chief and in their cross-examination fully corroborate that plaintiff performed all the formalities as per section 236 of the Mohammadan Law. The depositions of DWs. on this score are totally contradictory and not satisfactory On the question whether plaintiff is co-sharer or not, both the Courts below found from the history sheet and admitted by defendant that plaintiff is a co-sharer and entitled to pre-empt the case land. On the question of maintainability of the suit it appears that D.W.I in cross-examination admitted that plaintiff having performed all the formalities of Mohammadan Law, suit is maintainable.

15. On the question of which judgment will prevail., the Judgment under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or the instant judgment under the Mohammadan Law as pre-emption under section 96 State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is totally different for pre-emption under Mohammadan Law. This is the prime question to be answered.

16. On the question of which judgment got preference, Mr Ziaul Haque, learned Advocate relied on the case of Nuri Miah vs Ambica Singh, 34 Indian Cases 869, judgment was delivered by Mr Justice Ashutosh Mookerjee on 11 May, 1916. We tempted to reproduce certain portion of the judgment i.e. paragraph 11. "The true foundation of the right of pre-emption is explained in two passages in Book XXXVIII of the Hedaya. The first of these passages is in these terms: " 'Shaffa', in the language of the law, signifies the becoming proprietor of land sold for the price at which the purchaser has bought them, although he is not consenting thereunto. This is termed shaffa', because the root from which shaffa is derived signifies conjunction, and the land sold are here conjoined to the land of the shaft or person claiming the right of pre-emption." This indicates that the right of pre-emption is a right of substitution. The plaintiff complains that his co-sharer has transferred his share in the joint property to a stranger, and claims to be substituted in the place of the purchaser of the share of the joint property. If, before this can be affected, the property ceased to be joint property, it is obvious that the foundation of the right of pre-emption disappears. This view is, fortified by the second passage which is in these terms: "It is an express condition of shaffa that a man be firmly possessed of the property from which he derives his right of shaffa, all the time when the subject of it is sold, a condition which does not hold on the part of his heirs." (The author here deals with a case where the person claiming the right of pre-emption has died before a decree is made in his favour by the Qazi.) "It is moreover a condition that the property of the shafi remains firm until the decree of the Qazibe passed; and, as this does not hold on the part of the deceased shafi, the shaffa is, therefore, not established with respect to any one of his descendants, because of the failure of its conditions." It has not been seriously disputed by the plaintiff that the right of pre-emption, in order that it may be enforced by a Court, must not only arise on the sale, but be also existent at the date of the institution of the suit, for it is unquestionable upon the authorities that if a person who claims a right of pre-emption, ceases to interested in the joint property before the institution of the suit, he cannot obtain assistance from the Court. Consequently, the view cannot be maintained that the right of pre-emption which arises from the moment the sale is affected by the co-sharer is enforceable as it stands at the time of its origin; it is liable to be extinguished by events subsequent. The only point of difference between the plaintiff and the defendants is, whether the point of time with reference to which the existence of the right is to be determined is the date of the institution of the suit or the date of the decree by the Trial Court. In my opinion, for the reasons already assigned, it is plain that the right must exist and retain its enforceable character when the decree is made by the primary Court. This view was adopted in Ram Gopal vs PiariLal 21 A. 441: AWN (1899) 63 and Tafazul Hussain vs Than Singh 6 Indian Case426 : 32 A. 567: 7 ALI 715; these decisions are mentioned without dissent by well-known text writers such as Ameer Ali Tyabji and Wilson. It is also worthy of note that the Chief Court of the Punjab has accepted the same view in San-Wal Das vs Our Parshad 4 Indian Case 179: 147 PLR 1909 : 90 PR 1909: 159PWR 1909, though a contrary view had been adopted in an earlier case, Faiz Baksh vs Ramjidas 34 PR 1875. In the case just mentioned, which was decided by a Full Bench of eight judges, the nature of the right of pre-emption was fully analysed by Chief Justice Clark and Mr Justice Chatterjee. Mr Justice Chatterjee observes as follows: "A pre-emptor is bound to show that he was clothed with the right at the date of sale and also at the date of suit land up to the time of the final decree or should have this claim dismissed. If the pre-emptor loses his right within the period mentioned above, whether by his own act or from causes beyond his control his suit fails. The pre-emptor cannot get a decree unless he maintains the right on which he sues to the end." Chief Justice Clark added that conceding that the plaintiff pre-emptor must retain the prior right up to the time of institution of suit and even up to decree a plaintiff must have subsisting cause of action up to the time of decree. The possession of the property in which the right of pre-emption inheres is a part of his cause of action and if he loses that property either voluntarily or involuntarily before decree his suit must fail." This is obviously consistent with sound sense; for if the contrary opinion were accepted, the result would follow that relief by way of pre-emption May be awarded to a person who, according to the altered circumstances as they exist at the date of the decree, can show no reason whatever why he should be placed in that position of advantage."

17. We are of the view that this judgment is not exactly on the question which we proposed to settle.

18. Now let us proceed with our own decision.

19. Section 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure relates to definitions and sub-section 2 speaks 'decree' means the formal expression of an adjudication which, so far as regards the Court expressing it, conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and may be either preliminary or final. In AIR 1974 (SC) 1901, it is held that formal expression of an adjudication which the court conclusively and finally determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matter's in controversy in the suit. It shall be deemed to include the rejection of a plaint and the determination of any question within section 47 or section 144, but shall not include—

(a) any adjudication form which an appeal lies as an appeal from an order, or

(b) any order of dismissal for default.

20. Order has been defined in sub-section 14 of section 2 means the formal expression of any decision of a Civil Court which is not a decree.

(ii) Suit.—The expression 'suit' is not defined in the Code. "The word 'suit' ordinarily means and apart from some context must be taken to mean, a civil proceeding instituted by the presentation of a plaint.

21. Thus every suit is instituted by the presentation of a plaint. It means that when there is no civil suit, there is no decree. Thus, rejection of an application for leave to sue in forma paupeis is not a decree, as there is no plaint till the application is granted. It may, however, be noted that under certain enactment specific provisions have been made to treat the applications as suits; e.g. proceedings under the succession Act, the Arbitration Act, etc. They are statutory suits and the decisions given thereunder are, therefore, decrees. Therefore, a proceeding which does not commence with a plaint and which is not treated as a suit under any other Act, cannot be said to be a 'suit' under the Code and the decision given therein cannot be said to be a 'decree' under section 2(2) of the Code. A decision of a tribunal, even though described as 'decree' under the Act, it is adecree passed by a tribunal and not by a court covered by section 2(2) of the code.

22. A proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which though makes a formal expression of an adjudication conclusively determining the rights of the parties with regard to any matter in controversy, being not a suit as referred to in the definition of a decree in the Code of Civil Procedure, cannot be said to be a decree within the meaning of the definition of adecree given in the code as aforesaid.

23. From the settled decision essence of distinction between a decree and order seems to be in the nature of decision, rather than in the manner of expression. Thus the adjudication of a court which is not a decree is an order. Distinction between decree and order are as follows:

(i) similarities:

(a) both relate to matter's in controversy;

(b) both are decisions given by a Court;

(c) both are adjudications of a Court of law;

(d) both are formal expression of a decision given by a Court.

Dissimilarities:

In spite of above common elements, there is a fundamental distinction between the two expressions:

(a) A decree can only be passed in a suit, but an order could be given either in a suit presentation of a plaint or from by a petition or an application.

(b) A decree may be preliminary or final or partly both on the other hand there could be no preliminary order.

(c) In a suit there would be only one final decree, not more, but in a case of suit or proceeding, a number of orders may be passed.

(d) Every decree is appealable, unless otherwise expressly, provided, but every order is not appealable only those orders are appealable as specified in the Code.

(e) A decree is an adjudication conclusively determining the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy; an order on the other hand may or may not finally determine such rights.

Elements of decree:

In order that a decision of a court may be a decree the following elements must be present:

(i) There must be adjudication,

(ii) Such adjudication must have been given in a suit,

(iii) It must have determined the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit.

(iv) Such determination must be of a conclusive nature;

(v) There must be a formal expression of such adjudication.

24 It is further to be noted that decree of suit is on plaint but order can given either on petition, application, not on plaint.

25. As per decision of 28 DLR (SC) 91, order defined in section 2(14) of the Civil Procedure Code is analogous to a decree and generally has the essential attributes of a decree but as it arises out of a proceeding not being a suit, it does not amount to a decree. It is further held that an order allowing pre-emption under section 96(7) of East Bengal Act XXVIII of 1951 is an order within the meaning of section 2(14) Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, provision of section 36 of the Code will apply in the matter of execution of such an order "Proceeding" is a prescribed mode of action for carrying into effect a legal right. It means and includes all the steps and measures for prosecution and defence on an action.

26. Rule-14 of order 20 CPC relates to Decree in pre-emption suit i.e. Where the Court decrees a claim to pre-emption in respect of a particular sale of property and the purchase-money has not been paid into Court, the decree shall—

(a) specify a day on or before which the purchase-money shall be so paid, and

(b) direct that on payment into court of such purchase money together with the costs (if any) decreed against the plaintiff on or before the day referred to in clause (a), the defendant shall deliver possession of the property to the plaintiff whose title thereto shall be deemed to have accrued from the date of such payment, but that, if the purchase-money and the costs (if any) are not so paid, the suit shall be dismissed with costs.

(2) Where the Court has adjudicated upon rival claims to pre-emption, the decree shall direct.

(a) if and in so far as the claims decreed are equal in degree, that the claim of each pre-emptor complying with the provisions of sub-rule(1) shall take effect in respect of a proportionate share of the property including any proportionate share in respect of which the claim of any pre-emptor failing to comply with the said provisions would, but for such default, have taken effect; and

(b) if and in so far as the claims decreed are different in degree that the claim of the inferior pre-emptor shall not take effect unless and until the superior pre-emptor has failed to comply with the said provisions.

27. Theme of this rule is to provide the procedures of decree in pre-emption suits. Rights of pre-emption is the right to be substituted in place of original vendee. Right of pre-emption can be exercised only in respect of immovable property.

28. Law on the controversy mentioned herein above but it required to be applied. It is settled three classes of persons and no other entitled to claim pre-emption under Mohammadan Law, namely—

i) a co-sharer in the property i.e. shafi-i-sharik;

ii) a participation in immunities and appendages, such as right of or right to discharge water;

iii) Owner of adjoining immovable property i.e. shafi-i-jar but not their tenants in possession of such property without any lawful title.

29 Like section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, first class excludes second class and second excludes third class. In the case of two or more pre-emptors of the same class, they are entitled to equal shares of property in respect of pre-empted property.

30. As per section 24(10) of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and section 97(17) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, right of pre-emption under Mohammadan Law shall get preference as it lays down as 'Nothing in this section shall take away the right of pre-emption conferred on any person by the Mohammadan Law as such right is a personal right.

31. Mohammadan Law demand some formalities, which according to 19 DLR 759 (Mohammad Lokman Mondal vs Amir Ali Mondal and others). Same decision also reported in 21 DLR-211. are:-

"Requirement of making reference to talab-i-mowasibat, while making a talab-i-ishhad is set out in Mulla's principle of Mahomedan Law at page 22: in the following terms:

"Defendants for pre-emption-No person is entitled to the right of pre-emption unless.

(1) he has declared his intention to assert the right immediately on receiving information of the sale. This formality is called talab-i-mowsabit (literally, demand of jumping, that is, immediate demand): and unless

(2) he has with the least practicable delay affirmed the intention, referring expressly to the fact that that the talab-i-mowasibat had already been and has made a formal demand (a) either in the presence of the buyer, or the seller, or on the premises which are the subject of sale and.

(c) in the presence at least of two witnesses. This formality is called talab-i-ishhad (demand with invocation of witnesses).

32. It will, therefore, be seen that after having made talab-i-mowasibat, the pre-emptor has to affirm his intention with the least practicable delay referring expressly to the fact that talab-i-mowasibat had been made. It, therefore, requires the pre-emptor to make an express reference to talab-i-mowasibat. In this case there is no finding, nor has any evidence been pointed out to me that a reference was made to talab-i-mowasibat while making talab-i-ishhad. This omission at the time of making the talab-i-ish-had is indeed fatal to the claim of pre-emption.

33. In 16 DLR 45, (Monajal Huq vs Shafiullah and another) it is held as: "

7. A person entitled to pre-emption must make the immediate claim to the right of pre-emption called Talab-e-Mowasibat as soon as the fact of sale is known to him.

The right is lost if there be any delay in claiming it. This view is supported by authorities on Muhammadan Law.

34. In Hedaya, second edition page 550, it is observed:

"Claims to Shaffa are of three kinds, the first of these is termed Talb-Mawasibat, or immediate claim, where the shafee prefers his claim the moment he is apprised of the sale being concluded, and this it is necessary that he should do, in so much that he make any delay his right is thereby invalidated, for the right of Shaffa is but of a feeble nature, as has been already observed, and the Prophet, moreover has said the established in him who prefers his claim without delay."

35. If the Shafee receive a letter which, either in the beginning or the middle, apprises him of the circumstances of his Shaffa, and he read it on to the end, his right of Shaffa is there-by invalidated. Many of our modern doctors accord in this opinion, and it is in one place recorded as the doctrine of Muhammed"

8. In Baillie's Digest of Muhammadan Law Part I, second Edition, at page 487, there is the following observation in which the law on the point is stated :—

"The right of pre-emption is founded on contract and neighbourhood, is confirmed by tulab, or demand, and ish-had, or invocation, and is perfected by taking possession. The demand is of three kinds, tulab-i-moowathubut, or immediate demand, tulubtukreer, or confirmatory demand, also styled tulub-ishhad, or demand with invocation, and tulub tumleek, or demand of possession also styled tulub khusoomut, or demand by litigation.

36. By tulub-i-moowathubut is meant, that when a person who is entitled to pre-emption has heard of a sale, he ought to claim his right immediately on the instant (whether there is any one by him or not), and when he remains silent without claiming the right, it is lost."

37. 10. In the case of Jadu Lal Sahu and others vs Maharaji Jnki and others, the following observation was made by their Lordships of the Privy Council:

"The Mussalman Law insists that the first formality technically called the immediate demand should be observed by the pre-emptor or someone on his behalf immediately on receipt of the news of the sale otherwise the right of pre-emption falls to the ground."

38. Now to the point in our hand. In rare cases this type of conflict arises. After searching through different law digest of India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, I could find one such type of case reported in AIR 1936 Cal. 398 (Rai Nalinaksha Dutta Bahadur vs Kazi Abdul Pill), it is held as:

"On getting the notice the petitioner made an application for pre-emption under S. 26-F, Tenancy Act, in the Court of Second Munsif at Krishnagar on 6th June 1934. The transferees, namely opposite parties 1 to 3 were made parties defendants to that application.While this application was pending Muhamad Soleman instituted in the same Court a suit to enforce the right which he had to pre-empt under the Mohammedan law. The landlord was made defendant 10. This suit for pre-emption and the application under section 26-F were heard together and one judgment was pronounced. At the date of the order, in Misc. Case No.42 of 1935 the right, title and interest in the holding had already vested in Mohamed Soleman by reason of the pre-emption decree in the suit. There was no right, title and interest left to opposite par-ties 1 to 3 on which the pre-emption order, if made under S. 26-F, sub-section (5), can operate. That is to my mind a difficulty in the way of the landlord in the present case. The title in the holding which formerly belonged to the Kolas has now vested in Mohamed Soleman. There can be no order for pre-emption against Mohamed Soleman by reason of the provision of S.26-F, sub-section (1), Clause (a) ." Wherein it is held that competition between the right given under Mohammadan Law and right created under statutes, the right under the former will prevail. If plaintiff of suit under Mohammadan Law, whether heard analogously, simultaneously or separately, succeed on merits the application under the provision of statutes should be dismissed."

<u>39. As such we are of the view that the decision passed in the instant suit prevailed over the compromise order obtained in the miscellaneous case. In the present case, plaintiff did make the immediate demand, that is, he did perform the ceremony of talabe mowasibat immediately on coming to know of the sale and also talab-i-ishad in presence of witnesses, which the PWs univocally proved. Moreover, section 24(10) of Non Agricultural Tenancy Act and section 96(17) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act speak that right of pre-emption under Muhammadan Law shall prevail which cannot be defeated by these statutory laws. We find no substance in these rules.</u>

40. In the result, both the rules i.e. Civil Revision No.1769 of 2012 with Civil Revision No. 1772 of 2012 are discharged. No costs.

41. The order of stay granted earlier by this court is hereby vacated.

Before parting with the decision we appreciate both the parties particularly Mr Md Ziaul Haque, learned Advocate for enlighten us on this subject.

End.

parties:
Kumud Behari Sarkar
Vs.
Jogabandhu Sarkar
full_judgment:
Syed Md. Mohsen Ali, J;—This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 28-5-82 passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1566 of 1981.

2. The appellant, as plaintiff, instituted Title Suit No. 79 of 1978 in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Comilla for ejectment of the respondent from suit premises and for recovery of arrear rent. His case, inter alia, is that the respondent was a monthly tenant at a rental of Tk. 30/- per month, that he defaulted in payment of rent and he was as such an undesirable tenant.

<u>3. Prior to the institution of this suit one Shashi Kumar Sarker filed Partition Suit No. 163 of 1976 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Comilla against the appellant, the respondent and others for partition of properties including the suit premises. The respondent appeared in that suit, filed written statement and moved an application for stay of the further proceedings of the suit till disposal of the Partition Suit No. 163 of 1976 which was rejected by the learned Munsif by order dated 29-3-79. The respondent thereafter without moving against the aforesaid order dated 29-3-79 moved the learned District Judge, Comilla under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure in T.P. Case No. 306 of 1979 praying for transfer and analogous hearing of the aforesaid title suit with the partition suit. The learned District Judge, Comilla by his order dated 29-6-81 rejected the prayer. The respondent thereafter moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1566 of 1981 and the learned Single Judge, who heard the matter, by his judgment and order dated 28-5-81 stayed further proceedings of the ejectment suit till disposal of the partition suit. Against that judgment this appeal has been preferred.</u>

4. Mr. B.B. Roy Chowdhury, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant, has urged that having regard to the facts that the matter in issue in Title Suit No. 79 of 1978 for ejectment and the Title Suit. No. 163 of 1976 are not the same and the decision of the Title Suit is not dependent on the Partition Suit and the parties are not the same the learned Single Judge has committed an error of law in staying further proceedings of Title Suit No. 76 of 1978 for ejectment and the Title Suit No. 163 of 1976. He also submits that there was no prayer for stay of further proceedings of the title suit before the High Court Division.

5. It appears that a petition for stay filed by the defendant was refused by the trial court on 29.3.79 against which the defendant did not file any appeal. The present appeal arises out of an application under Section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure for the transfer of Title Suit No. 79 of 1978 pending in the 3rd Court of Munsif Comilla for trial with Partition Suit No. 163 of 1976 of the latter court as the suit properties of the Title Suit are also included in the hotch-pot of the partition suit and that the title suit is among the defendants of the partition suit which has been filed by Kumud Behari Sarker against the respondent as sole defendant for eviction from the suit property on the ground of bonafide requirement and default. In the Partition Suit No. 163 of 1976 filed by one Shashi Kumar Das he has impleaded as many as 74 persons as defendants wherein the plaintiff and the defendant of this ejectment suit are also defendants in that partition suit and the properties of the partition suit comprises 20 schedules of which schedule No. 13 embraces the suit property of the ejectment suit. The learned District Judge on consideration of the facts and circumstances was of the view that the partition suit will naturally drag on for years and as such, it is not desirable to tag on the ejectment suit to the partition suit.

6. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division concurred with the finding of the learned District Judge that the parties in partition suit and the title suit are not exactly the same nor the subject matter of two suits is exactly the same, nor the relief claimed in both the suits are similar nor they are pending before the same court and was of the view that both the Courts below rightly rejected the prayer for analogous hearing of two suits before the same court and there is no error of law on that count. In that view of the matter the learned Single Judge was not justified in staying the ejectment suit till disposal of the partition suit keeping it pending indefinitely till the decision of partition stilt No. 163 of 1976. The learned Single Judge having rejected the respondent's prayer for analogous trial of both the suits should not have stayed further proceedings of the Title Suit No. 79 of 1978 or ejectment till disposal of the partition Suit No. 163 of 1976.

7. In the result, the appeal is allowed Judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside. No order as to costs.

End.

parties:
Power Development board
Vs.
Sonali Bank.
full_judgment:
Anwarul Haque Choudhury, J.-This appeal at the instance of the Bangladesh-Power Development Board herein referred to BPDB is directed against the judgment and order dated 10.1.84 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Money Execution Case No. 4 of 1980. 

2. Facts leading to this in short is that Sonali Bank, the plaintiff-decree-holder respondent No. 1. as plaintiff instituted a Money Suit on 27.3.74 being Money Suit No. 26 of 1974 against M/S Conwell Ltd. and its Managing Director and one A.K.M. Moyeedul Islam as principal defendants, impleading BPDB and one of its Sub-Assistant Engineer as proforma defendant No. 4 and 5 respectively on the allegation inter-alia that the said M/s. Conwell Ltd. obtained an over draft facility to the amount of Tk. 2,25,000/- from the former Premier Bank on. hypothecating certain construction machineries belonging to the said company lying within the premises of Ghorasahal Power Station and though the said advance was payable with interest at 5% above the bank rate and the rate minimum 10% with quarterly rests and was payable and repayable by 31.12.71 but they did not pay. The further case of the plaintiff-decree holder was that the surety for the said over draft and revival letter and the letter of continuity was duly executed by the Defendant Nos 2 and 3 and also the demand promissory Note dated 21.10.71 in favour of the Premier Bank for Tk. 2,25,000/- It is in the further case of the plaintiff that the proforma-defendants No. 4 and 5 are denying and interested to deny the hypothecated took and machineries as mentioned in Schedule 'A' annexed to the plaint and it is asserted that if they continue to do so the plaintiff's claim a decree against them as well, having used or taken away the hypothecated tools and equipments duly certified by them to be in their possession which they cannot do "without repaying the amounts due to the plaintiff". 

3. In that suit the plaintiff's claimed a decree for Taka 3,50,000/- with interest at the rate of 10% from the time of filing of the suit till realisation and also prayed for such other further reliefs to which the plaintiff would be entitled under law and equity. 

4. The said suit, in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka was contested by the Proforma-defendant No. 4. namely, the BPDB by filing a lengthy written statement in which it was stated inter-alia that there is no outstanding bill of defendant No. 1 namely the Conwell Ltd. with the proforma-defendant and the hills were paid excluding the hire charges of the equipments of proforma defendant No. 4 which are to be realised from the security deposit of defendant No. 1 and from the tools and equipments lying with the proforma defendant. The value of the equipments and the amount of security deposit does not cover the total amount of liability of defendant No. 1 with defendant No. 4 and as a matter of fact defendant No. 1 have become liable to the proforma defendant No. 4 for an amount of Taka 14,00,000/- (Taka Fourteen lac) and the value of security deposit and equipment which are part of the contract do not cover the said total liability and the alleged hypothecation with the Bank of the tools and equipments being subsequent to the date of contract with proforma defendant No. 4 the said is illegal and inoperative in the eye of law and the plain-tiff, therefore, cannot get the relief prayed for rather the Proforma-defendant is entitled to appropriate relief towards realisation of his amount of Taka 14,00,000 (Tk. Fourteen lac) with cost. 

5. It appears from records that no other defendant appeared in the suit to contest but only proforma defendant No. 4, who for reasons knows to them all the time in the written statement described them as defendant No. 4 and not as proforma-defendant No. 4. It further seen from the record that on 17.12.75 the plaintiff filed a petition for passing an order of attachment before judgment of the proper-ties mentioned in schedule namely, the machineries and the equipments lying with the Bangladesh Power Development Board. The court thereon ordered to issue notices upon the defendants to show cause within 7(seven) days as to why they shall not furnish security to the extent of the claim and why the schedule property shall not be attached pending judgment and passed an adinterim order of attachment on that date. 

6. It further appears that the said adinterim order thereafter was made absolute. Further, it appears that during the proceeding on 29.12.76 the suit was taken up for ex-parte hearing when P.W. Abdul Quayum was examined and certain documents were exhibited in court and 27.1.77 was fixed for ex-parte hearing. On 27.1.77 none of the defendants appeared and the court after examining the deposition of the witness and the papers filed by the plain-tiff found that the case has been proved and ordered that the suit be decreed ex-parte with cost and interest and the plaintiffs do get Tk. 3,50,000/- from the defendants. The said decree was signed on 31.1.77. 

7. Against that judgment and decree which was ex-parte the proforma-defendant No. 4 preferred Miscellaneous Case No. 77 of 1977 under order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The said Misc. case was however dismissed and on appeal being F.M.A. No. 447 of 1979 before the High Court Division the Proforma defendant become unsuccessful. Thereafter, the plaintiff-decree-holder started the Money Execution Case No. 4 of 1980 for realisation of the decreetal amount with cost and interest upto 31.12.80 amounting to Tk. 6,08606/- and prayed for attachment of the main Development A/C No. SpI.36 of WAPDA-POWER DEVELOPMENT BOARD maintained in Sonali Bank, WAPDA Branch, Dhaka. 

8. In that money Execution case the Bangladesh Power Development Board namely, BPDB filed an objection on 31.7.82 contending inter-alia that the money execution case is not maintainable against the Power Development Board because no decree was passed against the Proforma-defendant No. 4 and that the assets and all properties of M/S. Conweil Ltd. was declaraed an abandoned Property vide notification dated 7.2.72 published in the Bangladesh Gazette, Extra-Ordinary dated 11. 2. 72 claiming that the alleged hypothecated tools and machineries of the said abandoned firm are not in the juridical possession of the Bangladesh Power Development Board and as the Government was not made a party in the said money suit and the Deputy Commissioner on 13.5.82 having taken over possession of the hypothecated goods, the decree cannot be executed against the Government also, they being not a party. That objection was heard on 10.1.84 and the Court rejected the objection petition filed by the Power Development Board holding inter-alia that the Sonali Bank instituted Money Suit No. 26 of 1974 against M/S. Conwell Ltd. and 4 others including the Power Development Board and got a decree in that suit against them and the court on examination of the papers and record found that the decree was passed against the Power Development Board also as they were in possession of the admitted hypothecated machineries and godown of the other judgment-debtors and as such they by agreement, are bound to pay the decreetal dues and the court found that the Execution case against the judgment debtors including the Power Development Board can proceed. Against that this appeal is preferred before this court which is heard and disposed of by this judgment. 

9. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant in the 
appeal having placed the relevant papers and the impugned order, had argued that in view of the fact that no decree was passed against the Proforma-defendant Nos. 4 and 5 by the order dated 27.1.77 of the trial court and no money decree having been drawn up against the proforma defendants, the executing court erred in law in rejecting the objection of the proforma defendants against the execution of the money decree against proforma defendants. He has further argued that the impugned order suffers from an inherent illegality because the executing court found that the decree was passed against the Power Development Board also as they are in possession of the hypothecated machineries when a reading of the decree itself would show that it was ordered that the plaintiffs are to get a specific amount from the defendants wherein the Power Development Board has been shown as a proforma defendant only and the expression defendants as used in the decree cannot be extended or made to include the proforma defendants because the executing court should take decree as it find it without any addition or alteration and cannot go behind the decree and write out a new order and decree in the name of interpretation which was in fact done in the instant case and therefore, the said order need be set aside being not warranted by law and according to the learned Counsel it ought to be held that the money decree is not executable against the proforma defendant No. 4. It has further been argued by the learned Counsel that there is nothing on record to show that any claim has been made against the proforma defendant No. 4 in the suit and that being so it cannot be said that the proforma defendant No. 4 would be bound by the judgment and decree arising out of a suit in which he has been added as a mere proforma without any claim against the said proforma by the plain-tiff and as a .matter of fact the said judgment and decree would not be a resjudicata between the plaintiff and the proforma-defendant in a subsequent suit, may be over the same matter and the proforma-defendant No. 4 being not bound, by the decree, which is a matter of fact had been admitted by the Power Development Board in their written statement, it cannot be executed against the Power Development Board. That being the legal position the impugned order has no basis in the eye of law and need be set aside by allowing this appeal. 

10. Mr. Ashrarul Hossain, the learned Counsel appearing for the Bank who is the Respondent No. 1 in the instant appeal and who is also the plaintiff-decree-holder had argued that there is no illegality and the impunned order suffers from no illegality which would need interference by this court for the simple reasons that in the money suit instituted by the plaintiff a clear claim was made against the power development Board and it was to the knowledge of the Power Development Board and the said was to the effect that the Power Development Board are denying and are interested to deny the hypothecated tools and machineries and if they continue to do so the plaintiff's claim a decree against them as well, having used or taken away the hypothecated tools and equipments duly certified by them to be in their possession which they cannot do without repaying the amount due to the plaintiff and therefore it cannot be said that no claim was made against the proforma defendant No. 4 in the suit. Further, the learned Counsel submitted that the proforma defendant contested the suit and made an adverse claim in the hypothecated tools- and machineries which were subsequently attached before judgment and the BPDB being a contested party in the suit would be bound by the decree and it will be executed against the said proforma defendant No. 4. In this regard the learned Counsel referred to a number of decision of the Indian Jurisdiction and particularly the one reported in A.I.R. 1947 (Bombay) page 217. In reply to that Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed the learned Counsel has referred to the decision reported in A.I.R. 1960(SC) page 388 to which we would advert at the relevant portion of the judgment. 

11. In the instant case the question to be decided is whether the decree that was passed in the money suit against the defendants would be binding upon the Power Development Board also who was described in the plaint as a proforma defendant and whether in the facts and circumstances of the case it would be executable against them also. 

12. The term 'proforma means for the sake of form only but we find that the said expression does not appear in any provision of the Code of Civil Procedure where the terms are only plaintiff and defendants and no proforma. A defendant might be a necessary party whose presence is a must or be a proper party who though not a necessary party but yet a party whose presence would be required before the court for the court to adjudicate all the points that are raised in a particular case before the court. in the instant case from a reading of the plaint it is seen that the plaintiff had made defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 as principal defendants. They are made so because defendant No. 1 M/S Con-well Ltd. is the firm which took the loan facility , from the Premier Bank initially by hypothecating the dispute tools and the machineries belonging to the said firm but lying in the premises of the Power Development Board at Ghorashal Power Station. The defendant Nos. 2 and 3 has been made a party because they were the guarantors. Defendant No. 4 was made a proforma because hypotheated machineries were in their custody and possession. But from a further reading of the plaint it is seen that the plaintiff claimed a degree against the defendant No. 4 as will as the plaintiff claimed that the proforma defendant No.4 cannot go on possessing and using the hypotheated tools and machinries without paying the amount claimed. This is a clear specific assertion in the plaint. This is a matter on record and there is no denial to this. Going back to the written statement as submitted by the Power Development Board it is seen that they clearly understood this claim made by the plaintiff in the plaint and they came out with a counter claim stating that the tools. and machineries are not with them for nothing but that the machineries and the tools which are hypothecated with the Bank and belonging to decedent No, 1, would not ever the amount due to be paid to them by defendant No. 1 and in the written statement the Power Development Board categoricall demanded Taka 14,00,000/- (Th. Fourteen lac) to be due from M/S Conwell Ltd. who are admittedly the owners of the tools and machineries hypothecated. They have not Only made a counter claim but also challeged the legality of the hypothecation itself stating that the hypothecation being subsequent to their charge the said hypothecation with the Bank Was invalid and had no basis in the eye of law. It thus, appears that the party namely, the plaintiff and the Power Development Board fought out the suit clearly undrstanding the issue and the claim they are making against each other as to the machineries and the godown belonging to the firm. If the proforma was for the ask of form only then they had nothing to decree Would not bind them. But in the instant 
case Power Development Board being the only defendant fought out the suit by filing a written statement and though the judgment and decree was passed in their absence it cannot be said that they being only proforma, the decree passed would not be binding upon them. 13. The executing court would not go behind the decree and write out a new decree in the name of interpretation. That is the law and there is no dispute as to that. The executing court, would however, in the facts and circumstances of each case be at liberty to interpret a decree and also the expression found in the decree, when there exists some ambiguity and uncertainty in the expression used, by taking into consideration to pleadings of the parties in the suit and the statement and averment made in the plaint itself. The court would do so to ascertain the precise meaning. In the instant case it appears that the executing court had gone behind only to ascertain the meaning and had to go to the pleadings of the parties and to the averment in the plaint made to the effect that the hypo-the cated goods and machineries are lying with the Power Development Board and if the claim of the plaintiff in those goods are denied they will be bound by the decree as well and a decree to the amount of the decreetal amount be passed against them also. We had occasion to refer to the provision of the Code of Civil Procedure and we found that the expression proforma does not exist in the Code but only plaintiff and the defendants who may either be a necessary party or a proper party and thus a proforma party but only because they were described as proforma they would not acquire any privileged position of any speciality if they choose to contest. 

14. in the case of Official Assignee Vs. Madholal Sindhu reported in A.I.R. 1947 Boni-bay at page 217, it was held that merely because parties were described as proforma defendant they would not occupy any peculiar or any privileged position deferent from that of an ordinary party. Their Lordships held in the relevant portion of the judgment, at last part of para 69 thus "The mere fact that no relief was claimed against him did not make him a proforma defendant. In any event once he had put in his written statement and joined in the litigation, he took the risk of any issue decided in that case becoming binding against him. At page 458 Edgley.1. observed as follows :—"We think that the law contemplates that even a proforma defendant should ordinarily be bound by a decree which has been obtained in his presence." With respect, I agree with this view if it means that a proforma defendant who takes part in the litigation would be bound by the decision." 15. We are in complete agreement with the observation made in the case under report which are in complete agreement with the view we have taken to the effect that a party though described as proforma in a suit would be bound by a decree passed in his presence after he has contested the suit by filing a written statement in which an adverse claim is made against the property in suit. He would be bound by the money decree in the instant case passed in his presence though he is described as a mere proper party namely, a proforma defendant. 16. We also hold that it has never been laid down, as argued, that when there is a defendant against whom no relief was sought and who is not a necessary party in the suit and who took no par. t in the litigation but claim to stand by and see others fighting the battle can still be bound by the judgment and the decree. If that being the position we would have allowed this appeal but we find that the position in the instant case is otherwise as in the instant suit a party was named a mere proper party and a proforma but against whom there is a claim made in the plaint categorically to the effect that the decree may be passed against them also and the proforma defendant having contested the suit by making an adverse claim and denying the claim of the plaintiff, the decree passed in the money suit in their presence would be binding upon them also, though they were mere proforma. 

17. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel has lastly submitted that the exparte order passed by the court below in the money suit had no basis because there is no evidence on record to come to a finding that the plaintiffs had prove his claim and further that the property being an abandoned property cannot be made subject to any attachment or sale in execution of a court's decree and more so when the concerned machineries arc in the custody of the Deputy Commissioner at the present moment. There is little substance in it because we are not hearing appeal against the decree itself and if the Government is in possession they are to agitate at the time of sale of the property if it is abandoned. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Counsel submits that this has also no basis in law because it has been decided in a number of cases by the Appellate Division of this court that if any claim exist prior to the coming into force of the abandoned property that claim cannot be denied only because the property became an abandoned property sub-sequently as the property cannot vest in the Government minus the liability incurred. 

18. We are not on this point in this appeal because it is not an appeal against the decree but here we are to examine the order of the executing  court and the mater for our decision in the instant appeal is whether the defendant also which we find in the affirmative in the facts and circumstances of the case.

19. That being the position we find no substance in this appeal which is therefore dismissed without any order as to cost.

The order staying all further proceedings of the Execution Case (being Civil Rule No. 439 (FM)/84) is hereby vacated the Rule is discharge without any order as to cost. The execution case is to proceed in accordance with law.

End.
